My main reason for purchasing this battery + charger was because the product page indicated that the car charger used a switching IC type circuit which apparently had all sorts of nifty protection circuitry built in. This is absolutely not the case, at least with the car charger I received.

Most frightening is that the battery works at 7.4 VDC, but because the car charger outputs the same voltage it receives (12-14 VDC), the battery is getting just shy of DOUBLE the voltage it should be normally operating at. Worse yet is that there is no actual charge circuitry - just a couple of resistors to limit the amount of current that can be pulled through the device. Go to Google and search for overcharged lipo batteries - they can be major fire hazards and have been directly responsible for burning down peoples houses and workshops. Finally, there is no diode present, so when the charger is plugged into the battery, the ends of the car charger have power on them. This could cause a short of the lipo battery, which is not safe. The only plus I can identify with this car
\\"charger\\" is that it has a fuse and ample room inside the case to modify it to have a proper charging circuit.

I'm reasonable confident that the battery doesn't have any kind of built in charge circuitry and will conclude that the car charger I received is very unsafe to use. The product page as it currently stands is misleading about the quality of the charger and I can confirm that NONE of the protection circuity is present inside the unit. Take a look at the pictures.

This mount is actually several pieces of different GPS/Device mounts from different brands that have been hastily modified to allow for iPad GPS mounting. The bag is actually a Bracketron Dash-Mat that weighs only 1.1 pounds compared to the iPad itself which weighs 1.7 pounds. As you might guess, this could cause some issues in terms of the bag holding the iPad still (since the dash-mat, according to the Bracketron website, is only meant to carry small mobile devices below 1 pound in weight). In addition to the lack of support caused by the inadequate weight (unless you contort the flexible goose-neck to a rather absurd angle, which doesn't help much either), there are several other issues. Primarily, the mount relies on a clip-on type backing that you attach to the iPad and then to the goose-neck mount. The problem with this backing is that it clips on far too securely and thus cannot be taken off for regular use of the iPad. During the time that I owned this product before returning it (which was scarcely a week, I might add), I was forced to leave the backing on the entire time, which made the iPad very unwieldy when not being used as a GPS. In the process of attempting to take off the backing the first time, I actually cracked the plastic of the backing, which can tell you alot about how cheap the plastics are in the product. Also, the adapter slot that is on the back of the iPad backing is NOT permanently attached or molded. You'll find that after enough force in attempting to remove the iPad from the goose-neck mount (which is even more ridiculously secure [in the bad sense] than the backing), it is easily possible for the adapter clip which had been hastily pressed on to the backing to completely come off. At this point, your mount could be rendered useless. Thus, in attempting to use it as a dash mount in my car, it was unable to support the weight. This could easily be an even greater issue for cars with smaller dashboards, where the iPad itself might hangover the end of the dash. I was forced to use the suction cup mount and attach it directly to the windshield. This held well enough, but it was not without problems. The pivot point on the neck, which allows you to \\"easily\\" reorient your iPad, relies on a giant plastic nut, which must be unscrewed and screwed every time the iPad is adjusted. EXTREMELY inconvenient. In addition, the neck's flexibility actually creates a ton of vibration, to the point where when I drove on mildly degraded roads, the bumps would cause my Navigon app to reorient into portrait mode for a split second, because the vibrations had caused the internal accelerometer of the iPad to jump. All in all, this product is absolutely terrible. Expensive, poorly conceived, and even more poorly made.     I would highly suggest instead the Bedox iPad beanbag mount, as it was custom designed for the iPad, weighs 2.5 pounds, has an adjustable ball bearing neck, and is also cheaper. I bought this mount as an alternative and am extremely pleased with how well it functions. Plus, since the Bedox mount doesn't rely on a backing to secure the iPad, I was able to instead choose my own case for the safety of my iPad.

The splash Raveskin is good looking (although the blue is not as bright as in the picture) and comes with a screen protector and a cleaning cloth. But it's a much thinner and looser rubber. It looks very nice on the iPod, actually nicer than the Pixelskin. But here's the problem. The rubber material is too loose on the sides and tops. The first time I put it in my pocket and then pulled it out, the top of the case had come off. I guess if you put it in bottom first instead of top first it might stay on.

Note: Both the Pixelskin and the Raveskin attract dust on the backside. The Raveskin also seems to attract more little crumbs of things normally found in the bottoms of pockets and purses and it's harder to wipe off because the grooves are narrower. Here's an interesting toy that fits the bill to be described as \\"it is what it is\\". It works for the most part as advertised, but probably isn't the ideal I thought it would be. I bought it because Hurricane Sandy had me thinking about how I'd entertain myself should the grid go down. I probably should have saved my money and bought one a little more high-end.

When you get it, it's put in a green-friendly box. The one-sheet manual tells you to keep the packaging - the inside of the box has a silvered piece of paper that some videos I've seen on YouTube were using as a screen, and another piece of cardboard that is meant to be used as a stand for the projector. Not the most ideal situation there - I'm expected to carry around cardboard in order to use this effectively? I'd rather just project the image on a light-colored wall.

I suppose it's well-built for its size - it's got a aluminum casing protecting the LED and lens. Lens is focused with a small dial on the top of the unit. Its dimensions are 3\\"x1 1/2\\"x7/8\\".

There is no internal speaker - it uses earbuds for audio, which are included. There are some minimal audio controls inside a menu, which, when I played with them, didn't appreciably change the audio coming through the earbuds. Maybe one of those little powered MP3 speakers would work better? Well, you could hear the audio from MP4 videos played through it anyway.

It's powered by a sealed-up rechargeable battery. No provision for external power at all. The picture projected is typical of a tiny projector - brighter the closer you get to the wall (Pretec recommends 9 inches, but in a completely dark room it could probably go a lot bigger. In a not-so-dark room, I could get a decent picture about twice that size.). Also, the MicroSD card that was supposed to be included - wasn't.

Testing it with a couple of MP4 videos was a mixed bag. My job is editing video, so I know a little something about making MP4s. I tried a downloaded video from YouTube, an MP4 of a Hollywood movie I had lying around, and an MP4 I made for a client. Both the YouTube and Hollywood MP4s played, but with monster digital artifacts. My best guess of why that is is that the MP120 has a 320x240 maximum resolution, and the thing is resizing the videos on the fly.That happened on both the 320x240 YouTube and the 720x480 Hollywood vid. Pretec does have a downloadable piece of software that's supposed to convert vids to MP4 that I haven't used yet. Maybe that will improve the video (though typically you don't want to recompress an already compressed video)? The MP4 I made from the client's file one way didn't play at all: make an MP4 from the same file with a different MP4 maker and it played fine. What does that mean? You have to decide.

- Nook(N) by barnes & noble
- Kindle 3(K) by amazon.com
- Sony Reader Touch(ST)

N: The Nook is epub friendly. As well as PDF, and many other formats.

ST: Sony reader is Epub friendly. pretty much the same as the nook.

N: $149 with wifi
ST: 169 NO WIFI
K: $139 with wifi(or $189 with wifi and free 3G)

*The Nook has a replaceable, rechargable battery. So it'll last awhile, but when its dwindling, you can spend 30 bucks and put a new one in yourself. For the Kindles, they are sealed inside. People have said you can do it yourself, but you must be tech savvy. Or you can send it away to Amazon for about the cost of $50+shipping charges and they'll replace it for you.

*You can expand your memory on the Nook and on the Sony touch. The Kindle you cannot, though the Kindle will hold 3,500 books, don't know if you need more space then that?!

*The new kindle now meets with the nook on their slim width. People used to say the nook was more comfortable to hold because of the width, now the kindle will be as well.

*Yet, the Nook is heavier by 3oz then the Kindle or Sony.

*The Nook battery life lasts about 10 days with wifi off, the Sony has 14 days, and the new kindle is up to a month with wifi off(3 weeks with it on)This wasn't a big deal to me, and I was more interested in the other features the Nook DID have, like replaceable battery and expandable memory.

All the money I spent sending those stupid lemons back could have bought us another Nook or Kindle AND it would still be working! (Our family's other e-readers are doing fine.) All this hassle doesn't make me want to buy another Kobo, that's for sure.

I've had my PRS-T1 for just under 6 months. The Wi-Fi has stopped functioning and won't detect any networks. When I undertook to have it repaired or replaced under warranty, I discovered that the warranty was barely there. If I was willing to settle for trading for a refurbished model, it would cost me $30. If I wanted to have mine repaired, it would cost me a minimum of $25 plus shipping, and I wouldn't have it for however many weeks it took. If the problem required replacing the screen, that was not covered and would be extra.

Either way, the rest of the warranty vanishes, to be replaced by 90-day P&L coverage. Sony should be utterly ashamed of themselves for this alleged warranty. Since this device costs about $40 more than most of its competition, that is inexcusable.

The display is more grey than white, but you do get used to this. The touch-screen is iffy, sometimes recognizing a swipe, sometimes not. I've learned to just use the \\"next page\\" button.

Forget the software that comes with it. The Sony software just blows. Hard to think how it could be worse. Fortunately, there's a freeware program out there, Calibre, that is better by leaps and bounds, and is also superb at doing conversions from Mobi (Kindle) format and others.

PDF is another popular format, but it's pretty bad on every reader I've seen -- most computer screens, too. There are very few books I'd suffer through PDF to read, most of them I'd rather do without than put up with it. Professional ebook publishers don't use it. PDF conversion is extremely difficult for anybody, and extremely problematic -- you've got to babysit the conversion and clean up all the dumb mistakes.

The Sony doesn't require you to divulge all sorts of personal information to sign up for a required account whether you want one or not, doesn't require you to agree to 160+ pages of legalese (B&N Nook), and doesn't contain software to \\"unsell\\" something you thought you had purchased (Kindle). This puts it ahead of either competitor.

Battery life is to die for. Plugging it in to my computer's USB port to load a book also recharges it, so in those 6 months it has only complained about needing a recharge twice.

Once you get accustomed to the way Calibre does things, it does them with the Sony better than it does them with any other reader. This will really organize your library conveniently. It uses \\"tags\\" or \\"collections\\", so you can tag a book in multiple genres, multiple subjects, etc., in Calibre and then find them that way on the Sony.

I should mention that the Sony \\"keyword\\" system does not work at all, is not described in the user manual and doesn't work. Apparently Sony never actually implemented it and just left the remnants behind.

The device runs Android, so it can be rooted and modified. One of the most useful mods (doesn't require rooting) is to change the list of \\"recently added\\" books, to \\"recently read\\". (Changing what they are, not what the screen label says.)

If you read multiple books at once, or need a reference handy all the time, or share the device with a spouse, this is invaluable. You have four books available at a touch, from the home page.

You can also root it completely, which makes the library of Android applications available.

The device runs into difficulties if the SD card gets up above 32 GB in actual content, slowing down a bit, so that should be the upper limit. The case for the reader needs pockets for SD cards, a significant lack.

The case's light has glare issues, requiring that the light be moved here for the top half, there for the bottom half of the page. Because of those two things I discommend the case and suggest you look at third-party products instead.

If you're going to get one of these things, get a Square Trade warranty to go with it as soon as you purchase it. If you have any problems that should be far better than Sony's vanishing so-called warranty.

There are a number of good design characteristics about this clock -- it's built into an aesthetically pleasing case, and the display, although somewhat small, is bright and clear. Furthermore, it's not a problem that the included mains adapter only fits European outlets, as the unit itself is powered by 5VDC. Included in the box is a cable that will get power from a USB jack.

Unfortunately, the user interface is pretty awful. The buttons are not especially well labelled, and they're not easily visible from the same angle as the display, meaning that you will constantly be manipulating the unit to see one or the other when programming it for the first time. This is made worse by the fact that the clock/calendar and alarm settings modes quickly time-out and return to the default mode. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, there seems to be no way to set an alarm to play MP3s. Yes, this clock does have wake alarms, and it can play MP3s... but only as separate functions. I blame this confusion on the clarity lost during translation of the feature list.

Amazon's site doesn't have a link for buyers to report this type of deceptive/incorrect advertising problem.  Amazon just accepts whatever description these independent 3-party sellers write.

Because of the low price on two different types of lightning adapters, I bought both types to see which one might work best. This particular adapter initially did NOT work at all. As soon as I plugged it in, my iPhone gave me an error message, told me it wouldn't work, and true to its word...it did not work at all. I could not charge nor pass any data to either my iPhone 5s or my wife's 5c. Luckily the price is relatively inexpensive, so these could be thrown away without too much regret. Alas, I didn't...and somehow, they began to work after a recent iphone software update. Not sure if it will work for you--but glad I didn't throw them away.

Of note, the other lightning adapters I purchased from Amazon worked like a champ. Those are sold by Cable N Wireless and you can see my review of those here on Amazon.

I suspect that diversity of reviews for both adapters is because of something in the Apple software plus a lack of manufacturing controls on these very cheap adapters. Remember that Apple is charging $39 for their equivalent--I purchased several of these cheap knock offs for about 25% of that price and ended up with two or three that worked and two or three that didn't. So, for about 10% of Apple's MSRP, you can find an alternative. I suspect that is why the Apple interface is so picky--if all of these worked Apple couldn't sell any of their own.

Bottom line: you get what you pay for--some of these cheap knock-offs might work with your iPhone, some won't. But in my opinion, this low price is worth giving some of these adapters a shot. In my case, this one didn't work, but another did.

Update: interestingly, after a recent iphone software update, this adapter worked fine on my iphone 5s. I am tentatively upgrading it to two stars and will further upgrade my rating if this adapter continues to work.

Pros:
I am able to turn up the volume louder on these than the 3M headphones. A plus if you're mowing.

I'm going to send these back and order another set of the 3M. Hopefully the new style is as good or better than what I have already.

The manual is written in chinese on one side of the sheet and on the other side in a very poor english, so I hope these paragraphs will help you get started with the CC-308:

Nice packaging, satin finish with magnetic closure on the front. The device is a lot nicer than others in its price range and functionality is good after you get the battery charged.

The battery charger has a mini USB connector instead of the normal negative cylindric with a positive pin connector which the CC-308 RF Detector requires. Fortunately I had bought another detector last year (model LD-RF1, which, by the way, wouldn't stop the charge on a full battery to prevent it from getting damaged; that's why I had to buy this device) and still had the charger with the cylindric connector and the correct power rating 5V @ 1000 mA, so I could proceed testing the device.

In order to charge the battery, you MUST turn off the device with the switch on its right side and connect the charger to the wall outlet and plug the charger lead into the CC308, the red light on the charger and the blue charging light on the CC308 will turn on for about 35 minutes until the blue light on the CC308 automatically goes off to let you know when the battery is fully charged. At this point disconnect the lead from the charger to the CC308 and unplug the charger from the wall.

The switch on the right side will toggle from off, to beep, to vibrator mode, there's a little knob for the sensitivity to radiofrequency (it is well marked from little sensitive to very sensitive), it is recommended that on an area that you know with no RF emissions you set it on the most sensitive and then lower it down to a point where no sound and maybe only one light is lit on the front. Then turn it off and take the CC308 to the area you want to check for radiofrequency sources.

The button on the front will cycle the lasers for the camera detector from off to slow blinking to off to fast blinking and so on. You illuminate slowly the area where cameras may be hidden and look through the round window with the red filter, then you will be able to see a bright point lit or blinking, depending on the state of the lasers, reflecting at you from the point where a hidden camera lens is located.fast blinking and so on. I've had the Clarion 675 for a couple of years now. It appeared to be exactly what I was looking for when I was researching it, integrated blue tooth, iPod control with video, navigation, etc. The system was expensive but looked like a long term solution so I had one put in my truck and one in my car so I'd have matching units in each. I had the navigation system, bluetooth, iPod, etc. all installed at once by a professional shop.

The good.

First, let me say that everything on the unit works by itself quite well. The navigation system is extremely nice and is more accurate than any system I've seen outside of aviation. The screen looks really good and video looks great on it. The bluetooth doesn't work as I'd like but is mostly functional. The unit looks impressive as a double din screen. The dedicated buttons mostly make sense except ISR (instant station recall). Who needs a dedicated radio function button anymore when you only have a handful of dedicated buttons anyway? Does anyone still listen to radio who owns a head unit of this type?

Now for the bad. I've just had one of my units pulled out to be replaced by a Pioneer avic-z110bt. All of what I expected the Clarion to be, the Pioneer is. I just couldn't stand the stupidity of the functionality of the Clarion any longer and despite repeated visits to my local audio shop, Clarions website, and internet, I saw no indication that any of the below would ever be addressed with a software upgrade, which is all that it would take to make the Clarion a great unit.

First, the bluetooth functionality of the Clarion is truly awful. I had a Parrott bluetooth hands free device in my truck that the Clarion replaced. I used it daily and absolutely loved it. It was so simple, and worked so well that I frankly didn't check the Clarion. I just assumed that surely the multi-thousand dollar (then) unit must at least work as well, if not better. The sound quality (of my voice, I could hear the caller) made the unit nearly unusable, which my local shop was kind enough to blame on my phone, not the Clarion. I had them install the Clarion bluetooth remote module (another add on and expense) to help with the sound, then to install a remote mic that I had to see if that would improve the sound. Nothing, 80% of the time I'd have to switch to handset in order to be heard. Despite the shops assertions that the issue was my phone, I had perfect hands free before installing the Clarion with the same phone so I'm confident this was a Clarion issue.

Compared to the Parrott, the Clarion supports voice only with bluetooth. No voice dialing, no contact synching, anything. So yes you have hands free, of sorts, but you have to dial with your telephone. No on screen keypad, no contact list, etc. Then, at least with blackberries, you cannot put your phone away, because it senses its going into the holster and hangs up. Yes, you can turn off that option but then you're butt dialing.

Another issue is the answer and hang up buttons take several seconds to work, unlike the instant answer and hangup I had on the Parrott and now on my Pioneer. You don't know for 5 seconds or so if you actually hung up or answered which leads to missed calls.

Lastly, and this is the most frustrating part, if you have a route selected and you are navigating by voice prompts, and then someone calls you on the telephone (a most likely scenario), the turn by turn instructions take priority over the telephone conversation, not just in overriding it, but it actually mutes the telephone so you can be reminded to turn left, again. I can see the turn coming up on the map, but I can't see what the person is trying to say on the phone. If you are downtown with turns every half mile, the voice prompt rarely shuts up. If you are on the phone in this situation, you may as well call them back later, you can't complete a sentence. To mute the voice prompts is several menusdeep, just what you need to be doing when you are going somewhere new, on the phone, and in traffic down town.

Another annoyance of the Clarion is the legal screen at startup. I know, they all have that, but the Clarion locks down all the buttons except the volume button. If you are going to work, jamming to some music and leave the volume up, when you get back in at lunch, probably with a guest in tow, the sound comes back to full volume. The mute button, the quickest fix to this, doesn't work till the legal screen is cleared. The volume button is an up/down button (as opposed to a dial you can quickly crank down) so it's several seconds till the volume comes back down to an acceptable level. Why block the mute button till legal is satisfied?

You have the option to have the clock set by GPS satellites or via the internal clock. My truck, like many vehicles, has the only clock in the radio. I do like having a satellite set clock that is always right. However, on the Clarion if you select set by GPS then until the GPS gets a fix, there is no time. This can be from 30 seconds to several minutes. I often get in the truck and say, ok, do I have time to get to A before I have to be back at B? Since which direction I turn depends on that answer, I can either haul out my cell for the correct time, or wait till the GPS synchs up. There is an internal clock in the Clarion, why don't we use it always, and have GPS correct it when it is synched so the time is always displayed.

Some others have mentioned the issues with playing video on the iPod. I know there are legal issues here, but the generational issue with different iPods, the lack of support from Clarion, and the BS of having to control video playback from the iPod are frustrating. It all was supposed to be from the Clarion screen when I bought the units, now there are half baked work arounds and still no clear solution that I am aware of. The Pioneer plays video just fine.

While the Clarion's navigation is quite good, the Pioneer has a function that I like very much that appears to be unique. If you are going on a route that you usually use, and the GPS for some reason likes another route better, you can tell the Pioneer to learn your route so it sees that you like this route as a priority. The road by my work for some reason is hated by GPS systems and they all try to route me down a parallel road. Unfortunately the road I like is much better than the GPS preferred road. I can teach my Pioneer to take me the better way, not the Clarion.

95% of the problems with the Clarion could be fixed with a software upgrade and I think that is the most frustrating part of Clarion ownership. It seems their answer is to just move onto another model and leave the existing units as is with no backward support. That's not the kind of company I like to do business with. When I quit smoking, I bought everything. An all out assault: The gum. The patch. Meds. And this Smoking Everywhere product. Being an avid product junkie, I read up on it and discovered competing products - that were touted as better/ cheaper/ etc. Here's what I found:

1) Although other e-cigarettes will claim they are different, they are all the SAME. Absolutely identical. The atomizer, the battery and the filter are exactly the SAME. In fact, the packaging on this Smoking Everywhere product is all that distinguishes it from competing e-cigs that are half the price. Trust me, I've ordered thrr different kinds. The HARDWARE is the same across the board.

2) buying the cartridges is a sham. They come pre-treated in packs of 5 that will last a typical smoker about 4 days. There are other companies (NOT Smoking Everywhere) who sell what they call \\"smoke liquid\\" or \\"smoke juice\\" which sounds kind of gross, but DEFINITELY the way to go. Companies like Smoking Everywhere do not want you to buy or have access to this liquid - as it undercuts their main profit, which is selling these cartridges. It's like buying a printer cartridge that lasts 10x a normal one, or a men's replacement razor that is 10x as sharp. Smoking Everywhere makes its profit from the carts. Dont fall into that trap.

3) do your own homework. I would have saved 100s of dollars had I done a quick internet search and read forums on the topic. There is info avail. There are also reputable companies that sell all items at a lower price point.

I hate the fact that most time clocks look so corporate and draconian.  It's like the manufacturers can't let go of the 1950's factory floor time clock design concept.    Now for the Cons:  First of all, it runs on USB - which sucks.  USB is designed to connect a personal printer, or a coffee warmer, or a flash drive shaped like a humping dog.  It is not, however, designed to connect key, centralized, always-on devices which should connect back to a server in a different location.  I mean, think about it, how secure is it to have a computer which has everyone's time data sitting next to the time clock.      Now, Lathem will sell you the fact that there is a way to connect RJ-45 (network) cables.  However, you have to buy additional converters (not too expensive), and do a little dance around a fire with a chicken to get the drivers to work correctly.  In addition, it's completely unreliable.  For the two+ years that we've had it, about twice a week every week, the terminals lose connection to the server, and the way this system is designed, once they lose connection, they're useless.  And, in the two+ years, Lathem has barely done any software updates.  Nothing.  Forget 64 bit support.  Forget Windows 7.  You're stuck with XP SP3.  It feels like Lathem puts a product out, and then completely divorces itself from it.      Lastly, as mentioned in reviews for other products, their tech support is a joke.  They keep banker hours, and when you do reach them, they don't know anything.  Their answer to any question is reboot or reinstall the software. It's a shame that a product that looks so good can't work well either, but I think I'm done with Lathem products.

I like Griffin, and they make one of the very few Apple-approved car mounts. This is why this latest version of the RoadTrip makes me sad. I thought the radio transmission on previous models was weak, but this one is weakest of all. If any car around you has their transmitter tuned to the same frequency, better stay 20 yards or more away, because otherwise you'll be listening to their music, not yours. Even the physical design of the unit has gotten worse. Granted, Griffin has *had* to make hard design choices to deal with the many different cases available for iPhone 4, but the new RoadTrip is simply not as good as its predecessors. The \\"neck\\", while solid, seems to move around more than in older units, so while I've only had to reposition my old RoadTrip once or twice in two or more years, I'm having to do it with this one at least once a month. The swivel top is not doing the unit any favors either.  This model does have some improvements over older ones -- there's now an LCD screen that shows you what's playing, and even sends it to your radio (for those who have a \\"Text\\" button). But, no Unicode support. I listen to a lot of international music, and the LCD is simply blank. Also, the new model turns off the hardware buttons 30 seconds into every song, track, or podcast, so if you want to use a hardware button on the Griffin  RoadTrip 31 seconds into the song, you have to press the button twice -- once to activate, and once again to actually perform the desired function. Why Griffin, why? Why make such a common task more difficult to perform than before? I hear you asking: \\"Is it really that hard to press the button twice?\\" Well, it isn't, but I don't count the seconds my song has been playing, so if I press it twice 31 seconds into the song it goes on to the next, but if I press it 29 seconds into the song I skip one song. It's sad to see such a once-great product become so much worse even as technology advances and more features are added. Forget features; getthe core functionality right first! You've done it before, Griffin, just not this time.

This radio has some good potential, but under the current firmware level it is barely usable.
Manual programming is similar to the Baofengs where the offset is ignored and one has to store the TX and the RX frequencies on the same channel. In the end, it can be done, even assigning channel names manually, but it is cumbersome.
Computer programming can be done using ANY Serial (or USB serial emulation) to 3.5mm stereo pin cable. The programming SW does not accept copy and paste, and the radio is not CHIRP compatible, as of the date of my review. If you run Windows XP, you need to worry only with the normal Prolific driver limitations. If you run WIN 7, you will need to fix the MSCOMCTL.OCX driver. After that, the SW will work on Windows 7.
The main issues I have with the radio are listed below:

1) Humming noise when volume is all the way down, even when using a signal clean battery as power source,
2) Loss of audio when the encoder is used to switch from/to an active channel
3) The loud beep sounds when the scan function finds an active channel (instead of playing the audio),
4) The RX interference it suffers when the vehicle is in motion and the radio is fed from the cigarette lighter cord that came with it.
5) The high cost to return it to China (around US$50), even if the unit is defective. Not Amazon nor the dealer seem to be willing to pick up the tab.

Therefore, in a $99 radio I would need to spend about 50% of its value to return it. This situation basically forces me to keep the radio and use it with all limitations described, or as paper weight.

I have seem other owners stating they do not hear the humming noise I described, and that is part of the "hit or miss" quality of my unit, but the main issues are firmware dependent. In a radio that has no capability to have its firmware upgraded, the only way to see a fix is to wait for 2 or 3 new firmware cycles and then purchase it at thattime. Your mileage may vary, but I am disappointed.

There are, admittedly, some good qualities to the Lonve. To wit:
* Color. Tinky-Winky purple! Need I say more?
* At 16 gigs, it holds a crap-ton of music. It took me more than a week to load my player with close to two-thirds of my music collection. Unlike my Coby, it did not reject my Hungarian and Turkish music, which features pesky umlauts in the titles. The Coby, perhaps being a tad culturally insensitive, prefers songs with comprehensible American titles.
* The metal case makes it a bit more sturdy than my Coby, which cracked after I dropped it on the pavement. On the other hand, I was sad when I dropped the Coby. I do not think I would regard a crack in the Lonve with as much regret.

Now, the bad:
* There is no randomizer function, so you can't listed to a Hungarian song, then a Tuvan song and then some kirtan music without manually flipping through the files yourself. Maybe this is a good thing, as artists often intend their album to be a complete opus, meant to be listened to from beginning to end. But for those of you who prefer a bit of chaos with your musical selections, not a plus.
* A small percentage of the massive amount of music I transferred to the device wouldn't play and I had to run a disk cleanup on the Lonve to address this issue, and then transfer a couple of those albums back.
* Most importantly: the thing randomly turns off when it's unhappy (insert bad dating reference here), which is a problem if you bought it to listen to music on your runs, like I did. When you're pounding out the miles on the pavement, you don't want to fiddle with the purple box. You just want it to play.
* Best I can figure with the stoppage issue: The Lonve doesn't like cold, probably owing to that metal case. And frankly, it wasn't that cold out: mid-20s F, which is shorts weather in upstate New York. I stuck the unit it my disgustingly sweaty running glove for a mile and it began working again without a problem. This isnot the unit you take when you want to reenact Roald Amundsen's discovery of the South Pole. This is probably not the unit to take when you visit the freezer aisle of your local grocery. While the Coby doesn't like being left outside by itself all night in the cold (who does?), I've never had a problem using it on winter runs.

The Lonve is a good purchase if you like to listen to a crap-ton of music in your car, slowly amble in the park to Beethoven, fiddle around with a piece of equipment so you don't have to pay attention to your relatives, or exercise in a temperature-controlled environment such as a gym, where you enjoy a periodic excuse to stop what you're doing and figure out what's wrong. It is also a good choice when you listen to a lot of music with umlauts and other diacritical marks in the title. But if you're a runner, stick with the Coby.

I've been in the market for an e-book reader for a long time now. I didn't want to get just anything and have been researching the iPad, the Kindle, Nook, and the Sony Reader. I chose the Reader because I liked the exclusive with Google Books, and it appeared to be the least-tethered and most-open of all the e-book readers. A week into it, I've had a complete change of heart, and am now contemplating the Apple iPad as its successor.

I've spent the last 4+ weeks looking at every single e-reader on the market. My wife and I love to read and when Apple came out with the iPad, she had to have it, and that pretty much ended the debate right there as far as her choice. I was a little more scrutinizing as far as what I was willing to spend, and what I wanted. I know that sounds like the typical male-versus-female shopping taste but I didn't want a $500 ebook reader, and didn't need a tablet computer--just something I could read books on, reliably, and was easy to use.

After having a few weeks playing with my wife's iPad, I had a good idea of what I wanted by this point. So following the recent price drop by Sony, I bought the PRS-600BC from my local discount warehouse store (not Costco, but close) and took it home to try it.

What I liked...
The size of the the Touch Reader is absolutely ideal and fits in my coat pocket. It's excellent as far as size and battery, can't say that enough. The included stylus that slides into the side of the screen is nifty, and I liked that the buttons were NOT ON THE SIDES of the reader (ala Kindle) so I don't accidentally hit them and turn the page.

What could be better...
As much as I thought I'd love the e-ink screen, I was slowly starting to dislike it in low light. I normally read in bed, or on the couch by a 60W lamp. I don't read in super-low light or anything but this book should at least be as easy to read as a paperback in bed. It isn't. I was finding myself straining to read The Apology (by Socrates, thanks to Google Books) in bed. In direct bright light, it's very easy to read but useless if you're used to reading paperbacks. Sony should have done their homework on this. The touch screen was descent but could be improved... it was sluggish to respond and options were not (at least for me) well laid out. While I liked that you could change the page orientation from Portrait to Landscape, it was only counter-clockwise (with the bottom 4 buttons on the left).

What I hated...

The first thing I noticed is that when I clicked \\"Help\\" in the Reader store (which looked reminiscent of the iTunes store) is it said, \\"Page not found.\\" I figured it was just down for the moment...but it wasn't. A week later, it still says \\"Page not found.\\" Strike one.

The first direct object of my fury of my scorn has to be the stupid Reader software that comes with it this device. I installed it on our home iMac and it was (to my surprise) part of a flash drive-like partition of the reader that downloads from the internet (rather than the reader). Ok, that's fine. However, after I had the reader software installed, it asks you to set up an account....two accounts....that must match...otherwise...your Adobe DRM will not match the Sony Reader site....and you will....have a problem. Why am I speaking with the ellipses? Well, it turns out that you must \\"authorize\\" each and every single device you wish to set up with the Reader store (like iTunes). That's fine, however, if you want to remove a device, you will need to e-mail, call, or chat with Sony each-and-every time. I found this out the hard way because I set up the Reader software on my laptop and decided to take it off....which lead me to the grand finale of hate against the person responsible for this abomination of software. Strike two.

If you are a Mac owner, you know how easy it is to remove software from your computer--you simply put it in the Trash, right? Ok, you would think it would be that easy on this, but it isn't. Sony expects you to know Terminal command lines to uninstall this lovely piece of software. I will spare you the details but here is a link to the Sony e-support site that contains the terminal command, albeit with the wrong path.

This is taken directly from Sony's website...

How to uninstall the Reader(tm) Library in the Apple® Mac OS® X operating system.
Solution

On the main menu, click Go and then click Applications .
In the Applications folder, in the right pane, double-click the Utilities folder.
In the Utilities folder, double-click Terminal .
In the Terminal text window, type the following: sudo /Library/ebookLibrary/uninstall-ReaderLibrary.sh ***
NOTE: There is a required space between sudo and /

Press ENTER on the keyboard.
A confirmation message will appear. Enter your password or leave blank if you do not have a user account password.
After a password has been entered or left blank for no password, press ENTER .
NOTE: You will receive the message that the Reader Library Uninstall is finished.

On the menu, click Terminal and then Quit Terminal to exit the Terminal application.
Close all other open windows.
NOTE: If the uninstall was done for troubleshooting reasons, you can now reinstall the software.

*** - This is the wrong path, Sony has yet to correct it on their website. The correct path is /Library/Reader \Library/uninstall-ReaderLibrary.sh

Sony 600 E-reader:    Bad Points:  -- Too much glare from screen.  Hard to read unless you angle it just      right.  Slightly less contrast compared to KOBO also.      (Apparently the glare comes from the touch sensitive layer that      Sony put over top of the screen.  The KOBO ZeroForce touch screen      doesn't have this problem, because it uses infrared beams from the      side of the screen to detect shadows created by finger tips.)  -- When USB cable is connected, you cannot read a book.  You either     charge or read, but not both.  (Unclear if you can read while      charging from the 5.2 volt adapter).  -- It does not accept MOBI format, however external Calibre      software can convert MOBI to EPUB which it does read.   -- No easy way to keep track of how far you got in more than one      book you are reading.   It seems to think you only read one book,      all the way to the end, before starting another, LOL.   -- A bit heavy (but I admit it did seem sturdy).      Good Points:  -- Touch screen is more responsive than Kobo E-pearl ZeroTouch screen.     (For example, note taking with stylus is possible.  On Kobo, precision     is limited to width of fingertip or thumb.)  -- It accepts a variety of book formats.  It seems to read PDFs fine, and      pulls the text out and re-formats it for its smaller screen.  -- I was able to read 3 books, of about 300 pages, using the XL font before     the unit needed to be recharged.  My guess is this was about 3600 page     turns more or less. (Since using XL font, each screen only displays      about a quarter of a printed page.)    -- It supports audio output, with a headphone jack.  Plays MP3 files,      etc.  This is a great feature for audio books, because the screen allows     better navigation within the audio book.   -- Apparently it takes Microsoft Word format directly, which is nice     if it works.     I think E-book readers are great, and they have terrific advantages over  paper. (My eyes started going downhill fast after age 40, so I appreciate being   able to use a larger font size, to make reading fun again).  I love Ebook   readers; the technology is great. (Great for the public, but not for the   publishing house of course.  Unclear if its good for authors or not.)    However this specific model of E-book reader has a serious glare problem.   The software is also a bit weak.  I can use it, but the glare is irritating.     I am already forming a list of what I want (and don't want)  in my NEXT e-reader:    Most important issue is SCREEN RESOLUTION/CONTRAST/ANTI-GLARE.   I don't need a colour screen.  Second most important feature is   BATTERY LIFE.   One Gigabyte or two of Flash memory   is fine, it comes out to many hundreds of hundred books.   I don't really need a touch sensitive screen, I think a well   designed interface with a few buttons would do fine.  I do not  need 3G cell phone connectivity to an e-store that sells   ebooks, since I download all mine from bittorrent anyway.   To avoid plugging the USB in all the time, it might be nice to   use BLUETOOTH or WIFI to move data from local PC to my ebook   reader, but it is not essential, since I have to charge it anyway.   An inductive charging dock system, with bluetooth or wifi   would be ideal. I also have no use at all for a built-in   dictionary or thesaurus. Similarly, I don't need a note taking  feature, or a dictaphone feature.     Here are some other useful things I will expect in my next upgrade:    a) I want to be able to read from the unit while it is plugged in      (via usb or optional charger).   b) I want to be able to turn on screen illumination, especially if      the unit is plugged in while I am reading from it.   c) I want unit to keep track of how far I got in any book I read.      I also want unit to keep track of things I recently read, so I can      easily go back to them.  Might be nice if it had a few folders to      keep track of personal bookmarks, if I share my e-reader withanyone     else.   d) It would be nice if the unit did a GOOD job of text to speach, but      if it is not good, then skip it... I will just dig around and find      an mp3 version of the text.   I definitely want audio output      capability, with good control features on-screen.    Cheers,     EricD

I have three important criteria for a screen protector for this type of product:  1) It should protect the screen well.  2)  It should be easy to install without leaving bubbles or uneven alignment.  3)  It should have a matte surface which dramatically reduces glare and reflections, making it easy to use the product in bright sunlight or with overhead lighting.  This screen protector is (1) Thick, sturdy, and protective; and (2) is fairly easy to install but impossible to eliminate bubbles in the process.  Unfortunately, this screen protector has very poor anti-glare properties which reduces the usability of the Kindle screen underneath it when used outdoors when the sun is shining.  Those who have claimed that this screen protector distorts the screen, should realize that matte non-reflective screen protectors do by necessity obscure some of the clarity (apparent sharpness) of the screen by including the non-reflective property.  Those who complained about the high price should be aware that a true non-glare anti-reflection screen protector normally costs twice as much as an ordinary shiny screen protector.  In my opinion, this screen protector neither reduces clarity nor reduces glare to a noticeable extent.  In fact, nothing on the package or instructions on the product i received implies that this is a non-glare (anti-reflective)screen protector.  It appears that the manufacturer did not design nor intend this to be a non-glare screen protector.  The description of the product should be changed so that it does not imply that it is a non-glare protector.  Amazon should also offer a true non-glare protector.

For the specs, it's a fantastic card that balances performance and cost and blows away GPUs from just a few years ago.

PROS: Overall solid specs at an incredibly affordable price. Great energy efficiency and doesn't require an additional 4- or 6-pin power cable

CONS: Graphic driver is horrible and the GPU randomly locks up on my AMD system. Also, this board is LONG and may block some ports on your motherboard -- it blocks one of my SATA connections, but I didn't need it anyway.

UPDATE: I have rolled back, updated, uninstalled, re-installed, and tried a variety of solutions, to no avail -- the card just doesn't want to run stable. I've plugged in a spare card and installed drivers for it, and I haven't had any issues; ditto with the integrated GPU on the motherboard. So it looks like I have a dud card. Thanks to Amazon's excellent customer service, this dud is packed and ready to go back.

Overall: This item is not an iPod.  It is a lookalike MP3 player with cheap construction and poor firmware programming.  The interface is not intuitive - from menu selections to the control buttons themselves.  It is, in essence, a flash drive device with a built-in MP3 player, and does not offer the convenience of the other (more expensive) MP3 players on the market today.      That said, if a person gets to know how to use this device, and takes advantage of the CD of drivers it ships with, it is a good way to carry 8 Gigs of music with you for a fraction of the price of more popular devices.    The BAD:    * The product images on Amazon.com show something very similar to an iPod interface, which is not the actual firmware offered on this MP3 player.  The interface is counter-intuitive, the buttons are confusing, and the menus don't always make sense.  * The buttons don't do what you expect them to (play/pause doesn't always play/pause and menu doesn't always lead to a menu).    * There is an audible click/pop at the start of, stop of, and between songs during MP3 playback.  * Horizontal images and video show up reversed, as in a mirror image.  I asked my seller about this, and he referred me to some manufacturer's websites, which had no solution to this problem.  Vertical images don't seem to have this problem.  * Construction is obviously cheap.  The materials used look like and feel like cereal-box toys.  The metal casing is not flush with the plastic end pieces.  The buttons don't always react, and you'll find yourself pressing them dangerously hard.    * Charging issues: the instructions warn not to over-charge the unit.  I don't know what that means, but it seems unreasonable to build a device in these modern times without some sort of charger shutoff when finished charging.  Is it going to self-destruct?  I'm worried that it might break irreparably simply due to charging.  * The E-book feature is completely worthless.  The screen is 16 characters wide and 8lines tall, so you can only read 128 characters on a screen at once.  It reads .txt files, and doesn't recognize word breaks.  This means the screen displays 16 characters across, and will do a line break right in the middle of a word.    The GOOD:  * Sound quality is pretty standard.  A lot of hiss is present on videos due to compression, but music sounds okay.  * iTunes or other software isn't required.  Simple drag-and-drop in Windows Explorer (in Windows XP and above) is easy and doesn't try to take over your computer or sell you stuff. (I'm obviously not a fan of iTunes or programs that require a sync.)  * Pretty cheap at $35 or so, compared to hundreds of dollars for name-brand players.  * Very light weight and very small - great for working out.    FINAL VERDICT: I got what I expected with this.  It's a cheap, sort of crappy MP3 player.  It has a lot of space, but is just short of fatally flawed in terms of design and programming.  Buy it if you want to save some money and are willing to give the time and frustration to read the poorly written manual and figure out how to actually make it work, then it's a decent, cheap alternative to name brand MP3 players.

I will never buy another Clarion deck after owning this unit. Sure the deck is a grand improvement on a stock deck, but for the price I'd rather own a high-end non-dvd deck (DVD being novelty in a sedan). This is the bargain barrel DVD touchscreen deck and it is not worth your time or money. The interface sucks and it is unreliable. I can't tear it a new arsehole though without giving it some positive feedback though, so here are some pros.

PROS:
Sounds better than a stock deck. Built-in Bluetooth mic works well for phone calls. You can watch movies on it when it lets you. Inexpensive for a DVD touch deck.

CONS:

AUDIO QUALITY:
The first next thing you will notice is the lack of mid-range frequency in your audio (primarily where vocals are heard). You can turn up the bass and treble, but there are no controls for Mid. So basically everything is thump-thump crash-crash and nothing in between. Songs I love to listen to at home and via headphones sound totally different and unremarkable through this clarion deck. It's probably good for rap and hiphop, but sounds like junk when playing rock or anything complex or melodic.

The next thing you'll notice is the sub woofer volume (if you own a sub). The range is from 0 - 7. The difference between 0 and 7 sounds like it should be the difference between 2 and 3. This is not a drastic or usable tool at all. I just keep it at 7 all the time. Dialing in the sub woofer isn't easy on this deck either as the controls are poorly documented and there is no section on dialing in a sub.

ANNOYANCES:

You will first notice this with the clunky behavior with iTunes. I got the separate iPod cable installed (extra $50) and the interface is horrible. I'd much rather use the iPod itself to navigate music. I usually only use Pandora, and that hardly interfaces at all, so I use my phone to navigate anyway.

The unit prefers bluetooth as an audio source, so if youare using the ipod dock cable and have bluetooth turned & auto-sync turned on it will play out the dock cable for 2 seconds when you start your car then turn off and switch to the bluetooth source once it connects. This means turning your car off and back on leaving your phone/ipod plugged in you have to change the source every time you start your car back up. This is very annoying.

Also, turning the screen off at night is a great feature. Except when it finishes a song and loads another one (at least on Pandora) it turns the screen back on, so you have to continually keep turning it back off to keep the bright screen out of your eyes at night. Ugh.

UNRELIABLE

It began to get picky on what CD I was playing (legit albums and DVDs only, it hasn't ever had a problem with burned discs somehow). It makes a clicking noise when spinning CDs up. This case at first glance is well made.  The faux leather looks pretty good and the stitching is done really nice.  The 5th generation Nano slides in from the top and has a strap that wraps around the bottom and uses a metal snap on the backside of the case just below the belt clip to secure the front cover.  There is a hole on the back for the camera lens.  It has a faux leather covered belt clip that securely holds it to whatever you're going to clip it to.  Finally, it comes with the sticky plastic screen protector.  Overall, I like the workmanship of the product -- it looks beautiful.    Unfortunately, there are a few things I don't like about this case.  The first is that the Nano fits fairly loosely.  There's a lot of wiggle room in there so if you plan on using the camera you have to make sure that the Nano is sitting in there with the the lens centered in the hole of the case.  Otherwise, the case is going to get in the way of the lens.    Second is the location of the front cover snap.  Where it sits gets in the way when you unhook it from whatever you have it attached to.  Either it's going to get caught on your belt/strap making it difficult to take off or it'll get hooked on your belt/strap undoing the snap.    Third -- and this is my biggest issue -- is that the access to the ports at the bottom is very poor.  The slot at the bottom isn't big enough to allow your headphone plug to seat properly.  Only the teeny tiny connector of the Apple earbuds would fit.  I did manage to get a headphone connector plugged in, but I had to push the Nano to one side of the case.  This caused the Nano to sit in the case in a cocked angle -- remember, there's a lot of wiggle room in there -- which then blocked all the information in the upper right hand corner of the display, plus it looks ugly sitting in the case all crooked.      I had the same issue with getting the iPod connector in there.  I had to squish the Nano to one side in order for it to plug in all the way.You can pretty much forget about having both a headphone and the iPod connector plugged in -- the slot just isn't wide enough.    So if you just want an inexpensive case to protect your Nano, then this is a good buy.  If you want to use your Nano while it's in the case, I wouldn't recommend it.

This dock (and the iPod Video in general) failed to meet my expectations in several important ways:

* You can't see the iPod menu on your TV, despite what the salesman I spoke with claimed. This is a huge drawback. In order to watch a slideshow, you have to get up, walk to the iPod / HomeDock, navigate the menus to your starting slide, start the slideshow, and only then can you sit down and watch the slides from your TV. (This is a limitation of the iPod Video, not the HomeDock. However, it's a huge argument for not buying the HomeDock -- it's better to just have a long A/V cable to your TV and use the iPod directly, at least then you can see and use the full menu while you're setting up your slideshow.)

* You can't control music while watching slides. Worse yet, pushing the wrong button while watching slides breaks you out of the slideshow. Given that I have my library of thousands of photos on the iPod, and given that you can't just resume a slideshow where you left off (a big gap in the usability of the iPod Video's slideshow functionality), it's extremely frustrating as there's no way to change music w/o breaking out of your slideshow, and there's no way to resume your slideshow if you do choose to change your music. (Again, many of these are design problems with the iPod Video, but trying to do the same functionality via the HomeDock's remote makes it twice as frustrating. Moreover, in slideshow mode, the HomeDock's remote has two unused buttons that should have been mapped to \\"track forward\\" and \\"track back\\", but don't touch them! Doing so will stop your slideshow and you'll be screwed.)

* I haven't tried watching a video yet. I imagine the same frustrations would apply, however, they might be less because, during a video, you don't expect to be able to control audio and video independently.

* I also haven't tried to use this dock with a computer. It seems to me that, unless you have a computer inyour living room, you're either using it as a computer dock or as a TV dock. (My wish for 2006 is an Apple computer that works flawlessly as an entertainment center hub.)

* The HomeDock's remote is not particularly responsive, and given the ease of bumping yourself out of your slideshow, this is extra frustrating.

* The base station has a place to put the remote when not in use. However, the remote is battery-operated, not rechargeable, so there's no need to \\"dock\\" it, and nothing substantial holding it in place when you do decide to \\"dock\\" it. The bad: if you bump the base station (and not even very hard) the remote falls down. The HomeDock is larger because of this extra \\"remote dock\\" space, and it also means you'll need to hunt for yet another obscure battery someday. The good: it does look kinda cool to keep the remote next to the iPod, and at least there's a place where the remote \\"belongs\\", which helps curb coffee table remote clutter.

Bottom line: I find the HomeDock unusable and prefer a simple A/V cable directly from iPod Video to TV. Until Apple upgrades iPod software to show the full iPod menu on the TV, and lets you control audio and video both independently while in slideshow mode, I would stay away from HomeDock (or any other expensive iPod accessory). Also, if you want to show slideshows from the iPod on your TV, you really need to arrange your slides ahead of time in iPhoto. Trying to do an ad-hoc slideshow with thousands of digital photos is too frustrating to bother.

Currently, I have all three sitting in front of me. The K3 is the biggest and heaviest, although not by much. After all, the K3 has a 6\\" screen with a keyboard, whereas both the Opus and PRS-350 have a 5\\" display and no keyboard. The K3 offers G3 connectivity in addition to USB, whereas the PRS-350 and Opus only have USB. So, as a Kindle owner, you can buy books anywhere in the world where a G3 connection works. In addition, you can transfer all those free eBooks found on the Gutenberg project or manybooks.com - just get the correct format.   One of the important aspects of an eBook is the readability of the Screen and that's where you see the generation difference: The Opus sports a first generation eInk passive display, whereas both the PRS-350 and the Kindle K3 have second generation displays. The K3 display is passiv, whereas the PRS-350 is touch sensitive, which reduces the contrast slightly. Held next to each other, the K3 has by far the best screen, followed by the PRS-350 and then by the Opus. The difference is most noticeable in dim light, where I can still easily read the K3, the PRS-350 to a lesser degree and the Opus requiring a clip-on light.  As for the haptic experience, I prefer both the K3 and the Opus to the PRS-350. The latter has a metal frame which feels cold. In addition, with the touch sensitive screen, I have to pay attention not to touch the screen inadvertantly.   In summary, for me, the K3 is the clear winner, both in terms of ergonomics and overall consumer convenience, followed by the Opus and trailed by the Sony PRS-350.  As for purchasing ebooks, I use my PC and not the K3. The PC screen and keyboard are still a superior browsing experience. However, due to G3, I can easily access ebooks I purchased from Amazon (USD 0.00 or higher) on the K3 (or smartphone etc) without needing to connect the K3 via USB. I also find it an advantage being able to keep purchased ebooks with Amazon, so I can download them whenever I want and I don't need to think about backing up my ebooks.

If you're a scholar and you're looking for an ereader with which to do serious research (read hundreds of pages and annotate them easily), and you *can* wait, I suggest you do at this point. I bought the BlueAnt S4 over a year ago. The product is useful, but deeply flawed.

The Good:

+ loud
+ battery lasts a while (or you can just leave it hooked up full-time)
+ voice interface
+ a2dp -- supports music, podcasts, reading text messages, etc.
+ supports multiple devices at once.
+ standard charging interface (MicroUSB)

The Bad:

- the hardware \\"buttons\\" are not very sensitive. I sometimes have to press them multiple times.
- the speech recognition isn't very accurate. I speak with the \\"General American\\" accent, so there is no excuse.
- the built-in menu doesn't have a simple \\"help\\" system. It should default to providing a help menu if no command is given. At the very least, it should recognize the word \\"help\\" to provide a list of commands. Instead, you have to remember \\"what can I say?\\" This is not printed on the device.

The Ugly:

- There are not a lot of built-in commands. You cannot add or remove items from the built-in phonebook, you can just transfer it from your phone -- maybe.
- There is no easy dial-by-voice built-in, so you have to use your phone's phone command capabilities.
- There are a limited number of devices that it can be paired with, and no way to remove devices using the built-in commands. This means that when you buy a new device, you might not be able to pair the bloody thing. The workaround is to reset the BlueAnt by making sure it's not connected to any phones and then pressing and holding both volume-up and volume-down. Why, oh why, didn't they just include a handy \\"unpair phone\\" or \\"delete phone\\" in the menu?

After this experience, I don't intend to buy another BlueAnt device.

Essentially this system of counting charge in/out breaks down from time to time and it somehow resets itself to a very low estimate of SOC that doesn't relate to battery voltage. This causes the system to shut down when the problem is too bad. The other problem is generator integration. You can't just plug a generator into this and get it to charge batteries. You need to program it and there is no documentation for the system parameters that control this. Even with very large KVA generators I can only get a few Amps of DC charging with this thing. My advice would be to get an alternative product.

While this seems like a quality cable, it just doesn't function with my automotive diagnostic software. The ELM327 chip  in this device must be a counterfeit chip. I did not open the case up to see if it were a genuine yellow ELM327 chip, but based on the fact that it doesn't work with my software and information which I found on the ELM chip manufacturer website, it is my best judgment to say that this is a fake chip. While looking for the latest driver on the Prolific software website I stumbled across the instructions for connecting the cable to a PC, which clearly state that if there is a yellow warning symbol on the com port in  device manager (in Windows) then it is most likely that the chip is a clone. Sure enough... I have the yellow warning label on both of my PCs. I attempted to hook the ELM327 up to 4 different software programs on 2 different PC without success. The software that comes with the cable does work , but is very basic and has a rather ugly interface (baud rate needs to be changed to 38400 for the port in device manager (Windows) and within the program in order for it to read the cable). I am sending my cable back and going to look for either a genuine ELM327 cable or get a stn1110, which supposedly is a superior chip set and works will all ELM327 software. Save yourself a headache and hours of messing around and buy a genuine cable.

Having relied on Xantrex and Trace inverters in the past, and having had bad experiences with lower quality inverter/chargers, I was a little nervous ordering a product with so little in the way of reviews or brand experience.  This unit has exceeded all my expectations, and performs better than any of my previous units.  To find a 3000 W inverter with charger (though description states 100A the unit actually provides 65A charge) as well as a built in 60 A MPPT solar controller was too good to pass up at this price.  The unit is extremely solid, and it appears very well manufactured.  If I had any complaints, it would only be that my unit shipped only with a specification sheet, and not a full manual, but that was easily remedied by contacting ZODORE.  I have not yet put the MPPT controller to use, but plan on tackling a solar array next, and the inverter and charger functions of this device are working well.  Update 2/16/2015.  Alright, well, when something seems to good to be true...  The inverter worked really well for approximately one week.  I have it on my boat, hooked to a deep cycle 12 volt battery.  After a week of steady use, I wrote the above review.  After I posted the review, I tried to run the inverter function off of a generator.  It appropriately noted the power and switched to shore power mode, but despite a steady meter reading of 115-120 volts, it continued to cycle back and forth from inverter mode to shore power mode.  I gave up, and turned it off, but on returning to shore, found it no longer charged, and did not work as an inverter - it would only pass through AC power from shore. I contacted ZODORE (available through Skype from China) and was initially happy that they seemed so willing to help.  They asked me to take a number of pictures, videos, and try a few things to get the unit working, then explained that the control board must have failed, and were willing to ship me a new one, as well as refund $100 for my time and inconvenience for performing the repair myself.  I put in the board, and no difference - it was still non-functional for anything but AC pass-through.  They had me take more pictures, and try more tests, but at the end of several weeks of frustrating back and forth (I frequently had to wait for their customer service person to speak with their technician, and get back to me with more questions or requests for pictures/videos, as well as time zone differences), told me that they felt the unit needed to be returned.  At this point I was starting to get angry, as I had no inverter, and no charger, and it had been weeks of frustration.  They agreed to cross ship a new unit to me to try and fix things ASAP, but insisted that I return the $100 refund they had given me.  Unfortunately, as I was desperate to get it working, I returned the money, and then shipped back the unit.  Despite promising me a cross ship, they decided not to send me anything, and contacted me after they received it back to say that they thought they could fix it, but it seemed to have been damaged in shipping, and so my repaired unit would be damaged.  I was very angry that they lied to me, and said so - then threatened to reverse the charges and file a bad review.  They relented, and sent me a new one, that I just received today.  I hooked it up directly to my battery, without connecting any other leads.  On turning it on, it came on in inverter mode for a few seconds, made a LOUD humming noise, and then turned off the inverter function and became quiet again.  It stated it was seeing 12.9 V from the battery and 0 V AC, which was correct, but despite checking the battery leads, powering it off and back on (again getting the LOUD hum) it would not supply any power to the AC output leads.  I went to Skype and started to type messages to their customer service agent, who immediately went to "away" mode, and has not answered me.  While typing, the inverter alarmed, made a loud POP, and started to smoke. I am not,by any means, an electrical engineer, however I work with a lot of electronics, do a fair amount of electrical wiring and circuit board repair.  The hook up of these units is not rocket science, but to have two units fail (one virtually DOA) is unbelievable. They customer service was friendly, if not honest or fast, but frustrating dealing with overseas. Update 3/27/15 Last update.  Despite a very rocky ordeal, Zodore has continued to have good communication, and has refunded me for this unit, as well as return shipping.  I'm still out the customs fees, $53, but I was honestly very surprised that this company was so willing to completely stand by their product and even after all this time, still issued a full refund as well as shipping.  Most vendors these days seem to use any excuse to leave customers high and dry, but they didn't. I keep going back and forth on what to rate this product. With the video instructions, installations was relatively easy, though I still had to use the second protector to get it right. I think the placement of the second tab made it a bit more difficult to see if I were lining up the protector correctly. I ended up overlapping too much and so there were bubbles in my first attempt at installation that would disappear. I don't think the cleaning cloth really did its lint-free job as it seemed that particles would immediately fall back onto the screen when I was trying to clean it so with a few lint bubbles and air bubbles from the lining up wrong, I ended up taking it off and reinstalling. Second time did go much better and it just seemed that I needed practice in installing the item as I really have never used a screen protector on anything before. Overall, with the installation video and a little practice, that part of this item was relatively good.  However, after turning on my Kindle Fire I was confronted with a terrible amount of pixelized rainbowing or whatever the proper term is called. Whenever there was a bright white or light background I would see these little pixels of color all over. It really distracted me and took away from the screen quality of this device and it really annoyed me. It it annoyed me more when I took a look at reviews and realized I should have read them first before buying anyway. The only time this rainbow effect does not impede the reading is when it is a black background with white words, but I haven't figured out a way to use that function for the PDFs I have to read for classes. I don't mind the smudging and fingerprints left behind as that was evident on the Kindle's screen without the protector. I don't think they show up anymore than they did before. I'm also the kind of person that will clean my screen obsessively after each use to keep it in nicer shape.  I have been trying to put up with this this screen protector for a fewdays to see if it gets better for me over time to use without noticing the screen distortions. It has been about a week now and I'm really do not think I will keep it on my Fire very much longer. I will probably look for one that is clear so as not to distort the images from the screen anymore.  As a protector I guess it does well, but it definitely distorts the screen quality too much, even for reading Kindle books. I would not recommend this product to anyone who wants to keep the screen quality the same.  As a final note, the only reason I went for an anti-glare screen protector was because a friend of mine had purchased one for her Nook Tablet for the purposes of protecting the screen and so there wouldn't be glare. I thought this would be a good idea as well, but on comparing my Kindle Fire with this product on it to her Nook and whatever brand of anti-glare screen protector she had purchased, the difference was amazing. I do not know if it was the brand of screen protector she had or if it was simply the settings she had active on her Nook, but there was absolutely no rainbow effect on her screen. And aside from all the smudges on the screen, there wasn't much detraction from the original screen quality. There was a softening to the images on the screen but there was none of the rainbowing effect that I have on my Fire with this anti-glare protector.

There are a number of things that I would like buyers to be aware of before ordering this unit. Some of them are for your information only, some of them subtract points/stars.

First the big issue that made me return the item: the outputs driving an existing car's power amps do not have output levels compatible with my E46 BMW's amp (which is by no means exotic). That means that even at maximum volume selected on the radio you still have very little volume in the car. This unit should have an internal parameter (or a dip switch) to adjust the output level. But it doesn't.

Another issue is that it is too deep, I can't mount it physically in this E46 convertible. While it is not much deeper than the original BMW radio this still doesn't work because the wiring harness clips into the back of the original radio (and hence \\"disappears\\") but the harness is outside with this Kenwood and there is no place for it to go. The RCA connectors were also causing too much depth with RCA plugs in them.

It didn't read my mp3 hardware player, although I think it should have worked. The player presents itself as a USB storage device to a computer just fine. There doesn't seem to be a way to diagnose this. The radio just doesn't like it and that's that. EOL.

The overall build is very flimsy and I bet the black plastic frame around the front panel breaks quickly. I wanted a Kenwood because the last Kenwood I had was built like a tank and lasted longer than the car I had it in plus the car I had after that. To my dismay I had to realize that since then JVC and Kenwood \\"merged\\" and that Kenwood is now a cheap brand in the JVC empire. This unit is directly labeled as manufactured by JVC. Sorry but I wanted a Kenwood, not a JVC.

The mounting frame doesn't have the latches that your bend in the right place to secure it in this BMW in any other place than the bottom. In fact the number of latches and overall depth (or lack thereof)of the mounting frame will be a problem in quite a few cars.

The controls on the left (input selection etc) are all small and the volume knob doesn't stand out enough for my taste. Very hard to use with gloves.

Just FYI, it has a 3-band EQ. I was hoping for 7 bands but it wasn't really possible from the website to find out, and of course the product page doesn't say either. No points subtracted. Just wishing for better information.

On the positive side the CD playing seems to work well, reading CD-Rs more reliably than other radios.

Although the features and price are tempting, the overall quality of the firmware (devices internal software) is below substandard quality.

Simple functions like finding and selecting songs is a real pain, requiring you to navigate through all songs available one at a time. With 2 GB of memory filled with files, this becomes real time consuming.

When you pause a song for only a few seconds, the player stops the current song completely and returns to the first song in the list. You must then find the song you were listening to all over again. There are no search functions available to help locate and play the song you want.

Many menu selections either don't work as expected or simply do nothing at all. Though I thought organizing songs into folders would make finding songs easier, the folder/directory selection feature doesn't select anything, and returns you to the first song in memory.

Although this items claims to play video, the one included on the player played great, all videos must be converted to a specific file format not standard in the US, using software included on the CD. The problem is the Windows only software accepts a limited number of video file formats, and I have had no luck with any files I have tried to convert.

Although connecting the player to a Mac OS computer was as straight forward as any other flash drive, connecting the player to Windows XP took several attempts, and all software on the CD only works on Windows. The Mac version of iTunes would not recognize this player.

Though headphones are included, the headphone jack does not accept a standard headphone mini-plug (it uses the smaller standard found on many mobile phones), so using higher quality headphones commonly available (like Sony or Koss) is not possible without a plug adaptor.

I would not recommend this player to anyone.
