Size: It appears a lot smaller in the photos on the website. I was disappointed that the battery cover protrudes  inch!, enough so that it doesn't slip cleanly in tight pants pocket.

Features: Jmtek did very well in this department. FM tuner, mp3, WAV, Voice recorder, back lit display, 5 audio modes, power save, key guard, even EXPLANDABLE SD/MMC card slot.
Unfortunately not all work so well. FM reception is spotty even with the `special,' ear buds that have a range extending antenna built in. I found myself holding the player in the air to get an adequate reception half the time. Back light creates interference when on.

SD/MMC card reader is a very cool feature (not sure why others haven't picked up on this yet?). Songs on your SD card will automatically be added to the play list no matter what format they are in.

Uploading: Uploading is very straight forward. Player needs no drivers and is instantly recognized by your system. My only gripe is the USB cable is NOT small standard as you might find on digital cameras, etc. So if you happen to forget it, or want to take your player to work you won't be able to upload without it....:-(

Battery life: I was disappointed to find the power save mode which is supposed to turn off the display after a preset time didn't seem to make a difference in battery life. I average about 6 hours on a single AAA battery, not that great considering Creative's MUVO micro gets about 12hrs and has nearly identical features.

General usage: I found that even changing tracks, play/ pause buttons were VERY difficult to use unless I was actually looking at the display. Additionally navigating the menu is dreadful!! The boneheads at Jmtek apparently tried to simplify the design and thus use only 3 buttons, with which to navigate through the menu, play/ pause, volume control, etc. The display is nice and bright and text is easy to read.

Overall: I would NOTrecommend this player. There are many players on the market that offer nearly all the same features for less money in a smaller package.

Other reviewers describe good sound. As an owner of Jambox (and Big Jambox), I can attest the sound does not compare.

I have used my Jambox and Big Jambox to connect to the Bluetooth (BT) on my Dish Network, as I have a large room making it difficult to understand dialogue on the TV. The Jamboxes work great, requiring no cord, provide great sound, and connect to the BT seamlessly. As I like to use my Jamboxes to listen to music from my iPad and iPhone, I was hoping to find an inexpensive BT speaker that would suffice for dialogue from my Dish Network Hopper. As several reviewers reported that the sound of the OontZ was decent, I decided to give it a shot.

For the purpose of video dialogue, the OontZ does the job. Spoken words, background music, and even music from music video type channels, is very acceptable.

HOWEVER....as previously reviewers stated, there exists several issues:

1) The manual is very poor. There is an LED on the front of the unit. The manual does not explain the meaning of the continuous blue, flashing blue, or alternating blue and red LED light. Thankfully, previous Amazon reviewers explained the meaning of the lights!

2) When connected to the BT of my Dish Hopper, the LED alternates blue and red. This is a little annoying and distracting. A previous reviewer explained that his contact with Cambridge SoundWorks described this as a firmware issue. When connected to my iPad, the blue LED glows continuously, which is, supposedly, how the light is designed to work.

3) The BT requires reconnection, through my iPad settings, Dish Settings, or iPhone settings, every time I turn on the OontZ. This is definitely a hassle. With the Jamboxes (JB), when BT is enabled on any of my devices, they connect right up with JB, with no issues. They reconnect and start working when powered on. Not the case with the OontZ.

4) When charging the OontZ, you have to have the power switch "On". This is very odd! The manual stats you can use the OontZ while charging. That is true. However, the blue LED flashes continuously while charging. It does not indicate when a charge is complete. I left the OontZ charging for 2 1/2 days while out of town, and the blue LED was still flashing when I returned. It must have had a full charge after this time frame! I connected my iPad via BT to listen to some music. With the charger still attached, the music cut in and out, as if the charging pulses were causing this. When I disconnected the charger, the music no longer cut in and out, and it worked fine. I don't believe that occurs if the battery is somewhat depleted and the charger is connected while listening to music.

5) The sound does NOT compare to my Jamboxes. Of course, the Big Jambox is MUCH louder (and much more expensive), but even the regular Jambox (also, over 3 times more costly), is louder and of better quality, especially for music.

For a relatively inexpensive speaker, the OontZ works okay, as long as volume is not required (I like to listen to music while preparing for my day, i.e. in the shower, etc. and the OontZ doesn't meet my needs). For low volume, in an office or room, it is good. Just be aware you'll need to reconnect often, the manual isn't helpful for the LED codes, you may experience unusual LED codes (iPad and iPhone seem to work okay) and it's not clear about the charging status.

One final tidbit, the OontZ does include a USB charger cord, and mini audio cord for non BT devices with an audio output, but no power adaptor for wall charging. If you do not own one, you'll need to charge via USB of your PC.

I initially gave this dash-cam a 5-Star rating. It was reasonably priced, pretty easy to set-up, and did exactly what it was supposed to do. I had literally no complaints. Unfortunately, I wasn't then able to take into consideration its longevity (or lack thereof).  About 4 months after I mounted it on my windshield, with almost zero handling in the interim, it simply stopped automatically saving the last file when I turned off the car. The last file is, of course, the most important one to have, should you get into an accident and need to stop the vehicle. It also automatically reverted to the on-screen Chinese instructions which I was unable to change back to English (though that was just a secondary issue). I subsequently contacted XIQI and was told the item was out of warranty and there was nothing to be done. After some up and back emails, and my threat to write a bad review, they reluctantly offered me a $10 discount for a new one.  Since I really did like it, I sucked it up and bought another one, figuring I'd just gotten unlucky. This time, about 6 months after purchase, the LCD screen suddenly become staticky when I started the car and the camera would essentially freeze up and stop working after a few seconds. Again, this was after almost never touching it once mounted. So you can't blame mishandling (or handling at all for that matter). I then took it off the windshield and after studying it a bit, noticed that if I jiggled the power connector a little (where it connects to the camera), it sometimes began working again. But after mounting and dismounting it about 10 times, I had to admit that there was a fatal short circuit or bad connection somewhere, and that I again had another bad one. I live in the Northeast US, and got this last one in late September 2014, so it simply hasn't been warm enough here yet to blame leaving it out in the heat-should overheating be considered a possible factor. After buying two units in the course of less than a year, I have to acknowledge that this item simply cheaply constructed and definitely NOT recommended. For a few dollars more than these two cost me, I could have gotten something more substantial, with a better warranty, and that's my plan at this point. Additionally, there have been a lot of reviews regarding knock-off versions of this dash-cam, but both of mine were clearly not knock-offs. So save your money, and very possible future aggravation, and look for something else!

I have two of these units, and have used them for over a year. This review is based on the Holux m241 with firmware v1.13.    If you need a data logger or track/distance measurer or want to geotagging digital photos, then take my advice and avoid this unit. Multiple failures resulting in data loss have lead me to start looking for something else. If you just want something to display your coordinates, or connect to a computer then it works well, but you can probably find other units more geared towards those purposes. As a GPS data logger, it is horribly unreliable. My advice, if you already have the unit, is to simply take photos of the Long/Lat screen so you have a sure record. And don't expect its logging feature to work every time.    Pros:     - The satellite signal is good. Doesn't usually lose its signal when in a car or backpack     - Battery life is good (but not enough for a whole day.)     - Can be powered by USB, so you can get a USB phone charger (2xAA) to extend the logging time to over 24 hours, or use a USB car charger and not worry about batteries while you're in a car. (These are third party accessories, and don't come with the unit)     - Has Bluetooth connectivity if you need it. Can even download your data via Bluetooth.     - Will start logging automatically as soon as it receives signal, but only if you set it to do so (Note: was not available in original firmware. Also note: like the device in general, it's unreliable.)     - When set to \\"Dist By: Point\\", the distance measure mode can be used for simple navigating (e.g. finding your car), although not reliably. See bottom of the review for details.    Cons:     - Critical fault: Sometimes it simply fails to record coordinates, even though the little \\"running man\\" logging icon is shown. I went camping for 4 days, and despite always keeping the thing powered during the day, and supposedly logging, the end result was exactly 0 records recorded. I've been using this thing for well over a year, but since this trip it rarely seems to keep logging (it didn't get wet or damaged in any way). There is no indication as to whether it is working or not unless you keep an eye on the free space screen. By the time you realize that it's not actually doing anything then it's too late.      - No Lock: There's no way to \\"Lock\\" the device. If you keep this in your bag or pocket you can accidentally switch it off or press a button, which could stop recording, lose your distance waypoint, or change settings, etc. The buttons are fairly difficult to press accidentally but it's still not something you want to rely on.     - No accuracy display. Can never be sure how accurate the coordinates are.     - Sometimes needs to be \\"jump started\\": power it via USB to turn it on (after that the inserted battery might start working by itself). This has been required at times on both my m241 devices. I tried multiple batteries (they weren't the issue)     - The distance measure is lost when you switch it off and on or press the right button (\\"enter\\"). So forget changing batteries if you want to use this feature and be careful not to knock it. (although the rubber buttons are fairly difficult to press accidentally)     -  Firmware / software is not reliable: The data format stored internally on the device changed between firmware versions (they increased its accuracy, which is good). All well and good, but if you use mismatched software+firmware when you download your coordinates you can end up with corrupted data, and think it was successfully downloaded. Too bad if you wiped your device after downloading the data from it, because your download is corrupt and there's nothing you can do. This happened to me after I used newer software to download the coordinate data from a device with older firmware. Note that I couldn't update the firmware without losing the data on there either, so it would have been a catch-22 even if I had known in advance that it was corrupting my data. I lost severaldays worth of logs because of this. Really wouldn't have been difficult for Holux's PC software to check the firmware version and deal with both cases. Instead they chose to have the software show success but silently fail. This is really lazy (or stupid) programming. Even if the issue is unlikely to affect me a second time, it increases my distrust in this unit, and I won't be buying anything with \\"Holux\\" stamped on it again.     - Buggy firmware: certain settings change other un-related settings. To reproduce this bug: Set the device to log by time (15 seconds). Then go into the settings menu and choose \\"Log Rcd\\" -> \\"Full Stop\\" (which is the default setting, and probably selected already). For no particular reason it will now have now changed back from logging by time (15 seconds) to logging by distance (every 100m). Note also due to the two-button menu system, once you enter the \\"Log Rcd\\" menu (e.g. to see what it's set to) then you can't escape out of it without choosing an option. Even by re-selecting the already selected option you end up changing the unrelated \\"Log by\\" setting. This makes for a very undependable device, as you can never be sure what your settings are and checking them changes others. I'm not sure if this is an isolated bug or if there are others like it.    - Annoying UI: The \\"Menu\\" button is also the backlight button. So to turn the backlight on for the current menu/screen, first you have to cycle through ALL the other menus/screens. This is a mere annoyance. (They could have solved the issue by making the first press ONLY turn on the backlight, and the next presses cycle the menu, rather than combine the two)     - Distance measure (\\"ruler\\" mode) doesn't tell you the direction of the reference waypoint. If it did, the device could almost be USEFUL for simple navigation e.g. finding your car (See bottom of review for details on how to do this anyway) As is, this gps is not even as good as an XKCD-407 for navigating, although in a pinch youcan use it as such.     - Frequent firmware upgrades have been required to fix bugs (e.g. the original firmware gave Northern hemisphere coordinates for the Southern hemisphere). Thank you Holux for fixing the bugs, but it still has a few.     - Software is Windows only.     - Windows software is not so user friendly. E.g. it forgets the last folder you downloaded to. Another issue is that to upgrade the firmware you have to hit the \\"disconnect device\\" button first. This really isn't so intuitive. (And it's very likely that you WILL have to upgrade the firmware, in case you're wondering)    Summary: It can do what it says it does, but don't rely on it to do so, and don't expect a pleasant user experience.    -----  How to navigate with this device: When you're at your car/bike/home/campsite, go the \\"ruler\\" mode and press \\"start\\", then you always know how far away you are. If the distance is going down, then you're getting closer. Up means further. However, this is really unreliable: You can't be sure if a fluctuating distance is just random or genuine (there's no accuracy display). The smallest unit is 10 meters (0.01 km). Also you have to hawkishly watch the display. If the device is switched off even momentarily or if the \\"enter\\" button is (accidentally) pressed then the location of your car is forgotten and you're on your own. I do not enjoy navigating with this device, but it's saved me in the past.    Note you must have \\"Dist By: Point\\" in your settings, and there is no way to tell if that's the mode you're using without going into settings and changing it. Fortunately, it seems you can swap between the two modes at will (by point, by path) without resetting either measurement.    I have never been desperate enough to try using triangulation to calculate the direction of my waypoint, although in theory you could do it too. How to do triangulation? This is an exercise for the reader.

This player runs ONLY on Windows XP. It WILL NOT RUN ON VISTA, and Philips have no plans for a firmware fix.    Also, it cannot handle Windows Media Player 11. You would have to roll back to v. 10.    A third problem is the CDs that come with the player. They don't actually produce any device-specific software; rather, they kick up Microsoft (not even Philips!) web pages telling you how to sync a player with WMP (ironically, the CD itself takes you to a WMP 11 page... even though the player cannot work with v. 11!).    I spent a frustrating week trying to make the player load and play consistently. Finally convinced I had a defective device, I called Philips tech support. That's when I learned that the device was fine; my media player was simply too new. And because I was in the process of migrating everything from my old XP laptop to a new one (equipped, through no choice of my own, with Vista), the device (I was told) would not work with my new laptop anyway. I could either roll back my media player AND wipe my new hard drive clean and install XP in place of Vista -- all for the sake of one single device -- or I could get rid of the Philips and find another player. I chose the latter.    So keep in mind that if you ever have to replace your XP computer or an automatic Windows update hands you WMP 11 (or 12 or whatever), your Philips mp3 player will become instant garbage.

I bought this case for my Zen nearly 6 months ago, but not through Amazon as it was not available at the time.  I have used it for 6 months and I usually carry it around in my jeans pocket - Zen inside the hard plastic case.  At first, I was excited about the case because it was a solid fit and it felt very protected.  I've dropped it several times and watched the player skip across the ground without it skipping a beat so I don't worry about dropping it or bumping it in any way.  However almost immediately after I inserted it into the case, I noticed that ever so slightly it dulled the colors on the screen - but it was a small trade off for the protection (so I thought).  Then after a few days, maybe a week, some scratches started showing up.  Again, not a big deal.  After about a couple months of normal use I noticed dust and other tiny particles slowly creeping their way into the case.  I didn't think much of it because I knew I could just pop off the case and clean it if I wanted to.  Well, I finally got around to doing that and I came to discover that, because the case fits so snugly around the player, whatever small, hard dust particles had been trapped between the case and screen caused little divots in the screen (rather than scratches).  This essentially rendered my case useless, because the main reason I wanted a case was to keep the screen from being scratched or damaged.  In fact it was the screen in conjunction with dust (and admittedly lack of maintenance) that caused the screen to be damaged.  I suppose it would only take a few small particles or maybe sand to work its way beneath the case to damage the player's face, and I would hope that regular cleaning would prevent this from happening, so be warned:  keep your case clean!    PROS:    Solid and sturdy case         Fits snugly         Small and Simple (no belt clip loop, no wire management, no prop stand)    CONS:    Will not prevent damage to the screen from dust or particles that   get inside.With normal use it requires regular cleaning to keep the dust out.         Scratches Easily.         Ever so slightly dulls the colors on the screen.

We installed these in a new Sienna van last year and here is the scoop.
They worked as advertised and the kids have enjoyed them but you should know a few thing that are not stated in the Amazon page.
First, intallation took a good big day and required some inovation to get the wires though the seats and sort of hide them so they don't get caught and tangled all the time. We used a 12volt plug in the cigar lighter and with the fuses and RGB connections it is still a pretty big wire pile under/by the front console.
Second, these DVD player only play about half the DVD that we try because of the region incompatability. So don't expect to be able to play all your DVDs, only a choosen few.
Third, One of the DVD players only worked about 4 or 5 hours and then quit. We still had the other player and could play one DVD and display it on both screens, but only one DVD player worked. I recently took the head apart and lubed it and cleaned the lazer eye and got it working again - lets see how long it lasts.
Fourth, Th FM transmitter transmits at 87.5 mghz and our van's radio only receives down to 87.7 mghz so we cannot play the sound through the van's audio system. This is a pretty major mistake in design. I checked some other vehicles and none of them could receive 87.5 mhz.
Fifth, The volume on the internal speaker is really, really, low. It is pretty well useless as far a listening while on the road. The IR headsets work pretty well as long as the kids can tolerate them, but they are pretty tight on their heads so after an hour or so the kids complain and it would be nice to be able to listen through the van's audio system or through the DVD player's internal speakers - neither of these work. The infrared headsets are strickly line-of- sight so the kids in the third row of seats have a hard time getting the headsets to receive consistantly.
Sixth, The headrests are not really well built and solid. The little plasic shims arenot tight in the seat sockets and so there is some wobble. The faux leather color did not match our van's interior very well, but tolerable I guess. The zip off covers do not come clear off so they only flop down at about a 90 degree angle, so they are kind of in the way for getting in and out of the van.
We have used these for about a year and we are probably going the change them out for something that we hope will work better. When you spend this much money I think you should expect something that the details are worked out better. They work, but not well.

This is the 4th e-book reader I've had in the last 10 years. In all these years there have been very few improvements because manufacturers want to sell e-books, not e-readers. E-books are expensive and produced mechanically. They show inferior quality and are riddled with typos and other irksome imperfections. Publishers don't want to pay professional proofreaders to check the quality of their e-books.

The Kobo Touch advertises itself as being able to read many different types of formats; it's really not suited to read anything but EPUB files. If you think you can read PDFs or DOC with this e-reader, look somewhere else.

The unit is not very touch responsive; sometimes you hit the page or swipe it and get no response; that is very frustrating because there are no other buttons to advance the pages. Display is not that sharp. Software updates promise improved capabilities and better touch response, but so far this reader has been very disappointing.

I give it two stars because the only positive attribute this e-reader has is its ability to accommodate different typefaces. Not all work well, but you have to experiment and find the one you prefer.

I don't know if all e-readers as like this one; if they are, books are in no danger of extinction.

The good: As I approach middle age, my eyes are betraying me, so being able to enlarge the font from, say \\"large\\" to \\"largest\\" is awesome. It really does make reading enjoyable again. The screen is much larger than it looks and it is backlit, meaning you can read it in a dark room. Other e-readers tout the so-called \\"e-ink,\\" meaning the screen looks exactly like a piece of paper and it behaves like a piece of paper, meaning you need a reading light. The Literati mimics a computer screen and is in full color. This isn't important if all you read are novels, but if you subscribe to magazines and newspapers as I do, or if the book you are reading has color photos or maps in it, then of course color is essential. The Literati uses the incredible Kobo Books (think of it as iTunes for your Literati). You create an account, buy books and they are yours for keeps. What's cool is that you can buy books right off the e-reader itself because it's wi-fi. Setting up the wi-fi was a snap, by the way. Or you can buy books on your computer or smartphone via the cool Kobo app. If you use your computer, say, you simply sync your Literati the next time you turn it on (it stores your Kobo password, so you are always logged into your account when your wi-fi is on) and your new purchases appear in your library. Oh yeah, you may also delete books from your Literati with the push of a button but they remain yours, housed in your Kobo account. Very thoughtful feature. The thing is lightweight and relatively easy to hold and it comes with a nifty leather folio. The battery lasts for a few hours (not a few days) but if you keep your wi-fi on, it decreases your battery life. If you lay the thing down and forget to turn it off, it turns off automatically after a few minutes. Conclusion: The Literati is, as far as I am concerned, thoughtfully designed and packaged and is what it is: an good, reliable e-reader.

The bad: There is only one thing about the Literati I don't like, but it's a deal breaker. It is painfully SLOW. It takes forever to \\"boot up,\\" and if your book is long, like say the Bible, it takes literally MINUTES to load the book. It is true that the e-reader automatically bookmarks the page you stop at and when you return to the book it opens up to that page (you may also insert bookmarks automatically and highlight passages, another \\"pro\\"), but it is unbelievably slow in EVERYTHING it does. Think of the old days with dial-up Internet and you'll have a good idea of what using the Literati is like. I gave this product 2 stars because of the abundance of misinformation about plugging into ipods and the use of products that plug into the docking port like this one.  Taking the signal from the ipods dock port does not bypass the ipods built in amp. It does however take a maximum amplified signal from the ipod that bypasses only the ipod volume control and will drain the ipod battery accordingly.  What you are getting from the ipod dock port is the signal that you would get if you plugged into the ipod headphone jack and turned the volume all the way up. If you have both cables Try it.  I think most of the reviewers praising this product have low powered FiiO portable headphone amps that need the ipod pumping out full power and therefore sing praises to a bad set up, the set up in fairness does sound better than no amp at all though. This same group is experiencing short battery life with their ipods and has simply not been exposed to how to do things better.  A better way to go, first plug into the ipods headphone jack FiiO makes a great cable for this the L8. Second adjust the volume of the ipod to no more than half volume. (this will quadruple the battery life of your ipod over taking the signal from the ipods docking port) Third get a amp with enough power to operate in this mode. If you want to go portable you don't want any of the FiiO portable amps they are under powered or marginal in the better cases such as the highly touted FiiO E7.  My sugestion - buy one of the CMOY amps, these come in all kinds of cases or not in cases at all. You need to find somebody who packages the excellent CMOY amp in what you think is a nice case, I use the CMOY amp by Zigis audio lab, you will find Zigis on ebay under CMOY amp, I like the black plastic case version with 9v battery, gold metal face and blue led power light. I paid $48 plus $9.95 shipping. The CMOY amp will sound better and have more power than other portables. I am not associated with Zigis.  You can find manyplaces to buy the CMOY amp in many different packages. As far as I know they all have the same guts. So shop around and find what you like.  Now you know, if you decide to take your audio signal from the ipod dock port like this product does it will make your low powered portable amp happy but be sure to keep your ipod battery charger handy. There is a better way.

I installed my JBL MS Bass Pro in my 2006 Acura TSX with its factory stereo. After I installed it I noticed bass started coming out of the sub and the car was not even on. I had to turn the volume on the sub all the way down to stop the humming. I called JBL but they do not know what the problem is and they stated the sub should not give any sound if the car is off and the keys are out of the ignition. Once the car is started I can turn the gain up all the way and I do not have the loud humming or bass tone coming from the sub. I do not want to ship the unit back but that is what JBL recommends I do and they will send a brand new one. Putting this problem aside I was surprised at how loud this little thing is. The sound is pretty impressive for something this small. However do not expect this thing to hit 20Hz like it states in the specs for frequency response. I have a bass CD with test tracks and the lowest frequency I was able to get out of this thing was 30Hz. The problem with it being so small is that it rolls around in the trunk very easily. Since I have had it my trunk I have to drive very slow around turns so it does not roll around too much. The good thing is this little sub is very loud for its size and looks very nice and clean. JBL did a good job making this thing look nice. Installation was easy as well. I ran an 8 gauge power wire from my battery to the trunk and an 8 gauge ground wire to an existing ground point on the vehicles chassis. Also pay attention to the price on amazon because it does jump up and down. I got my Bass Pro about a month ago from amazon and it costs $409.00 at that time. I just wish it would hit 20Hz and JBL supplied something to strap it down. I will try to create another ground point in the car and see if this resolves my issue with the loud feedback I am getting from the sub. If I did not have this issue I would easily give this product 4 stars but it is a pain in the ass to start my car then go to my trunk and turn up the gain every time I want bass.

I'm thankful I bought this product at Costco, because I could take it back for a full refund. The idea is appealing, and a good deal - you get a lot for a good price. But on closer inspection, there are a couple of significant problems:

1. The contents are redundant.
- Cassette adapter gives better sound than FM transmitter in many cases. If you have a car with a cassette player, you wouldn't need the FM transmitter. If your car doesn't have a cassette player, why would you buy a package with a cassette adapter in it?
- Similarly, at home, you'd get better sound on your stereo by using the cables vs the FM transmitter, even if you do have a tuner.
So unless you plan on using your ipod in a car with a cassette player, a car without a cassette player, and with your home stereo system, having cables, a cassette adapter and the FM transmitter is redundant. You may come out cheaper by buying the components you need separately.

2. The case is TERRIBLE! Honestly, if the case had been good, I would've overlooked the redundancy and likely kept the entire package. But the case was a key component for me. The case in this package covers the iPod on the front, back, sides, and bottom. Since the belt clip swivels, to prevent the iPod from falling out of the top, the case has a suction cup (no joke!) on the inside of the back panel. The case opens up in a flip-down style by un-velcro-ing the side panels. You nest your iPod into the case, sticking it to the suction cup, flip the front of the case into postion, and stick the side velcro strips together. Between the case itself, the suction cup, and the bulky belt clip, the iPod is more than twice as thick in the case as it is alone. It's also significantly wider.

My advice - keep shopping.

First, and most important, it is *not* really HD. Fine, they can say \\"1080p HD\\" due to the size of the picture, but nobody looking at this would consider it to be high definition. Why? Because the camera's recording rate (data rate) -- even on the highest speed SD cards -- is quite slow, measuring in at only about 8kbps. That, if there is any motion whatsoever, results in a grainy, pixelated picture. And this data rate is with the \\"highest\\" resolution and image quality selected in settings.

If you bought a television advertised as \\"HD\\" and got a picture similar to what the BlackVue dash cam produces, you would surely return it immediately. You'd also likely be annoyed that whoever sold it to you wasted your time by claiming it was \\"HD\\" based on a technicality when the actual display is anything but.

Despite what BlackVue seems to want you to believe, you CANNOT read license plates on vehicles unless you are FULLY STOPPED, and the other vehicle is directly in front of you. If you're moving and a car side-swipes you and drives off, their license plate is guaranteed to be a useless blur based on my experience. If you witness a hit and run, my guess is the BlackVue cam will be of NO HELP in identifying the suspect vehicle's license plate.

Quite simply put, the picture quality is what you would expect from a very cheap camera. Even most smart phones take better video than this.

For some reason, it accepts only 8, so if you think you're configuring it with a 9 or 10 character password and then try to use that password to connect, it will fail. Type just the first 8 characters of the password you want.

I kept this camera too long, hoping the company would release firmware to make the picture clearer, and they did eventually bump it up a bit, but it's still far too low for being able to use it for much more than entertainment or a conversation piece. The metal strips (tangs) that plug into the wall socket have no strain relief on the interior of the white housing.  After a couple of insertion/removal cycles into the AC outlets, one of the tangs pulled out of the housing rendering the device unusable.  Upon inspection of the interior, it was observed that the rear of the tang was cold soldered to the wire that connected to the PCB.  While I may be able to grind the surface of the tang to obtain a suitable surface on which I may re-solder the wire, I may just chose to wire a replacement AC cord directly to the PCB, preventing a repeat failure.    Good news is that the PCB is still functional even if the housing is not.    Caveat Emptor

I didn't buy this from Amazon, but feel the need to warn others. This looks like a very fun thing to have if you have an older car stereo with only a cassette player, and you don't have any other MP3 player (such as a smartphone) that can simply be "adapted" into the cassette. I realize, this is almost no one nowadays, but I'm one of them :-\  This product has two considerable design flaws which, if they didn't BOTH exist, wouldn't be that big a deal, but together are DEVASTATING to the usefulness of the thing. The first flaw is that it does not have a shuffle play mode, like most small, cheap players with a very limited UI. Rather, it simply plays the MP3 files from the beginning (in the order they were copied onto the memory card) until the end of what's there, and then loops back to the beginning again. OK, maybe you can live with that.  However, it also does NOT remember where you left off listening when you power it off! In other words, each time you power it off and back on (to save the battery, naturally), it starts playing from the beginning of the memory card again! So..... you're always hearing the same music over and over again. Uh, I guess you can FF (click through) the songs you've heard, each time, but imagine you've loaded 7 hours of music onto the card. You'll basically NEVER hear the music copied onto the card towards the end.  One gets the impression that someone came up with the idea for this thing (as I did, myself, and then went looking for it, and found this), designed it on paper, said "cool!", and went straight to production without actually building a prototype and trying it out. Of course, the way people are these days, it also wouldn't surprise me if the designers recognized the problems I've described, perhaps too late, but manufactured it as-is, because to fix the flaws would have been too expensive or troublesome :-( It comes with a car charging adapter, and I thought, "ok, I'll just leave it plugged in and chargingwhile it plays, which should alleviate the problem somewhat", but of course the USB cable sticking out prevents the thing from being fully loaded into the tape deck, and it just gets auto-ejected right away. One more thing: the manual claims that using the REW/FF functions on your cassette deck will skip ahead/back in your playlist, but this did not work for me. At least they had the foresight to include a remote control with it.  Heck, it's still fairly useful as a USB SD card reader :-) Imagine if they had actually given a crap and wanted to make a superb product.... they could even have engineered it so that the inevitable spinning of the cassette deck spindles recharged the battery! Fat chance. Well, you've been warned.

Bought this waterproof MP3 player to replace another more expensive one which had headphones that just kept dying due to corrosion of the wires in the plug (upon taking it apart for further examination, found sketchy molding process/QC). Since it uses a smaller size than the standard headset plug, you pretty much are limited to the factory replacements and that was getting expensive given their short lifespan.
After using the QQ-Tech waterproof MP3 player for a few surf sessions this is what I found:
The sound is pretty decent through the included headset and the cable length is just about right for my needs. It does take some fiddling to make them fit comfortably although they will lose their seal on occasion. The radio is much better than expected. Good reception, unlike the other MP3 player both on land and out at my local surf spot. The display set on maximum brightness could be seen even in broad daylight which made selecting tracks or radio stations much easier during lulls between sets.
This product is definitely not user-friendly - the instructions are somewhat helpful, but the best way to learn is to just try all of the buttons until you get the hang of it. However, two shortcomings prevent me from recommending this MP3 player to others, especially if it will see use in water. The first one being a selectable \\"random play\\" mode in the menu which only plays the same number of songs (around 10 or so that the player chose - at random?) and that is a bummer. I do not like listening to my music in a set list, much less being limited to hearing the same songs during a surf session. The second, and perhaps biggest flaw I discovered was evidence of water intrusion in the headset jack and plug after rinsing the unit off and drying it with a towel. Not good. One would think something designed to be waterproof would have something like a gasket or o-ring seal in that area. The other MP3 player I have actually has a screw-on plug with a rubber gasket which works great at keeping the water out of the unit. Though the QQ-Tech MP3 player is still working and there does not appear to be signs of more serious water intrusion in it - yet (condensation in the display screen). It gives me doubts about the long term reliability of the player. The search for a good waterproof MP3 player that is not a modified i***d shuffle continues...

This is major cheap - if it works for you, great, but you need to know:

1. The power source is a linear regulator - this means that the difference in voltage (between your car's 12V and the 5V USB plug) gets turned to heat. If you're using a lot of power, say, an iPhone or Android, it's enough heat to temporarily burn-out the display and ultimately melt the plastic. Even a fancy music player like a Zune can be too much for this thing.

2. The radio transmitter works, and surprisingly well for something this cheap. I suppose it depends on the relationship between the cigarette lighter and the antenna - it's not enough for me. Sometimes the signal is great, sometimes I end up fiddling with stations when I really should be driving.

3. I've never succeeded at having it read a USB mass storage device and I'm not sure what formats it supports (haven't tried them). The headphone jack works correctly, but be careful about touching the connector after unplugging it - I burned my hand (see #1).

Although, given the price, it might be worth the risk - I can see this working just fine for some people. Good luck with it!

In order to fix it, I had to drill a tiny hole in the center and insert a little screw to make the spring-loaded center contact about 3mm longer.  Now the device works well, I may even file a patent for my invention and charge the manufacturer a royalty fee.  If you want something that works in all cars, look for another device, unless the manufacturer fixes their defective design.

I parked my vehicle outside today (4/20/2013) in 90 F heat in order to see if the BlackVue would stand up to high temperatures. The peak outside temperature probably wasn't reached, so I'll do further tests when I can leave the vehicle outside in the sun for a longer period of time.

When I took the BlackVue out of my vehicle it was too hot to hold for more than a few seconds without having to switch hands. The micro SDHC card seems to have recorded continuously without fault for the 3 hours I left the vehicle outside. Temperature of the BlackVue at night (60 F or less) I would characterize as being \\"hot\\" not \\"warm\\".

Daytime video quality is very good. Nighttime video quality is OK. Sound recording is OK (slight hiss).

One of the reasons I chose to buy the BlackVue was the wi-fi functionality. Some of the permissions you must accept in order to download the wi-fi-access app to your smartphone or tablet include:

1.) Directly call phone numbers
Allows the app to call phone numbers without your intervention. This may result in unexpected charges or calls. Note that this doesn't allow the app to call emergency numbers. Malicious apps may cost you money by making calls without your confirmation.

2.) Modify or delete the contents of your USB storage modify or delete the contents of your SD card
Allows the app to write to the USB storage. Allows the app to write to the SD card.

3.) Add or remove accounts
Allows the app to perform operations like adding and removing accounts, and deleting their password.

Number 1.) falls into the category of \\"WTF?\\"
Number 2.) is reasonable assuming it's limited to YOU directing the software to doing the modification, deletions, and SD card writes (other than the recording and write-over permissions the BlackVue unit needs to do)
Number 3.) another \\"WTF?\\" permission

So, essentially, one of the primary reasons I chose the BlackVue is rendered useless since I won't accept the Draconian permissions required by the wi-fi app.

UPDATE: 4/22/2013--Apparent GPS-chip failure.

I noted that for my parked-in-the-sun test of 4/20/2013 that the BlackVue had recorded the correct number of video files for the for the 3 hours that I left my vehicle outside.

Initially I didn't look at all of the files for the test, only the first few and the last one. There was something in the video clips that I didn't notice at the time, but after I looked at some video clips recorded early today (4/22/2013) I saw that while driving down the road the MPH indication was \\"---\\" and the GPS-signal icon, in the viewing software, was red. There was plenty of time for the GPS unit to have obtained a satellite lock.

It was because of the \\"---MPH\\" display that I decided to reexamine my parked-in-the-sun-test video clips. I found that the first few video clips correctly showed \\"000MPH\\" (although there were some anomalous readings of \\"005MPH\\", etc.). At approximately 1 hour and 20 minutes into the test the \\"000MPH\\" had become \\"---MPH\\".

Perhaps I got a bad unit. It was working OK prior to my parked-in-the-sun test. I suspect it may be heat-failure related, but I don't have a way to determine if that's true, being mindful of \\"post hoc, ergo propter hoc\\".

Anyway, I'm going to return it. Instead of getting a replacement just now, I'll wait a while to see if others report similar failures. If there aren't reports of bad GPS units I'll probably reorder, in spite of the fact that I won't be using the wi-fi app.

I hope others will do parked-in-the-sun tests too and report the results. It's good to know if the BlackVue (which runs hot--at least mine did) will stand up to closed-vehicle summertime temperatures (a lot of 90-95 F with the occasional 110 F, or so, where I live).

UPDATE: 4/22/2013--later in the day: apparent BlackVue failure.

With my vehicle in the garage at ambient air temperature of 91 F (about 80 F outside, for what it's worth) I plugged the BlackVue in--time 1:58pm. At 2:53pm I stopped the BlackVue and took the micro SDHC card to be read on my computer. The micro SDHC card contained 4 files; the first 3 files were 3 minutes in length, the 4th file had 51 seconds of video. The BlackVue had been plugged in for nearly an hour but recorded only 9 minutes and 51 seconds of video (I'd occasionally walk in front of the vehicle and give it a shake).

The blue wi-fi light was working when I powered-down the unit to retrieve the micro SDHC card. In the video files the speed indicator read \\"---MPH\\" and the GPS-signal icon was red. The chrome-plated annulus around the lens was quite hot to the touch.

I've previously bought Cambridge SoundWorks products, and have always been happy. Not this time. When the Oontz works, it produces quite good sound for such a small speaker. But, they seem to have major quality control problems.

I have bought and returned two Oontz now. The problem: the ability to play music through the AuxIn port is extremely unreliable. The instructions on how to do this (Turn unit on. Push source button once) unequivocally DO NOT work. After a lot of fiddling, I figured out how to (sometimes) make it work: Turn unit on. Hold down source button for 3 seconds to initiate bluetooth pairing (even though I don't want to use bluetooth). Wait a few seconds while LED flashes red & blue. Press & hold source button down for about 1 second, and wait for LED to start flashing blue only (you may have to repeat this step a few times). Then, hit play on your music device.

However, even after going through the extra steps, the Oontz will only play music for around 10-60 minutes (even when powered) before it abruptly cuts out. Once it cuts out, you seem to have to let it "cool down" for an hour or two before it will work at all.

All of these behaviors were the same on both Oontz that I've had. It's really disappointing that they were so successful at the "hard" part -- making good sound come out of a small speaker -- but they apparently aren't willing to spend a few more dollars on the easy stuff, like the basic electronics. I would have happily paid $10 or $20 more for a reliable, easy-to-use unit.

I don't typically write reviews, but have to say something about this deck.  I have this deck in the mini-van for about 8 months and I finally made the call to get it replaced.  Here are some of the problems we have with it:  1. The time sets itself and is rarely correct.  Usually it is off by an hour.  Sometimes it is off by an hour and 20 or 30 minutes.  It's possible to drive for 15 miles with the time being correct on the onset, incorrect by an hour plus within a few miles, and back to the correct time when arriving at the destination.  It could be wrong for days or it might be correct for days.  If you get this deck, buy a watch too.  2. The navigation system takes a long time to enter an address.  With most navigation systems, if you want to find an address that is close, you can just put the street number and name.  With this thing, you have to start with the country, then state, then city, and it narrows as you go.  So it is never quick to enter an address.  3. Using the bluetooth for calls makes it sound like you are in the back of a long deep cave.    4. We have 2 displays, the in-dash and rear display.  It's impossible to have the navigation directions on the in-dash while a movie is playing on the rear display.  5. It's not intuitive to switch between navigation and DVD play.  After 8 months, I still can't make the switch while driving.  You might think I'm technically challenged, but I'm a computer programmer.  6. The straw that broke the camel's back was the LCD tray not ejecting properly.  At present, the tray starts clicking when coming out of the deck.  It gets about an inch out stops while making a clicking noise.  It sounds like some plastic gears are grinding and it will only proceed if we pull the deck and help it along.  It has some really cool features, but the User Interface is pretty bad and the features don't all work very well.  Some of the high end features I have enjoyed include the USB port on the front and the ability to play music viabluetooth.  It's still under warranty, so we'll just return it and get another deck.  No more Eonon decks for this family.

This is a very cheap unit and no one should be surprised at the price point this unit is offered. It does what it says it will do using the free software Audacity.  Here are the surprises I ran into:  1) Cheap, cheap, cheap! All plastic. I would not at all expect this unit to get me through my 200+ cassette tapes.  2) Cassette tape does move while the pinch rollers revolve therefore the quality of sound is unpredictable. Just picking the unit up while it is playing will cause the music to \\"stretch and twang\\".  Tried playing the unit without the lid on (lid down was applying too much pressure on the cassette and altered the sound greatly) but that caused a great deal of loss of contact with the play-head so volume dropped considerably.  3) The mini-CD contains an old version of Audacity.  Just go to [...] to download the appropriate file. Be careful where you download from.  Some of the audacity files from third and fourth parties may have ads or malware added.  I found the zip file straight from the audacity website to be the easiest to use install Audacity on my PC.  4) Be sure to download the more comprehensive manual from the Audacity website.  It tells you not just \\"what\\" is in Audacity but equally important is \\"how\\" the process works to get the best conversion.  5)Surprise! Can only record one side of each cassette.  6) Next surprise, must download a codec (dll) file from Audacity so that the Audacity file format can be converted to mp3.  7) Before converting there are listening styles (similar to equalizer) settings in Audacity that you can use that will be applied to the entire file (can be one song, two songs, or the entire one side of a cassette.  8) You can listen to the cassette while it is playing and being recorded by the PC, but watch to make sure that Audacity software is selected so that it is playing stereo and not the default mono.  9) Lots and lots of white noise is produced. Deal breaker right there for me, as if that hasn't already happened by this point.  10) This process is slow - slow - slow and labor intensive! Not for the working man or woman.  11) No useful troubleshooting help in anything that comes in the product manual.  I had to change my settings in my PC sound drivers in order to get stereo recordings on Audacity and to be able to hear the cassette recording on my computer speakers.  E-gads, not what I expected!  I just had to play around with those PC setting (not Audacity settings0    Note: Possibly using a stereo patch cord from the stereo headphone output jack of a quality non-USB (maybe that old cassette deck you still have hanging around?) then port the cassette player deck from headset to the sound card input of the PC would produce as good, if not better results.    A quality deck with a USB output probably would be preferable.  However still not finding what I'm looking for.  I am looking for is:    1) A solid (not necessarily \\"tricked-out\\") USB output cassette deck.  2) Similar to the software in a digial camera for the fully automatic option for being able to simply insert the cassette and pushing play and a quality recording at the PC is created with a Wizard for minimizing white noise while minimizing depreciation or distortion of the music or voice content of the cassette.  3)For those wanting to use equalizing settings, that option needs to be included as it is in Audacity.  4) Cassette detection for chrome tape or Dolby or any other special tapes or technology are detected and sound is balanced accordingly.  5) Cassette deck auto switches to side B so that the entire album is recorded with each song segregated as a separate recording automatically.  6) Software would have ability to search Internet libraries upon user-entered album titles for song titles and other information so that setting up the tags can be automated.    The point is to be able to pop a tape into the deck, hit play on the tape deck and press record on the PC software so that I can set it up then be able to forget it and come back after the recording has completed and find the songs in mp3 format in the music folder title with the album's name or artist name or whatever option I have chosen.  This way I could pop in a cassette on my way out the door to work in the morning and another before I go to bed for the night and in 100 days I'd have 200 cassettes recorded, titled, labeled and heck even album cover completed. Please feel free to build on these specs.  Hope this helps to see the huge delta between what is available out there on the market (which is a lot of these walkman type units vs. what most of us want in order to preserve our libraries of cassettes.  I do not understand why no one is doing this as it's not new technology even the application has been around for several years now.  The economics are there too, it would not be expensive to take a current design and either smart it up or dumb it down to accomplish this cassette to mp3 conversion with quality and under $100 for everything needed to accomplish the above.

After having a similar 4 gb coby flash drive/player for 2 years, i figured that another cheap flash player is the way to go. Unfortunately, this was not at all worth the 10 dollars (and 2 dollar shipping) that it costs.    On the actual player interface, every function is slow. select the next track, and you'll have to wait for up to 5 seconds for it to begin playing. And the transition from one track to another? rather than just playing the track, the player fades out of one and fades in to the next, a process which will shave the first few seconds off of every track. This is especially annoying if every track you have doesn't begin with a few seconds of unimportant ambient intro.     And Sound Quality! I have never before heard a player that so thoroughly neuters your audio! In the past, I had attributed audio quality and fullness to the original mp3 attributes, and the quality of the headphones used. For that reason, I encode all my music files at a minimum of 320, and use quite high quality headphones.     Alas, this player totally destroys the sound quality of your files. Either there is a low-end roll off that begins around 0hz, or the player just refuses to reproduce those tones. This is somewhat manageable when you plug the player in to another system that has its own eq, like a car stereo. At least then you can bump the low end up to make up for it. But if you just listen with headphones, audio will sound incredibly tinny, thin, and weak. Even going through the handfull of pre-set eq options, with the most 'bass heavy' selected, you will find incredibly weak sound.     Forget listening to modern electronic music, drum and bass, dubstep, footwork, or uk funky - the experience will leave you incredibly disappointed.    AVOID THIS MP3 PLAYER - spend twice as much, and get the similar looking, but far far superior coby flash player. With this player, you literally get what you pay for.

I don't know if the mount would work if the clips were longer and extended past the end of the vent louvers (with or without end hooks), but it's a moot point because it's not built that way and in my car the clips themselves do not exert enough pressure on the louvers to hold the mount in with the GPS attached.

The GPS sits higher and is much easier to see in my peripheral vision while driving than when it's down lower on the Mini's center vent.

Other comments here say it works fine on other cars, and when that's the case without falling out, I'm certain it's quite satisfactory, and it will lock the Nuvi GPS at essentially any normal viewing angle with the twist wheel you can see just in back of the ball which fits into the Nuvi GPS unit, and the unit is also independently adjustable on the ball itself.

Despite this item being clearly described as containing chargers for \\"Barnes Noble Nook Color, Nook Tablet\\" it DOES NOT CHARGE a Nook Tablet. It has the wrong physical and electrical specs. The Nook Tablet uses a modified micro-usb that is longer than the standard one, with extra electrical connections. In addition, the real Nook Tablet charger is rated for 1.9A while the charger here is a standard micro-usb and is only rated at 700ma. When you plug it in the device clearly indicates that the battery is \\"not charging\\".

While it may be possible to charge it over a few days with a standard usb charging, it is NOT a charger designed for the Nook Tablet. I don't have a Nook Color, but I believe it's the same story there.

The description is completely misleading and should be changed or just taken off the market. I plan to return it at my earliest convenience.

UPDATE: Wanted to give an update. We were contacted by their customer service, and they were very helpful and pleasant. They sent us a second charger that they believed would work, but it still had the same problem, when you plug it in the Nook clearly says \\"Not Charging\\". I can't give full stars based on that, but to their credit, it does seem that if the screen is off the Nook tablet can slowly charge (e.g. overnight). If you're using the Nook when it's plugged into a normal usb (which this is) then it's still likely to use more power than the usb supplies. Nevertheless, it is not equivalent to the actual BN Nook Tablet charger, and not really a substitute.

However, based on the response from Bluemall I would be happy to do business with them again for other products. They were very pleasant and did their best to satisfy us.

We recently decided to drop our landline and go all cellular.  I purchased one of these XLink units and a new cell phone from Verizon to go with it (it's a Samsung Convoy and supports all of the latest bluetooth profiles).  This phone is dedicated to the unit, meaning that the cell phone sits next to the XLink and never moves.  The XLink then connects to our 5.8Ghz base station, which services six wireless extensions.  The phone, the base station, and XLink are all on top of the same table.     Pairing up the cell phone to the XLink could not be easier.  It was also easy to connect the XLink to my computer to download the latest software update.  Then things went downhill.  As we used the system over a period of a week or so, we ran into two major problems.    1. The sound quality was considerably worse than our landline. There was no static, so I don't believe it was an interference issue.  Rather, the sound was very much like a speaker phone. When a person was not talking, the line sounded dead, but when they spoke, the first word of their sentences would be clipped. Conversations were not duplex--two people could not talk at the same time or overlap in their speech. Again, just like a speakerphone.  The overall sound quality was a bit distorted too--like the gain on an amplifier being turned up too high.  Anyway, I contacted XLink support about this and they said that this is basically typical of a bluetooth connection and there is nothing that could be done about it.  Strike one.    2. In addition to this problem, I had repeated connection problems.  This happened three times before I finally decided enough was enough. After two days of being connected, like clockwork, the phone would get into a kind of weird funk.  The blue light indicating a valid bluetooth connection remained lit, and you could both receive and place calls, but you could neither hear nor speak to the other caller.  It was like the phone was fully muted.  The only way to fix the problem was tounplug the XLink and re-pair.  XLink support suggested that I download the latest software, but I had already done that.  After three instances of this along with the first problem, I was starting to wonder if I had made a mistake in disconnecting the land line.  Strike two.    Being rather frustrated, I re-read some of the reviews here, and based on a hint from one of the reviewers, I went down to BestBuy and picked up a vtech DS6321-3 system just to try someone else's technology (Amazon also sells this).  This unit has a bluetooth compatible base station and three extension phones for just $89--only $10 more than the XLink.   I brought it home and was immediately amazed at the sound quality.  It was night and day over the XLink. Almost indistinguishable from the landline--and full duplex too.  No clipping or distortion.  I have not had any weird connection issues with it either.  It just works.  You also get full bluetooth integration with the vtech, such as the ability to download your phonebook to the handsets and notification of voicemail. I will need to buy a few extra handsets at $18 a pop to fully replace my old system, but the difference in quality is well worth it.  Strike three.  The XLink is on its way back.

Unfortunately the leather lining the polycarbonate edges on the bottom of the case began to fall off within 4 months of moderate use. Then as the pieces of leather fell apart, the rest of the case started to disintegrate. The one sturdy piece was the leather top cover with the aluminum backing which covered the iPod's touchscreen. Then the back leather cover tore off after the pieces of the leather lining were falling off. The iPod remained well-protected in spite of the disintegrating case, but the case looked horrible-- like a derelict property.    Proporta has a lifetime warranty for its products. As an ER doctor constantly on the move, the iPod Touch fell out of my scrub top's front pocket while I was on duty, and sadly I've lost my iPod Touch to either the hospital's trash compactor or else to another scarier, unknown fate.    Overall, the Alu-leather case for the iPod Touch 2G/3G would have been a 4.5 star product due to its beautiful looks, the sturdy and attractive leather-aluminum top cover. I listen to a lot of audio books so I suppose the RCA Lyra RD2850A 20G HDD mp3pro Player seemed like a great Christmas present for me. And I have to admit that having an mp3 player with more capacity than my PC's old D: drive was a bit of a kick. The unit is pretty large so it doesn't hide unobtrusively in my jeans pocket like my old Creative MuVo did, but that's ok, I'll clip it to my waistband and hope it stays there.
As an engineer, I don't usually RTFM. I didn't. The Lyra has a USB I/F and a FAT file system, so Windows 2000 automagically recognizes it as a Removable Disk. I proceeded to drag and drop 20G of audio books into it, almost 1500 files, into the directory called \MUSIC\. That's a lot of audio since I listen mostly to low bit rate lectures. Impressive!
A little bit of random button-pushing got the device to profile the contents. This took a while to complete, but that's fine, consider it part of the initial setup. After that, some more random button-pushing (a million monkeys, eh?) got some mp3s to play, and even captured my favorite radio show as an mp3. Nice. It was all a bit jumbled in there, though, and sorting by Artist or Artist/Album or even by track title didn't make it possible to locate a 12 lecture series, much less pick out and listen to the 6th lecture. Hmmm, seems the tags are messed up, I'll have to fix that. Ok, let's install the software and get serious.
Well, that's where the fun began. The Lyra comes with an application called Lyra DJ. Lyra DJ has a simple user interface - a big orange button labeled \\"Analyze Device\\" and a little gray button labeled \\"0 Sets\\".
\\"The main advantage of a simple user interface is that it prevents the user from actually doing anything.\\" -- banth
Push the button and voila'! Wait several hours for it to analyze the device. The analysis failed several times. Ok, I'm a trained professional. I can handle it. I deleted most of my audio - a mistake, I realized, but that's what happens when you're wrestling with new hardware at 2AM. This time the analysis actually completed. In retrospect, if I had moved the files out of the \MUSIC\ file tree I would have saved myself a lot of hassle.
I decided to continue at work, and this is where I realized that having a separate USB cable with a non-standard plug is a disadvantage. My old Creative MuVo plugged right into the USB port so I didn't have to worry about forgetting the cable.
Back at home again I ran the analysis and pushed Lyra DJs little grey button. It only took a minute or so to create 15 LDJ sets. The device itself calls these playlists. Very kewl, *now* I can listen to some audio books... what the....???
According to the blurb, Lyra DJ uses \\"advanced acoustical analysis\\" to \\"create sets of related content\\". I'm sure it does, but my tiny engineering mind wasn't able to discern the relationships between the items in the plain vanilla .m3u text-based playlists created by Lyra DJ. I suspect that if you listen to music and in no particular order, this won't be an issue.
I won't bother you with the irritating misspellings on the Lyra DJ app. Most engineers can't spell anyway.
I briefly considered editing the playlists manually, but as I juggled several open files cutting and pasting I realized that I just don't have time to futz with it, especially if I want to load another 18G of audio. I was going to have to use another app to generate playlists.
I also considered modifying the ID tags to enable the RCA Lyra itself to present them in a logical manner. I don't &$^$ think so.
The RCA Lyra also comes bundled with MusicMatch software. Throw the installation CD away. Save yourself some trouble and use something already installed on your computer to create playlists. I settled on WinAmp. So here's how to do it:
Arrange your audio files in a neat, structured manner as subdirectories in the RCA Lyra \MUSIC\ directory.
In WinAmp, create a new playlist.
Also in WinAmp, Add a folder from your RCA Lyra directory structure to the playlist. Make sure the files are sorted correctly in WinAmp - if ID tags are messed up the playlist will be scrambled.
Still in WinAmp, Save the playlist to the RCA Lyra \lyra_playlists\ directory.
From the RCA Lyra menu system, profile the device.
It's important to save the playlist to the RCA Lyra so that the .m3u file has the correct paths.
Simple, eh?
I'm failing to see the benefit of carrying 20G of audio files when a 512M Creative MuVo carries an entire work day of audio.
But that's ok, the RCA Lyra RD2850A 20G HDD mp3pro Player is a serious Guy Magnet.

It has the usual play-all/repeat-one/shuffle-play options. You can skip to the previous / next song, but there is no fast-forward / reverse within the same track. It remembers the track it was playing when power is shut off, and will automatically restart at the beginning of that track when power is restored. At first blush, the Pioneer DEH-6300UB has all the right features and a reasonable price.  I bought the Pioneer unit to upgrade a factory unit in a 2002 Toyota Celica, a car which features an orange-backlit instrument cluster.  Since most aftermarket stereos like to blast the user with shades of blue and white, the adjustable color option sold this unit over several otherwise-equal competitors.  I obtained a factory wiring harness to minimize the damage and tangle in the dash, and went to work.  Before long I had a working MP3 head unit...or so I thought.    Unfortunately, it wasn't quite that simple.  Granted, some things do work well -- the remote, for example, is not just a gimmick, it offers fast access to some sub-menus and settings that otherwise require tedious button pressing and scrolling on the head unit.  The CD player is also very quick to pick up a track, and avoids skipping over all but the worst possible potholes.  The detachable front face feels a bit cheap, but not unreasonably so for this price range, and has a reasonably clean and uncluttered layout.  So what's not to like?    First, the backlighting is appropriate for daytime, but far too bright at night.  The darkest available shades of orange and red still shine brighter than the instrument panel.  The keypad and LCD can be separately changed to any of three dozen different hues, yet nobody in R&D though to add a high/low brightness control?  Worse, the polarization on the LCD display is oriented such that an ordinary pair of polarized sunglasses almost completely blacks it out during the daytime, unless you rotate your head.  Part of the Celica's IP is LCD, yet doesn't have this problem -- you have to rotate your head to black it out, which is how things should be in hardware that was expressly designed for use in a car.    Second, the USB has some quirks.  I had no problems loading up a couple 8GB thumb drives and playing them through the head unit, but then something funny occurred: I pulleda drive to add and remove a few files and folders, and on next access, the head unit failed to fully re-scan and re-sort the drive.  Instead, it appended the new file structures at the end of the index.  The scrambling will persist until the head unit is either fully disconnected from power, or the drive is wiped and inserted into the head unit, which seems to clear the index.  Pull the USB stick while it is playing, and instead of switching over to next source, the head unit shuts off; eject a CD, and the unit will switch over to the next input source as expected.  Huh?    Third, I can't get the high pitched squeal out of this thing.  Noisy power and ground wires are common in modern vehicles, but so far I've tried a couple different noise isolators on the power wiring, I've tried a ground-loop isolator on the preamp outputs, I've tried reworking the grounds in several different configurations (including bypassing the harness and going direct to chassis), and I've tried disconnecting the sub entirely from the head unit, leaving only the new head unit and the factory amp and speakers.  It just won't quit.  Usually this is indicative of some shortcuts taken in the head unit's power supply filtering, and I'm at a loss what to do next.  The factory radio and CD player had no such issues.    In short, this unit may work for some applications but it sure isn't working for mine.  Everything is *almost* right with it, but then the bugs start showing up in ways that indicate the design was never properly field tested.  It still gets three stars for price and features, but my suggestion would be: keep your receipt in a safe place, as you may need it.

What we DO like about it is that it does NOT have back-lit screen, which is easy on the eyes. (My 8-year-old reads lots of books on this, so that's important for us. No \\"glazy, red video eyes\\" after staring at this thing for long periods of time.)  It can be read exactly like a REAL book: Anywhere you have daylight or a light, you can read it. It's size is also nice (big screen but small footprint,)  It's great, too, that you can download free books off the internet (I use Gutenberg.org exclusively.) As long as you choose the .txt files, it's quick and easy to get material onto the JetBook. We need nothing fancy (don't even WANT internet capabilities with it since our kids use it,) so the simplicity of the JetBook suits us fine.    We also LOVE all the classic books that come pre-loaded when we bought it new. My son uses a literature-based curriculum for school, so many of the books he needs to read were already on this (White Fang, The Jungle Book, Moby Dick, Shakespeare stuff, Mark Twain stuff, etc. etc. etc.)    What I DON'T like about our JetBook -- and from what I've read we're not alone in this -- is that it will freeze often and need to be reset. It also has frozen before on me and I couldn't even reset it; it just stayed frozen on until I think the battery just died down. Looking at Ectaco's website, I kinda wonder if they care very much about this product? It's never advertised -- and they do much more with language translating type units and software. Perhaps this was just a little side-project for them? In any case, if they don't fix the stability of the JetBook, no one's gonna want to buy it.

I purchased this product with the two add-on solar panels, bringing the total number of panels to four (inclusive of the one on the main unit). Unfortunately, the panel connector part arrived broken (seems to be a common problem). I was able to use a twist-tie to \\"fix\\" it, so I thought I'd give it a shot. I followed instructions and let the unit charge via USB power prior to first use (I did this several times even though the manual said to do it once--as I saw comments here before I ordered saying that it's better to charge/discharge via USB 4 to 6 times prior to placing in the sun). Using this method, I was able to fully charge my HTC One smartphone twice on this charge level. So far so good.

With the unit drained after 5 charges/discharge cycles on USB power, I then tried charging it in the sun. I have a large, sunny backyard so I thought this would work well. However, even after a full day in the sun WITH the add-on solar panels, I couldn't get the unit above 50% charge. I thought it might be a fluke so I left it out all day in direct sun the following day. Still the unit wouldn't charge above 50%. Finally at the end of the third day it showed 3/4 full, so I decided to see what I could get out of it. To my disappointment, I was only able to get my HTC One charged 75% of the way before the unit showed no power. This doesn't make sense since I was able to get two full charges by USB with 4 bars showing, whereas I only got 3/4s of a charge with 3 bars showing.

Worse, after a few more days the charge capacity grew less and less--I wasn't even able to get it above 50% under any length of time in the sun. I thought I could still live with it but then the unit's flashlight began turning on by itself. I'm now no longer able to turn the flashlight off, so whatever power I'm receiving is immediately being wasted. Time for a return.

Hopefully I'll have a good return experience. If so, I'll append this review.

----Update----

The seller, Accessory Genie, shipped a replacement panel connector part for free. That did the trick. Apparently the poor charging issues and the inability to turn off the main unit's flashlight were all connected to the damaged panel connector. While I appreciate their honest and excellent customer service, I still don't feel that the product deserves more than 3 stars since it is very fragile and doesn't charge anywhere near as rapidly as promised. However, it is adequate for its purpose and if used carefully it may yet prove to be a fair source of backup power to charge one's phone or ipod when no other power is available.

You never know what can happen while driving your car, so having a video recorder can be a handy device to capture any event while behind the wheel.

The Dostech HD 720P Dash Cam is an affordable entry level car dash camera that provides a simple recording method.

It comes with a car Charger, a mount (suction cup), a USB cable which connects to your computer to transfer the video, and a remote control.

Some nice features include a rotating camera (340 degrees) which can capture the road ahead, the sky, or yourself driving. The video is nice and clear during the day and can be powered on automatically when the car starts and powered off when the car is turned off. To record you will need a TF card (not included) and supports up to 32gb.

This device does have some room for improvement. The box mentions some form of night vision but it does not really perform well at all in the dark, unless something is lit up. Also the mic for sound is subpar. The camera seems to only record at 720p/30 FPS in AVI format.

To sum-up I would say this dash-cam video recorder is for someone who is interested in recording strictly video in their car at an affordable price. It's a simple piece. This could be handy for a parent who wants to be able to see their children in the back or just wants an additional level of safety or insurance while behind the wheel. This could also be handy if you are on a trip or driving and would like to record the surroundings or scenery.

For these reasons I give this product ★★★ out of 5.
