UPDATE 1/21/06: One thing I have noticed since my original review is that if you set it to play random songs in a particular folder, it will play through every song in the folder ONCE, and then it starts playing random songs on the entire disc. This is highly annoying and drops my rating from 4 stars down to 3.5.     I just picked up one of these for my new '05 Kia Spectra. I've never owned an aftermarket head unit and therefore I've nothing to compare it to, but I'll give you my impressions so far. My main requirements where an MP3/CD player and an auxilary input that I could hook my iAudio G3 flash mp3 player to (mostly used for audiobooks - car CD/mp3 players don't do audiobooks well, mostly because of a lack of any kind of bookmarking capability).  I decided to purchase this unit because of the auxilary input on the front, as opposed to other units where the input is in the back. I'm starting to question the wisdom of that decision because it might've been better to have the 3.5mm audio cable coming from the back of the h/u with the end of it in the compartment under the dash instead of having a cable dangling off the front of the radio. That being said, the G3 sounds amazing when hooked to the aux input, possibly even better than the CD player :)  The unit is a definite step up from the factory radio it replaced in terms of sound quality. It wasn't quite as big of a leap as I could have imagined, but it definitely gives the speakers more power.  The CD player supports auto resume for both audio CDs and mp3s (haven't tried WMAs) and fast forward/rewind is there too (though it's not nearly as smooth with mp3s - it jumps about 9 seconds instead of 4-5). The EQ settings are pretty basic - treble, bass, fade, etc. There's 5-6 presets so that you can save your own settings for different styles of music. This is a good thing because the CD player has much more of a bass boost than FM (assuming you even listen to FM these days), so it's important to have at least 2 different settings. The buttons are small, which is sort of a bummer. The Mode button (used for various functions, such as turning on/off suffle, random, and mono on FM), is sitting right beside the preset buttons, which is extremely aggrevating because if you're like me, you'll find yourself pressing it constantly while flipping through presets. When are manufacturers going to learn that putting buttons the same shape/size right beside presets is NOT a good idea? This is the only thing I REALLY don't like about this radio.  As for the mp3 capabilities, pretty solid. You can switch the display to either scroll or not scroll and display either tag or filenames, whatever you want. However, the display is limited to about 8 characters (not a problem for me since it scrolls). Also, you can't view the clock and track information at the same time, so anyone without another clock on the dash may want to consider other options if this is a big deal to you.   I honestly have no idea if it does playlists, but you can store songs in individual folders and then have it play randomly all songs on the disc or all songs in a particular folder, so I suppose that kind of does the same thing.  I don't have Sirius in the car, so can't comment on the h/u as a satellite controller. (BTW: For all of you computer geeks out there who are paying for more than one sat radio, you need to research a program called TImetrax.)  All in all, I am quite pleased with the product. I could easily have gotten something much more 'stylish', but I live in an area where car break-ins are quite common and nobody even pays attention to car alarms. So, the less I can advertise to car theives, the better :)

I've tried several mounts over the years for my TomTom920.  This is the best one so far.    Pros:  +The base is heavy and the bottom is a material that does not slip easily, so it stays in place well on my dash.  +Includes a loop on the base and a small hook that can be stuck to the dash for added stability if you need it (I didn't need it).  +The arm is solid and does not vibrate (like the flexible goose-neck mounts that are available from other manufacturers).  +The suction cup that holds the arm to the base is a very good design with a lever that creates / releases the suction.  +The half-circle shape of the base ensures enough clearance so that the GPS unit can mount without hitting the padding (this was a problem with the full-circle designs).  +Easy to take with you or hide without leaving the tell-tale suction cup mark on your windshield that might encourage thieves.  +Doesn't fall off while you are driving (like the suction cup mount that TomTom includes with their GPS).  +Doesn't run afoul of any laws that prohibit you from sticking things to your windshield.    Cons:  -If your dash is curved, the base may wobble a little.  -Vibrates a little more than when mounted directly to the windshield with the standard suction cup mount because the base wobbles a little.  But, vibration is not too severe and the GPS is still easy to read.

I am not really a fan of back-up cameras- I sort of majored in parallel parking in college, and can amaze myself at some of the spaces I have finessed my Jeep into. But I also use the vehicle to tow a number of carts and trailers, and often have trouble getting the ball centered under the hitch. Usually it ends up requiring a helper or multiple trips around the back of the vehicle to see how close I am. This little gizmo solved that.

=== The Good Stuff ===

* The unit is designed to mount to a license plate frame, and it would have fit perfectly on my Jeep mounted this way. But since I didn't plan on permanent mount, I didn't want to deal with screws. Instead I used two pieces of sticky velcro on the top of my license plate frame with the mates on the camera bracket. Not the most secure of mounts, but works well enough to get the trailer attached. For power, I cut up an old trailer wiring harness, and just hardwired the power supply to the backup connector in the trailer harness. Connects in a second. (I actually wired it to the tail-light connections, this way it stays on the whole time instead of just when my reverse lights are on. Works better for me).

* The unit is nice looking, with a shiny chrome finish. Truth be told, it sort of sticks out on my Jeep, and I would have preferred a black anodized finish, but since it is seldom installed, not a big deal. The unit is about 9 1/2 inches long, and the bracket will mount to license plate screws anywhere from 6 3/4" to 9 1/4" apart. The camera sticks out about 1" from the bracket, and the whole unit weighs in at 5 ounces.

* The image is reasonably clear, even in low light. The biggest problem I have is the license plate lights on my Jeep can sort of burn out the image at night, but there is still enough detail to make out the hitch.

* It appears that there are two little torx screws which would allow you to rotate the camera within the bracket. I didn't try this, since the camera has a wide enough field of view for my needs.

=== The Not-So-Good Stuff ===

* I wish there was a way to turn off the parking aid markers in the camera. I just find them annoying.

* The manual is a bit limited, but the whole thing is pretty simple. The manual lists specifications for three different cameras, but I have no idea how to tell which one I have.

=== Summary ===

The only concern I would have is how robust the exterior components are for a use in which it is permanently mounted outside the vehicle. The camera lens seems well sealed, but without disassembling the unit I can't comment on how well the electrical connections are sealed. Also, the video phono plug is already assembled, so if you were to try to bring this inside a vehicle, you would either need to clip and reattach the plug, or have a 1/2" hole for it to pass through. Likewise, the power plug does not really strike me as "weatherproof", especially in harsher climates.

For my application, it worked great.

I recently obtained the Alpatronix AX100 Capsule Speaker, and I was decently surprised by its quality. The size of the speaker is fairly small, which makes it convenient to carry around. For such a seemingly small speaker, it has great volume control and can play music very loudly when needed. So far, I've tested it with everything from instrumental music to rock songs, pop songs, and songs from live performances. I've found that the Alpatronix AX100 Capsule Speaker captures all songs quite well. That being said, the only slight setbacks I've encountered thus far are the wire and sound clarity. For me, specifically, the wire used to connect the speaker to my device seems a bit short, and it sometimes can be inconvenient (such as when my device is at the edge of a table and there is no room immediately next to it for the speaker). Of course, that is just a personal preference, and it may not be a problem for you at all. The other little thing is the sound quality. I've noticed that, as the volume gets louder, the sound tends to become a little blurred or, for lack of a better word, echo-y. In other words, the sound is not earphone-quality, but that can be expected as it's not meant to block outside noise or play music straight into your ear. Again, this is very slight and probably won't be much of an issue for you because it does not happen unless you play the music impractically loudly all of the time. Overall, I think that the Alpatronix AX100 Capsule Speaker is a great, fairly reliable product,and I definitely would recommend this product to anyone needing a portable speaker. -Tuonglinh Bui

I purchased this dash cam from an Amazon vendor, Stuntcams, and received it in just two days. Excellent service in that regard. I'm sure I won't be shown as a verified purchaser of this product because my wife purchased it on my behalf under her Amazon account. Nevertheless, it was purchased through Amazon. As far as the camera is concerned, the user manual is very poorly written and is almost useless but after experimenting for a few hours I think I have most of it figured out. When I first started using it I considered returning it but after using it some more I've decided I like it. The five things I dislike about it the most is:

1) the small screen makes it almost impossible to clearly see the icons unless you have 20/20 eye sight or better and many of the icons have no explanation as to what they mean in the manual. If I ever have cause to purchase another dash cam I would definitely select one with a larger screen even if it costs more but I do think DOD makes a good product.

2) the LED lights on the top left side of the screen that show the camera is on is almost blinding at night but a small piece of slightly translucent masking tape should solve that problem.

3) the speed display is in metric units only, in kilometers per hour. Unless you manually convert the speed to American units or your speedometer has a dual display, the speed display and speed alarm on the camera is useless and quite annoying. After a short time the display screen starts to only show the speed (standby screen saver?). I'm not sure how I was able remove this function, but I did and it now it only shows what the camera is seeing and of course the current functions icons but I still have to learn what some of them mean. Also, there is a button marked EV and I guess it adjusts the light exposure of the video. On one occasion I was following a friend recording her less than perfect driving and the video turned out too dark to be able to clearly show her her poor driving habits. I guess I hit this EV button by mistake when installing the camera in my truck that morning. When in doubt, hit the default settings selection in the menu and I think a person will have good results with the recordings.

4) there are two LED lights on the front of the camera that you can turn on but I don't know what they're for yet but I'll experiment with them some more the next time I drive at night but it seems to me they would only cause glare reflecting off the windshield as they appear to be white LED lights and certainly not infrared lights. Maybe they are for taking close up photos or videos in low lighting or dark conditions. Again, there is no explanations in the poorly written user manual.

5) I've only viewed the recorded videos on the included DOD video player software once and the GPS location on the intergraded Google Maps display is way off. It shows the vehicle's location on the map as much as a half a mile off where the vehicle actually was. This also makes be doubt whether the calculated speed of the vehicle from the GPS is correct or even if the GPS is correct. You can install the DOD video player from the camera once it is connected to a computer but I now only view the recorded videos in Windows Media Player or VLC media player but I'll be trying the DOD player some more in the future and see if it works better then with the Google Maps function. Something else I don't know for sure is whether the TS format video files are uploadable to Facebook or YouTube but I assume they are as I've seen reviews of the product on YouTube with actual videos taken with the camera.

Positives: In daylight, the camera takes stunning videos that are seamless and at night in the city with street lights it's really pretty good considering what the camera's primary function is which is to record any traffic altercations or accidents. Additionally, the audio recording function works very well and is also seamlessand the audio recording function can be turned off so that the camera doesn't record any audio. I've had the camera only a few days and I like it pretty well for the price but since this is my first experience with one, I really don't know how to compare it with others that are available. Something else. With some slower computers you may have to download the videos to the hard drive to play the videos. With a little faster computer you can easily view the video files directly from the microSDHC card with it's card adapter (which is not included with the camera).

From my limited experience with the product I would recommend that new users select the default functions in the settings and then just select the time/date function and use your variance from GMT settings for your time zone. This setting is relatively easy to find in the menu. You will have to know what your time zone variance if from GMT (Greenwich Mean Time) but that is easy to find out on the internet by just typing in GMT in a search engine. Something to remember, GMT doesn't observe Daylight Saving Time so you'll have to subtract one hour from your variance when you're observing DST in your area.

In summation, this camera is a good value for the price but if you have a little deeper pockets, select one with a larger LCD display screen. You'll really enjoy the stunning videos and if your ever in a traffic altercation that is not your fault, this camera should easily pay for itself. The manufacturer, DOD, would be well served if they would provide a much more comprehensive user manual. The one that is included with the product is very poorly written but you can figure most things out by just fooling around with it. That part is really sort of fun! Also, being aware that your camera is recording, I think it will make your diving habits a little better and that's a plus.

I hope you find my review helpful.

I've been using various car DVR/cameras for a long time, tried many models - some were good, some were pretty bad... Recently I've tried this BlackVue model. I've purchased it for a lesser price, with a \\"proper\\" English firmware (1.005 version), so your experience may vary if you got one with different firmware.

First, the good things:
-The packaging and the physical build quality of the camera is excellent - it feels very sturdy, the fit and finish is very good, there are no \\"misaligned\\" parts or anything like this. All of the necessary installation components (the power cord, the \\"sticky\\" holders for power cord and a spare \\"sticky\\" holder for camera's mount) are included and the instructions (I got a proper instruction manual with English language) are easy to follow and well-written. The memory card (I got 16GB version) came pre-installed and the package also included a tiny USB reader for the card.
-The camera's mount \\"ring\\" makes it very easy to remove the camera from it or adjust its vertical angle - very convenient, haven't seen such system on other models...
-There are plenty of features for this camera - normal recording, event recording (when the camera uses built-in gyroscope to detect sudden increase of the vertical/horizontal movement, like in case of a vehicle collision... b.t.w, make sure to decrease the sensitivity for it - the default settings are too \\"sensitive\\" for rough road surfaces), parking mode recording (when the camera only records if it detects motion in front of it and if car hasn't moved for a certain time... This may drain your car's battery, though - disable this feature if you don't need it), choice of video compression (make sure to select \\"normal\\" - the other setting will lower the bitrate and lower the quality of video), choice of resolution, adjustments to voice guidance and blinking lights (you can turn them off or on), etc. All these features are easy to adjust using the software for PC, Mac or from your iOS/Android smartphone, using appropriate apps/programs (the English manual explains all of this). The programs for Mac/PC will be located on camera's memory card - just make sure to power the camera first with the card still inserted into camera so it will format the memory card and write these programs to the card. The apps for smartphones are available at appropriate App Store (just search for \\"blackvue\\").
-The visual quality of recording seems to be pretty good, both day and night.
-The camera doesn't get too \\"warm\\", like the previous model which tended to overheat.
-The built-in GPS sensor is very \\"quick\\" to lock-on onto GPS signals and stays \\"locked on\\" even with tall buildings nearby.

The not-so-good things:
-The camera has a very wide angle lens, which produces \\"fish eye\\" effect at the edges of the picture. If you dislike this - you can eliminate this by purchasing different lens (this camera uses standard M12/0.5mm screw-on mounting for lenses) from third-party sources (with narrower view angle), but it will require full disassembling of the camera (you can't unscrew the existing lens without it), which is not very \\"user-friendly\\" procedure... The picture quality is pretty good even with stock lens, though - just make sure to mount the camera as close to the \\"center\\" of windshield as possible and make sure that it doesn't get too much of the sky view (the bright skies can make its automatic brightness adjustment pretty \\"jumpy\\").
-The camera does have a WiFi connectivity for your smartphone, and it does work, but the speed over such connection is pretty slow (also the camera decreases its recorded FPS while you're trying to view/transfer video files over WiFi, so only do it when you don't need the camera to continue recording the video), so prepare to wait for a few minutes for each file transfer... If you're impatient - just remove the memory card from camera and connect the card to your PC/Mac, the file transfer will be much faster this way.

Aside from those couple of issues I haven't noticed anything negative about this camera and overal am pretty satisfied with it and would recommend it to anyone looking for a full-featured, compact car camera/DVR with built-in GPS. This is a beautiful case.  I bought the red one for my iPod Touch 3G, and I love the metallic red color.  I even think the wavy line across the back of the case where the two halves join is pretty attractive.  It does not add a lot of bulk to the iPod touch and feels very smooth and comfortable in my hand.  The sleep and volume buttons are very accessible, as are the dock port and headphone port.  The screen protector that came with it is easy to put on, fits very well, and the edges end up under the lip of the case where it comes around the front.    I've had it for about two months now, and so far very little dirt or dust has gotten trapped underneath (as there are openings for the buttons, I'd expect some dirt to get in there).  It is easy for me to slide the two halves apart to check for dust, and so far there hasn't been any.  The screen protector hasn't started peeling around the edges, probably because the edges of the screen protector are protected by the case.    There are three caveats though:    1) As the other reviewers mentioned, it is a tad loose.  It hasn't come apart on me, but if I pull on all 4 corners at once, the two halves jiggle apart a bit.  I have been considering buying a protective sticker-type cover for the back (similar to the screen protector for the front) to make the fit a little tighter.  I am pretty gentle on my iPod touch, however, so it has never been a problem for me.  If I were to regularly stuff this device into my back pocket and take it running and such, I would probably either buy another case or tape this one together to ensure that the two halves wont' separate.    2) The opening for the volume buttons is rather large, and exposes part of the back of the iPod Touch.  Not a lot, but it exposes more of the iPod than any of the other openings.  On the one hand, this allows the part that is exposed to get scratched, but on the other hand it makes hitting the volume buttons much easier.    3) While the Apple charging cable plugsnicely into the iPod while the case is on, some 3rd party chargers/docks do not.  If the the plastic part of the dock/charger is wider or thicker than the exposed metal part, the bottom half of the case must be removed in order to charge the iPod.  In all fairness, my friend has a one piece silicone case that has the same problem - she says it would be nice to be able to just remove the bottom half in order to charge the iPod.  It is not much of a factor for me because my cables have a fairly thin connector.    All in all, the case works quite well for me but those with different requirements may want to consider a different case.    EDIT/UPDATE:  I bought a second one for my iPod Touch 2G, and it seemed a little different.  There are two tabs on the side that lock together; these tabs seem to be made of flimsier plastic than on the old one, and it was a bit tricky to slide the two halves of the second case together.  Also, the screen protector that came with the new one was hard - one side was sticky, and the other side was already pretty scratched up and dull.  The screen protector that came with my original case (for the 3G) was not hard, and was just one of those stickers that you put on any small device screen.  It was much easier to put on - I couldn't get the hard one on easily and I don't think I'd want it anyway given how easily scratchable the non-sticky side was.  I think I will buy a different screen protector.      The two halves seem to fit a little more tightly, although I'm not sure if that is because there is a very tiny size difference between the 2G and 3G iPods or because the cases were very slightly different.  Other than that, the plastic tab issue, and the different screen protector, both praises and criticisms from my original review apply to the new case.  About the screen protector:  if you leave the original one that came with your iPod on, the case covers the edges pretty well.  I'm sure the case would perform just as well on another screen protector that was soft and stuck to the screen.    I'm pretty sure I ordered the same case, since I went to the Amazon orders page and just re-ordered the one I had ordered before.  I gave the previous case a 4 (4.5 really, but I you can't give half stars), but I'd give this one a 3 - mainly because I have to get a new screen protector.  However, while the product quality and the screen protector type seem inconsistent, the case itself is still pretty good.  I'd down-rate the seller but I still think the case itself deserves 4 stars.

Still I do wish this case had been cheaper, soif the price or shipping goes down, I'd recommend it more strongly.  - The fit for the iPod touch was a pretty tight squeeze to slide it in.  However, I didn't have any problems getting the iPod into the case.  I just am used to it being looser.    Overall, I do recommend this case. My original key's buttons had worn away straight through the soft rubber. Seemed like a great time to upgrade to a flip out key. I'm so glad I did.
It didn't come with directions so here's how I made the switch.
The lock/unlock chip comes right out if the old key, just pry it open with a small screwdriver. The transponder chip is a bit more of a challenge. Other reviewers suggested using a heat gun or hair dryer to loosen the glue. I didn't want heat to possibly damage the chip, plus I don't own either of those, so I carved it out with a utility knife.
The lock/unlock chip sets right into the new key body, but it is rotated 90 degrees from the original orientation. There is a little pocket in the new key for the transponder as well. The transponder could be glued into the new key, but I didn't, just in case I want to get it out in the future. Even without glue the transponder is held securely once the cover is in place.
Once I removed the key part, I had it cut at a local locksmith shop.
While everything is open this may be a good time to replace the battery in the lock/unlock chip.
Pay attention to how everything comes apart for reassembly later. Make sure to "wind" up the spring with the small cover before reattaching it to the body of the key. This gives the spring the tension to swing the key out when the button is pressed. I found that 180 degrees of winding is perfect, any more and the key wants to pop open when bumped.
All in all this is a great key with a great price. The only reason this product didn't get the 5th star is the material quality is not what you would get in a factory/dealer key. Don't let that stop you though, this is a great product.

Having ordered this for my Sony PRS-950, I was surprised to see a sticker on the box when it arrived stating \\"Brown Executive Case for Nook.\\" I thought for sure they had run out of the model I ordered and just sent me the next closest thing. Actually, based on the website of the manufacturer (VanGoddy), they make just one model: it is designed for the Nook and happens to fit the Sony PRS-950.   In fact, it fits quite well, with just one non-trivial problem: the elastic strap that holds the PRS-950 on the top left completely covers the power switch. This is a major problem for turning the unit on or waking it from sleep mode! While it's somewhat possible to adjust the strap to expose enough of the switch to use it, it is not very comfortable or convenient since the switch must slide side to side (if it were a push-button it would be easier).   Similarly, but not so critically, the straps that hold the unit at the other corners block access to other things as well, including the SD card, the wireless switch, and half of the volume rocker switch. However, in this case, I kind of like the protection this offers since I so rarely remove the SD card or switch off wireless, and it's the Volume Up side of the rocker switch that is covered, which is a push button (but I rarely use the MP3 player anyway).  In summary, it seems to be a good product, but you should know you are buying a Nook case that just happens to fit the PRS-950. The statement in the Product Description that indicates \\"Reading with the cover on, you can easily access your device ... power switch ...\\" is simply wrong: there is nothing easy about accessing the power switch with this case. It is nice, however, that you can access the device's stylus and plug it in to charge without removing it from the case.

I wanted to make duplicate keys with transponder chips. Instructions were hard to follow but thanks to reviews posted on Amazon I was able to figure it out. Worked on windows 7, all the fuss about XP is probably about 32-bit operating system. It didn't work (more like software registration) for me on windows 8, but it was 64bit OS. I switched to 32-bit windows 7 and it ran fine. Video instructions in .rar file were not applicable to this version (mostly for registration)
Pre req
1)Install Java
2) 32 bit OS

Installation: (V9.10.037)
1) Run Mini Vci Driver from the folder
2) Run techstream
3) Run TISKEY
4) Plug in USB end of your Mini VCI and let windows take care of driver installation etc.

To duplicate keys: (This will allow you to create keys that would start the engine)
Pre Req
1) One Master/valet key to duplicate the code from.
2)Get the keys from Amz/Ebay with empty transponder chips (got it for $7/key)
3) Get it cut. Walmart refused to cut, so went to local locksmith and got it cut (Charged $8 for two)

Installation
1) Turn your Ignition to ON (do not start engine) plug in MINI VCI to OBD port.
2) Connect USB port to laptop, launch techstream, connect to vehicle.
3) After establishing connection, it should pickup VIN# and make/model/engine type. Select weather it's with or without smartkey, as far as my understanding goes smartkey also means that you have push start button. In my case it was W/O smartkey.
4) From the \\"System Selection Menu\\" chose \\"immobiliser\\"
5) Select \\"Utility\\" on the next screen and then Key registration.
6) Follow the prompts from the registration wizard in timely fashion. It will require Master key and then the newly cut key with transponder chip to successfully register.

This device is stated as 1Gb ethernet with USB 2.0 HIgh Speed connectivity. The USB ports are powered, seemingly up to the standard 500mV per port to power host-powered devices. The device is smaller than the pictures imply but the curved back/bottom plate means only two strips of contact area for mounting on flat surfaces .

I use these USB bridges to enable wireless sharing of USB devices between laptops, in this case a standard scanner and a printer. The scanner, when plugged into the network, will try to grab a DHCP address making setup, if you took the time to preconfigure your network for its new little friend, quick and easy. Software installation on Windows 7 Pro x64 was seemless and quick and, most importantly, actually had full functionality with seemingly no conflicts with other drivers or software. The program stays running in the system tray and, if you configure it so, will automatically connect and disconnect your computer to a shared printer whenever a print job is run. As per the Keyspan, other devices such as scanners, disk drives, etc., must be manually connected and disconnected to allow usage - the control panel, accessed from the system tray shortcut, makes this quick and easy. The software even allows sending electronic requests to other client users who have not released a device sharing lock - if the other client responds, they can disconnect and unlock the device in order to allow you access again (every device can only be connected to one computer at a time).

So far the Silex is significantly faster on myUSB device usage versus the Keyspan.; the USB-powered scanner plugged into the device no longer suffers from the start-stop data feed operation while the network 'catches up' and printer operation is significantly faster. I only quickly tested the unit with a disk drive attached - my personal recommendation, if you want to have shared network drives, is to either plug it into a computer or (better still) get a NAS as a USB to Ethernet bridge must handle device-level servicing of the drive which is much more bandwidth intensive than the SMB network-level sharing of computer-to-computer or computer-to-NAS.

So, pluses:

- small size
- powered USB ports
- stable, functional software and drivers with auto-connect printer abilities
- 800mHz processor leads to better throughput than other bridge devices
- Win7 x64 functionality tested

minuses:

- only 2 USB ports built-in; more ports will require USB hub
- no status lights for USB devices or complete network link status
- only status lights on ethernet port surround, not as easy as front mounted
- still not quick enough to truly recommend as drive device sharing for the impatient, but does work

Overall, if you know what a bridge device does, are knowledgeable about some of the network setup required and are aware of pluses and minuses of such a device, this is probably one of the best small SoHo devices out there that does this. Fast, small, not really expensive and works great!

I've had smaller USB battery packs, like the Motorola P893. They're fine in a pinch for adding ~30% to your battery charge before going empty.

This 7000mAh pack, however, is in another class. It can take my phone from Low Battery Alert to 100% charge several times, even after sitting in the bag for weeks. Just the ticket for travel, where finding an outlet in a foreign place can be a hassle.

The on-board LEDs are a bit.. muddled. They all merge together to where it's hard to tell precisely how much charge is left. The good news is that it doesn't matter much -- the thing generally has plenty of power to go.

It puts out 1A on one outlet, and 2A on the other. iPad3 and Nexus7 benefit from the added current available on the 2A port. The 1A one is great for most modern phones that exceed the typical 500mA of a standard USB charger. The difference is dramatic -- topping off a phone in 1 hour instead of 2.

The included cable is odd. It's a tightly coiled cable with a USB connector on one end, and then a coaxial connector on the other. Included is an adapter for mini-USB and micro-USB. I would have preferred to have two separate cables, one mini & one micro. The coaxial connector tends to pull out easier than the USB and the fittings are easy to lose. This is a double problem because of the short cord and tight coil. Really, your phone has to be right next to the battery pack. You can use other USB cables, but not all of them have the right signaling to indicate to the phone that 1A or 2A is available. Test stuff before travel, of course.

Anyway, the biggest feature is right there in the title.. 7000mAh. Sweet. Having this kind of power on-tap is useful in new ways. I can rent a WiFi hotspot on travel, couple it to this battery, and leave it on all day long. No more worrying about how long the little internal hotspot battery will last.

It's the kind of thing that doesn't get frequent use, but when you need it, it's awesome.

I bought both the tweed and the red/black versions of these cables.  After getting braided cables, I don't think I will ever get regular PVC cables again, where possible.  These cables just seem like they are more flexible, and they seem really durable.      The problem though, is that one of the cables was suffering from horrible clicking/popping static whenever I so much as touched it.  I took off the end, and after fiddling with it for a while, found that the problem was that the prongs were not properly pinched in place.  Whenever force was put on the connector, the prongs would slide in the housing and the wires on the back would move closer and maybe spark.  By using a pliers and pushing the connector tabs from the back of the connector, they got jammed in place, and upon reassembly, everything worked great.  So, these are fixable if you initially get static when moving them.    Also, a minor qualm is that these smell a little bit like chemicals, but not too bad, think new shoes or something.  I've seen much worse.  My fender Vintage-Volt braided cable had the same problem, but my Spectra-flex did not.  Both of these other cables cost 2-3x more than these, so they aren't in the same category.    So overall, considering that these are really inexpensive, and that they only require SOME tweaking if you get a \\"bad\\" cable with static, these are 4-stars.  Maybe even 5 stars if you get a good one to start, my red/black one was fine to begin with.  These are probably just as good/better than 90% of mic cables out there, at this price, I say go for it.

My wife didn't want my new Garmin unit on the dash and I don't like sticking it on the window so I went looking for alternative mounts. Basically there were vent mounts and there were cup holder mounts. For the weight of the unit I could only see disaster coming my way using the vent mount so I chose the cup holder mount.    First off the Gomadic mounts are not model specific but they do seem to be product specific in other words I could use the mount Gomadic sent to me to mount any Garmin current size of Garmin unit - 4.3\\" right up to 5\\". It comes in two parts the support stem and the holder.    You put the support stem into the cup holder and turn the base counter clockwise and viola the base expands to fill the space of the cupholder giving a firm hold  and support for the unit. I expected the neck of the base to be articulated but it isn't however it bends well into the position that you want.    The holder is where I ran into trouble. It has two halves which expand to fit the width of your unit. However my Garmin unit was 5\\" and was larger than the maximum expansion. I said a few bad words and wondered how the folks at Gomadic could get my order so wrong and vowed to call them after lunch to give them a piece of my mind. I puzzled the problem and after lunch I turned the head 90 degrees and sandwiched the unit vertically instead of horizontally which obviously was the way to do it. I then attached the holder to the stem and rotated it to the proper orientation.     I love having my Garmin next to the instrument cluster and not out my windshield. The screen is at my fingertips instead of me having to lean forward to punch in addresses. I do have to look down and take my eyes off the road to check the route but I can't think it is any less distracting than having it on the dash or attached the windshield.    Next though the stem is 6\\" and even with it firmly planted in the cup holder my Garmin unit vibrates with the motion of the car. No a big thing but if you were expected rock solid it comes as a little surprise.    All in all a good accessory to my GPS unit.    And oh BTW Gomadic folks a little 'how to' piece in the packaging would have been nice. At the very least a slip of paper that directed the buyers to a YouTube video of installation would have been welcome. I still may call you and give you what for; I did spend my lunch hour mulling the problem after all.

Being a student, I was looking for something not too large, I didn't want an eReader broken in the backpack due to tweeking or twisting, but I wanted it large enough to read without constantly moving the document around on the screen like you have to on a smart phone.  I did a lot of research for an eReader and settled on the Sony PRS600.  I don't regret the make of the reader as it suits the needs of a student very nicely.  I only wish I'd had the money for the PRS900 Daily edition, I think it's a slightly better unit and the overall design of Sony's readers are solid.  Anyway, after putting the money into the reader, I wanted something that would protect my investment.  I've done roughly the same amount of research finding the protector for my reader and have settled with the M-Edge Latitude Jacket.  I didn't care for the Leisure Jacket as it didn't protect the screen as I wanted when the reader is in the backpack.  Other items I have researched either required the reader be pulled out when in use, or simply didn't protect the reader well enough for my investment.  The Latitude has a soft, plush type interior lining which is excellent for the protection of the screen when rubbing against other items in the backpack.  It has four durable, sewn-in ... holders?, one in each corner to hold the reader.  These are large enough and durable enough to hold the reader nicely, without worrying about losing the reader because of floppyness or weak holders.  The zippers (there's two) will roll around the edges to allow full open flexibility so you can leave the reader in the case when using it.  I've had comments that it appeared I was reading a regular book in a cover, or that I was reading a CD case or CD holder.  They were impressed when they discovered it was an eReader.    The reasons I gave it four stars instead of five are these:  There is a pocket on the front cover with a zipper. Nice for small items like an SD card or Sony's memory stick.  But nothing more, it's simply too tight. It is suggested by the makers of the M-Edge that you can put your sync cable in it, but I wouldn't trust it, it's too tight and may damage the screen of the reader by mere pressure.  There are two open pockets on the back cover, one is designed I believe for a light.  A mounting pocket I presume.  The other is larger in size, but still very tight for anything thicker than my student ID. I had a hard time even putting a pencil in it.    My wish list:  First, I wish the 'holder' in the upper right corner that holds the eReader was a little bit bigger than the others.  It is rather difficult to get the stylus of the Sony eReader out of its holster with the current configuration of this holder.  Second, I wish there was a finger loop on the outside spine of this case.  I find the excellent material it is made of can be rather slippery at times and when it is open to read, there's nothing to hold unless you wrap your fingers around the bottom or the top.  Perhaps I am just use to the large textbooks that lay heavily open in the palms of your hands.  But it would still be nice to have something to put a couple fingers through for that extra sense of security in holding such an expesive book.    Overall: A touch pricy perhaps (for my budget anyway), but well worth the security of protecting my eReader.  The material is durable and I know it's going to last the life of my reader as I use it constantly in my classes.

Despite the complete lack of reviews on the internet, we decided this Kenwood receiver would be perfect for our boat. We were looking for a marine receiver with a front USB drive that didn't look incredibly cheap and was easy to use, all for a reasonable (i. e. less than $200) price. This Kenwood KMR-350 receiver definitely fulfills all those requirements.

The product arrived well-packaged in its original box, and the box also includes easy-to-read instructions and a wiring harness. My husband actually installed the receiver in our boat, which took all of about 60 minutes. This time frame also included installation of our 2 Polk dbi 4\\" marine speakers and running new wire from the receiver to the speakers. The whole setup sounds very respectable, particularly for merely (2) 4\\" speakers.

The receiver itself includes a CD player that also reads MP3 CDs, front facing USB and AUX ports (an integral plastic cover is attached so that you can cover the ports from the elements when they're not in use), a radio, and Ipod and Pandora compatibility. Thus far, we have only used the CD player and USB player for the Ipod, but both work well. The CD player has been able to read a CD that I frequently have trouble with in my own car. The Ipod compatibility will allow you to either control the Ipod through the stereo, or directly through the Ipod, and its very easy to switch back and forth.

The volume of the receiver has a nice range - it can be cranked halfway, and we'll still be able to hear the music even speeding over the water with our outboard engine just a few feet away. Naturally, its also soft enough not to interfere with our fishing or conversation.

However, don't take the word of just my review - go see for yourself! That's what we did - the radio was on display at our local Bass Pro, so we checked it out prior to buying the receiver from Amazon. In sum, it looks decent, Kenwood is a respectable name so we feel like we've gotten a reliable product, and the front-face USB ports are almost impossible to find on a well-known brand-name receiver in the $100 price range.

Update 8/15/2013
We've had this radio for over a year now, and it still works perfectly! CD player still works great, USB function still works great, and I believe the radio does as well, although we don't get anything beyond two static-y AM stations out on the lake. Last year we made the effort to take the face off the unit during the week; this year we haven't been as diligent, and yet, no harm done (not that I reocommend not treating your unit with care). I will note that we do at least keep the cover on the little box where the unit sits, however. Don't use the Pandora function at all because we mostly just plug an iPhone into the USB port, and both of us have Pandora and Rhapsody on our phones, where the app is a lot more user-friendly than going through all the buttons.

Last, radio still cranks up loud enough to be heard over the outboard motor (and we have a bass boat, so the motor is RIGHT THERE next to the driver seat). Great radio and would continue to highly reccomend!

When I set the SM-900 to full mono-bridged power, it would hum slightly. When I set it stereo-bridged, it would shoot out 260 at 8 ohms per channel. That’s not a lot of power. This amp has a bunch of features I never used.

There’s 2 three-band semi-parametric EQ’s. You can combine the 2 EQ’s together. Never used it. it got a little confusing when you combined them. Each knob will cut/boost so many decibels. I don’t remember if it’s 12db or 15db. And when you combine the EQ’s to work together, they will cut/boost 7db. So I only used one EQ.

This amp head also uses an EQ footswitch to toggle back and forth between the 2 EQ’s. Never used it.

This amp also has a built-in crossover to send hi frequencies to one cabinet and lows to the other. Never used it. I think it’s best to send the full range to all the cabinets.

It also has a stereo FX loop to send a dry signal to one cabinet and wet to another. Never used it. I had a SanAmp RBI rack that I ran thru the mono FX loop.

I’m glad I sold it but I miss the tone.

I have owned this system for one month and can tell you that it is a solid system.
What sets this system apart from its competitors is the power of its amp. It is probably the only microsystem out there with a 140 watt amp (70 watt x 2 channels); most microsystems are typically 30-50 watts (that's total wattage). Besides this it has excellent speaker design, the cabinets are solidly built and even though it is a faux laminate wood siding I think it is still handsome (you won't fool anyone into thinking its solid wood, but its not bad). The speaker wire that is used is of thicker gauge then the average cheap mini system (you know, those thin black wires). The wires are connected by a proprietary connector, the positive of this is that there is a firm connection leading to better sound than the average spring clamp. The downside is that you can't connect other speakers, not that this matters since the system is bi-amped which means that any other speakers could damage both the amp and the speaker itself.
Instead of pre-programmed \\"equalizer\\" settings this one has independent Bass and Treble controls. While it is not as good as higher quality (and priced) systems it does the trick. Basically you have four positive settings and four negative setting for both treble and bass. Because this is a microsystem, don't expect that turning the bass all the way up will get the room bumping. Overall you will not be disappointed in the sound quality. On a slightly different note one control feature I really like is the volume knob which is slightly dampened, when you turn it there is some smooth resistance.
Sound quality is excellent for a small room/bedroom and the powerful amp means that it really rocks when you crank it up. Volume setting goes up to 30 but for casual listening 13-17 is fine (and I like music loud). Radio reception is fairly good with the coaxial FM antenna, where I live there is really poor radio reception so it may work better for you. There is a tape deck cleverly hidden behind the display, I don't know how good it is because I don't use tapes.
The display is a no frills LCD that has a bright orange backlight; it's hard to see/distinguish track numbers, etc. from far away. I have owned systems in the past that have fancy blinking lights and colors with cool demo-setting visuals, the problem is that I can't go to sleep at night because my bedroom is lit up like there is a strobe light on. This system is either on or off, the LCD is not too bright to light up a dark room but when you turn it off it does not default to a blinking/flashing demo setting (which, I feel is a plus).
Cons... There have to be some...
1) It is a single disc player. If it had a CD changer (lets say 3 discs) then this would be my dream system. Nope, you're going to have to get off your butt to change the CD.
2) Does not support MP3 playback. I am very surprised by this since most mini/micro systems these days support MP3 playback as a basic feature. For a system of this quality (and price... I got mine for $299) you would think MP3 playback would be standard, but no... On the other hand many of the higher priced/ upscale systems like Denon and Onkyo don't support MP3 playback either.... Why? I don't have a clue...
3) The remote. What can I say, the system is very attractive and elegant but the remote is a clunky piece of crap. Not only is it much larger then it needs to be but it feels awkward to hold. The button layout is poorly designed as well, there is nothing intuitive about it except the power on/off button being a different color (green in this case) and at the top corner of the remote. Important buttons such as skip forward and backwards are tiny specs while the equalizer controls (which most people don't use that much I'd imagine) are huge. I wish electronics companies spent more time on remote control design because it is an accessory that most people use quite often (also, for this system you need a remote to perform some actions like setting radio stations).
4) There is a flimsy switch on the front of the system, next to the volume control, that is used for tuning radio stations, skipping tracks on CD's or fast forwarding/rewinding on CD's. It just feels like it will break off with enough use and for the functions that it is assigned to frequent use is what it will get. To make the system better they could have used a spring-loaded knob (sort of like jog dials that are found on some remotes).
All in all this system is worth its money. Sony could make a few improvements and create a dream system, but I am plenty happy with my purchase as is. Hope this review helps.

My first reader was a Sony PRS-500 (the original model.) The main complaint I had about it was its horrible battery life. Simply put, the unit never \\"shut off\\" and despite the ad literature saying it only used power when \\"updating the display\\" it was an out-and-out lie. Basically, the battery would never last more than about 1.5 weeks while sitting regardless of usage. After my reader was stolen I replaced in with the Cybook Opus. Sooo...

I'll start with the cons first:
* Sluggish start up - takes about 18-20 seconds from startup before you can start reading.

* Accelerometer - quirky. Works but often takes a shake or two to register the movement.

* PDF support - works and decent but rendering isn't the greatest.

Pros:

* Battery life - unbelievable. I have no idea how it holds the charge it does. I've charged it 3 times in a little over a year and then only because I had it plugged in via USB while updating the books on it. Battery has never fallen below 50% and rarely falls below 75%. It sits in a drawer most of the time and I have no desire to plug it in on a regular basis - I never have to. It's always ready to go. I realize this is probably the main reason for the sluggish start-up. The PRS-500 was ready in about 5-7 seconds, but it was usually dead when I wanted to read it. Worse, the PRS-500 couldn't be charged via USB (though the newer ones can.) The slow start-up is a fine trade-off for it always being charged.

* Simple to use and navigate. Also doesn't require any proprietary software to load books, just drag and drop.

* Screen: Standard E-Ink, identical to the PRS-500. Easy to read, little glare. I wouldn't say its \\"like reading paper\\" as the ad propaganda does, but certainly much better than any LCD display by far.

** Update: I've since learned that Cybook has released an updated firmware for this unit which vastly increases the start-up time but, according to comments and cybooks own website, kills battery life. They now estimate it at \\"2 weeks\\" like numerous other readers. I, for one, have no intention of updating. Incidentally, it is presently selling on Amazon for about $400. You can buy it directly from bookeen for about $140 (as of 2/2012.) I think you can only buy it with the latest firmware though. With the latest firmware, I would not recommend this unit as it's other features are only mediocre and plenty of other readers are available for half as much which will perform just as well.

I owned a Sony Walkman that was about seven years old when the headphones went kaput. It was an original Walkman with Noise Cancelling, and of course, seven years later, there are no replacement headphones to be found anywhere outside of Japan, and I can't even get them. I could, of course, plug in normal headphones to the old Walkman, but the built-in NC feature of the unit won't work.

Imagine my disappointment when I found there are no Sony Walkman models with NC available in the USA anymore (apparently we only buy iStuff these days in America?). I knew Sony still made an NC Walkman, as I'd seen it on a lot of the tech sites I frequent. Only available in Canada and Europe =/.

Luckily, a seller here on Amazon has them imported from Canada, and I snapped one up, not sure what I was going to get (though all the reviews I'd read were great). I absolutely love that the earbud cable is long enough to not be restricted to ONLY using it with an armband holder.

Some positives:

1. Sony Walkmans still sound awesome. I had an original cassette unit growing up (I'm old). I had an original Discman (it was terrible unless I was perfectly still). I own an iPod, a Sansa, and I've owned a Zen. I wanted a Zune, but Microsoft gave up the fight and yet the Zune is still premium priced... but without NC. For me, by far, the Walkman (my 7 year old NWS-716 with NC unit and my brand new NWZ-584) sounds superior. Yeah, I've heard iRiver or something is great, but I love my Walkman too much because of #2.

2. Built-in Noise Canceling - It's too exquisite to describe the feeling of using a lawnmower, weedeater, air compressor, terrible reality TV shows that my wife watches, the neighbor's dog that never shuts up and should be bleeding from the throat by now after the 2 1/2 years of non-stop barking, it doesn't matter. This thing blocks out just about everything. I wouldn't go firing a pistol with these in (well, I might, but I'm really weird and I do things just to give my wife something to complain about to her friends, which is probably why she doesn't have friends haha).

I write fiction novels for a living, and to keep from flying into a homicidal rage with every little interruption or distracting sound, I put these babies in, crank of my Killswitch Engage and DevilDriver, and ignore everyone. I do worry that one of these days, my brother, wife, or maybe even a Red Army soldier might sneak up behind me and remove me from this world, but to be honest, I'd be listening to heavy metal and wouldn't hear a thing, so might not really be as bad as I'm making it out to be.

3. It plays FLAC files. However, I can't really tell the difference between the 256k / 320k MP3 files and the FLAC files. I can easily tell the difference on the home theater, but not really on the Walkman. But at least the Walkman can play them.

4. Gapless playback - I always laughed when people complained about this. I still do, because I could care less about it, but after seven years, I finally hear the next song kick in instantly (especially nice when one song leads into another without a break). Again, at least it has it. It's nice when listening to certain albums.

5. It has good options for sound quality, good playback options, a bright, easily readable screen.

6. The earbuds are comfortable, and it comes with different sizes.

7. The volume button is nice and big finally. This is kind of bad sometimes, though. But mostly good. I'm awkward and end up turning it down to a whisper, or turning it up so loud blood leaks out of my ears, just by leaning up against a counter or sitting wrong. Accidentally turning it down too low is okay, but accidentally turning it up too loud is like George McFly waking up to Marty blasting Van Halen in his ears. I knew I could work a "Back to the Future" reference in here somewhere.

8. FM RADIO! I know, right? Who listens to the radio anymore? Well, I do. I'm an NPR nerd when I'm not listening to thrashy metal stuff. I love NPR. NPR + Sony Walkman = something positive, but I can't think of anything specific.

Some bads:

1. The most egregious, and the reason I can't give this thing 5 stars = the shuffle 'breaks' about every other day. Suddenly the Walkman will no longer shuffle the songs, and plays them in order. First impressions:

This is not a radio for new users to start with. I may be spoilt from simple mono banders and the simple & basic programming the Baofengs with CHIRP, but programming the VR-6600Pro manually is a chore.

But once you have it programmed it is easy to use and a powerful rig. I would just not recommend it to a novice user who is just starting out in radio. Once I had the radio programmed it was a piece of cake for my daughter to operate the radio, but difficult for me to remember the steps to make changes. I would find myself having to scroll through bands via the [B] key a lot if wanted to toggle from VHF to UHF and back to VHF, because there is no backwards with the [B]. One Press to go from VHF to 220Mhz, another press to skip the 300Mhz band , then 6 more presses to go back to VHF, as you have toggle through the extra bands. Even when you disable the wide RX coverage, you still have Line In, AM and FM bands to toggle through. I have sent a feature request into VGC to see about getting Line In, AM and FM moved into the expanded section. I would like to just have 144, 220 & 440 on my mobile rig!

While not a lab grade test, Amelia and I were able to have a QSO in simplex VHF from our house to a ham in Tracy 39 miles away as the crow flies with 50 watts. All our on air reports have been favorable, nothing out of the ordinary either pro or con. So no objections to on air performance at all.

My theories on the overall feature set and radio operation are the following:

* VeroTelecom is a land mobile radio company where features, adjustability and flexibility are king. The radios will be programmed by a technician, who has time to study and configure the radio for a semi static operation. The average business will not reprogram frequencies often and will mostly just use the memory function. This leads to a lot of advance features, but less focus on simpler operations, programing ease and the User Interface/Experience.

* VeroTelecom is innovating with the APRS features, but again, it is deep in the feature set and not a novice grade set up.

* When I sent in a feature request that would make manual programming easier for hams, the factory politely vetoed my suggestion to retain maximum flexibility. I think this is due to the land mobile vision.

APRS Setup

I have the APRS module ready to set up, I downloaded APRSdroid for my Android phone, I sent off and got a passcode, but have not had time to set up APRS on the radio. I will get the APRS function set up as soon as I mount the radio.

Quick Reference

There are a couple short cuts and quick references I will be setting up for the radio. Little things that can make a hams life easier. Keep an eye out on the VR6600 Facebook page.

If your intention is to record something extremely loud, such as a guitar/bass amp, this microphone does not perform well in that environment as it clips REALLY BADLY. It's not as good as some of the other mic's I have heard, but for the price it is a great value. Nothing you could get at this price range can come close to this, aside from maybe the Blue Snowball, which I have 0 experience with but have only heard good things about.

As an ambient mic recording a room full of people this mic works stunningly well. It is very sensitive and has very minimal buzz or hum, all of the buzz or hum can be easily equalized out. It is very sensitive to pops such as those resulting from the P or the B sound at the beginning of a word, and it does not come with a pop filter in the set which would have been nice but there are ones for like 20 dollars at guitar center... or you can use the 'ol stretched pantyhose over a coat hanger wire trick and that works well too.

Mic response is pretty bassy, and is very susceptible to the proximity effect. When you are right up to this microphone, any noise you make will rumble out of your speakers. This is good for some thing but it is annoying at other times. You need to make sure the singer/player stays relatively the same distance from the mic at all times, else their voice will change slightly in the recording.

The mic itself is very sturdy feeling my klutzy friends have dropped it, knocked it over and (in a weird case I would rather not explain) thrown it around... and it still preforms the same as it did when it was new. Though I would not recommend being rough with it intentionally.

The built in monitoring only works right in the included Pro Tools. All other DAW's treat it as just another audio interface, which works but is not ideal.

ProTools is not my DAW of choice. And the stripped down version that is included in this set is not very good. Registering is a NIGHTMARE, and once registered you must always have this mic plugged in even when you don't want to use it. This becomes nightmarish when you want to record using a different interface and have limited usb ports (such as on a laptop) or limited space, as is the case in many small home studios. The software itself is very usable, the stripped down version automated many of the most confusing aspects of big kid Pro Tools, and if this is your only option it is a very good choice, though many better options exist.

The included stand is tippy but its better than nothing, just make sure the mic is aligned with one of the feet and you should be ok...

Overall I would say that this is a good choice for someone looking for a good sounding mic on a budget.ame as it did when it was new. Though I would not recommend being rough with it intentionally. Got the radio for Camaro 1998. Replaced Dual HD radio head. Reviews keep talking about time correction adjustments, well in my case that was only partially successful. My setup is 2 Polk door speakers in custom airtight fiberglass boxes, 2 Rear Polk speakers that reproduce excellent accurate deep bass that will thump thru your chest without any subwoofer thanks to this car's rear speaker placement position. Equalizer works great, Bluetooth works great and clear with KCE-400BT adapter. But I had mixed results with time correction adjustments. When following directions for time correction from the manual, I noticed right away the center of sound did move to the center for Mid and Hi range, but it negatively affected Bass from rear speakers. Mid bass was gone and no time correction tweaks were able to fix this. I suspect delay caused elimination of bass Standing wave frequencies, produced when all speakers work in same phase (no individual speaker delay). Standing wave makes BASS really pronounced inside the car. Since I don't have sub, that was unacceptable. I left time correction for front speakers since they don't produce deep bass due to enclosure size but reset rear speaker correction to 0 and bass came back right away. By the way you can listen to music while adjusting delay which was cool to see effect right away. I suspect if you were to have sub, may be it would overwhelm rear speaker loss of base, but just be aware that time delay correction can cause negative side affects as well. But at the end for the money, its an excellent piece of equipment.

I have a 7th gen 160GB Classic iPod and wanted to take advantage of its large capacity by recording family events and stories and the little kids' priceless comments. Basically the unit works well, but isn't perfect. After some experimentation, here are my findings:

The little mic is easy to use once you get the hang of it. When it's attached to the iPod, it takes a minute but then a new category appears in your main menu--Voice Memos. Although there is an 'instant recording' button on the device, I didn't get that to work, however by selecting Voice Memos from the menu with the click wheel, you'll get the Recording screen where you can 'Start Recording' using the click wheel. You pause the recording with the click wheel too, then resume the recording or save it via menu options. You can play back any of the recordings you've saved, each of which is labeled with time and date. You can delete any you don't want to keep. When you sync to iTunes saved recordings are automatically uploaded to a newly created playlist on your computer called Voice Memos.

When I first started recording things, I wasn't alert to the red 'record' dot that shows on the iPod screen. Anything I recorded before the dot showed up wasn't picked up. I also found the quality of my recordings was far better and had much better volume when the 'Gain' switch was in the off position, contrary to the directions. Overall, I didn't find the directions all that great, but with some experimentation I was able to do everything I wanted to. I tested recording quality both hand held and up to about 6' away and was very satisfied with the results.

Bottom line, the unit doesn't feel top quality, but seems to do a good job of recording. The drawstring carrying bag that comes with it is big enough to carry my iPod Classic as well as this small mic attachment.

Sound quality:
So so. It sounds like a mediocre box from the '80s ( although better than most things that are available today)..not bad, but nothing to write home about. It does not hold up to the better boxes of the past, but that shouldn't be surprising. The treble frequencies are reproduced clearly with little or no harshness, the same for the midrange. Bass response seems to roll off at about 100-120Hz.
The good news is that it has separate bass and treble (-7 to +7 Db) controls, so your not limited to (often useless) pre-set eq settings.

Radio:
AM reception is improved over the older model (i931), though still not exactly great. It will pull medium level, and strong stations, but you can forget about anything weak or even slightly weak at all. Selectivity isn't that great either. I'd say it's less than average.
With an iPod in the dock of course it's much worse as they put of quite a bit of r.f.i. (static).
With that said it's still an improvement as the last model was practically deaf on AM.

The FM still overloads when close to a relatively strong station. It's not the most sensitive or selective, but it get's the job dome. Again less than average. It is capable of switching to mono, and that helps with fringe reception.

MP3:
The USB port reads your PMP/MP3 player like a disc (you can't use the controls on your player), and also charges the device (you may not want to do this if you are running \\"D\\" cells as it will drain them). The card slot works as it should and is HCSD (lager than 2GB) compatible.
Navigating is done by browsing though folders (F01 F02 ect.) and by clicking though ff (next) and rewind (back) just like a CD player. There is no menu or way to scroll through a list of files available. Holding down the FF or REW button will scroll though the file at a very slow 2x or maybe 3x normal speed making long files such as podcasts or audio books very difficult to navigate through. Thereis no resume feature, nor does it remember what track you were on should you change functions or turn it off..
Formats are limited to MP3, WMA, and WAV/PCM.

IMHO you're better off running your PMP/MP3 player though the AUX port

Pros:
- Very fast shipping and well packaged.
- Color matches very close with the existing dashboard trim (not perfectly, but can't really tell the difference)
- Perfect fit with existing dashboard hardware (brackets, screws etc).
- Easy install, matching wire harness, doesn't need any wire work.
- Nice, large screen. Brightness adjusts with night/day based on headlights on/off switch.
- Good radio reception.
- Clear sound.
- Customizable home screen (there are some limitations listed in the Cons).
- Easy Bluetooth connection.
- Good iPhone/iPod connectivity (for iPhone 5 and up an lightning adaptor is needed).
- Good USB options - movies play well (some limitations as I only got the AVI files to play)
- Steering wheel controls are customizable and work fairly well.
- Good Remote Control.
- Decent GPS software with POIs.

Cons:
Phone book doesn't transfer all contacts from my iPhone. I observed that contacts with more than one phone listed (such as home, cell, work etc) don't show. Only contacts with one phone number show. I wrote to Eonon customer support and they replied: "We would like to tell you that it can show the 2-3 phone numbers such as home, cell, office." I am still to figure this out, as most of my contacts have more than just one phone number.
- No voice activated commands (for phone dialing).
- Only 4 speakers work, the two located on top of dashboard don't work as unit only has amps for 4 speakers.
- No support for MP4, MKV, MOV files - so far only AVI movie files work.
- Home screen can't erase icons that are not used (such as TV or TPMS which my unit doesn't have).
- TPMS system no longer available from EONON - I really would have shed $125 - $150 to buy one.
- Relative lagging in overall functions, including scrollingthrough the 4 screens of the Home Display.
- DLNA and Miracast are buggy - not very easy to work around; screen mirroring is still a work in progress.
- Watching movies during daylight can be difficult, as screen is not very bright. No problems at night.

Other thoughts:
- GPS antenna can be nicely routed in between the dashboard vents, then lift the section with the dashboard clock (it is relatively simple as there are only clamps holding it in place) then put the cable on the right (passenger side) next to the windshield and the GPS antenna will be nicely located in between the dashboard and windshield, with perfect exposure to satellites, and snug fit in place - almost unnoticeable.
- Overall installation time is ~2 hours, with a lot of attention to details. Second install can be done in under 30 minutes.

Overall the unit appears to be a good investment, as my OEM unit failed to play CDs and displaying an error that didn't allow to go from CD to Aux input for iPod (which I use most). Now the playback options have increased and kids appear to be excited with the movie option.

I have long wanted a quality GPS driven running watch but could never quite afford the $200 minimum pricetag.  For Father's Day this year, my wife and kids came up with a pretty good alternative in the Nike Fit+ Sportband.  At around $60.00, it is much more affordable than a GPS watch and is pretty darn good for the price.  There are just a couple of points that anyone considering buying one should consider:    - You DO NOT HAVE TO PURCHASE NIKE SNEAKERS TO USE THE SPORTBAND. Nike would tell you otherwise but the sportband system works just as well with your favorite brand of running shoe.  You must simply find a way to attach the sensor to the laces of your shoe.  I initially used a folded over piece of duct tape holding it in place under my laces.  I looked online and found numerous devices designed for this purpose specifically, ranging from $2 to about $10.  I picked a latex case that attaches to my laces and holds the sensor in place.  It works as well as the Sportband is expected to work.  Thank goodness because I personally find Nike running shoes overly expensive and of poor quality.    -The Sportband is generally pretty accurate. It is surely accurate enough for everyday use.  Even without doing calibration on the system, it is generally within 1/10 of a mile on my workday morning 5 milers.  The only place I have found that it falters is when I try to include speed work into my routine.  When I do my usual 8:10-8:20 miles the accuracy is as I mentioned, however, if I speed up my run to under 8 minute miles, it changes my gait and, clearly, this effects the accuracy of the unit.  On such runs I have \\"lost\\" up to 1/4 mile on the same 5 mile route I run 4-5 days a week.  This is not an enormous deal except that when training for a race, my pace is very important to me and I don't trust the pace that the watch is telling me since the mileage is clearly inaccurate.  I can do the adjustment in my head but isn't that why I wanted a running watch in the first place?    Within these parameters, the Sportband is a good purchase.  It won't stop me from getting a GPS watch when I find the money to do so but it has provided a good substitute in the meantime.

This little player is lightweight, compact, and good for the price.  The 2Gib model is available at Microcenter for under $20.  The features are FM, video 160x128 AVI/MTV, MP3/WMA/WAV, voice and FM/voice record at 64kbs 8kHz 4bps. In addition it has the usual repeat/shuffle functions, a simple tone control, and 4 extra speeds of playback so you can slow it down or speed it up by 2 steps.  The unit can be purchased in 2Gib, 4Gib, or 8Gib capacity.  The screen is of course too small for good videos, and the record function may be OK for capturing an interview, or just to remember a song by.  But the recorded music will sound very bad.  But at this price an lightweight, having this capability is very good.  The unit will run for 6hrs or 3hrs with video.    The manual is almost written in English, but it is fairly complete.  The controls are not consistent in that sometimes menu is used to select things and at other times the play key ||> in the center is used to select.  This can be confusing.  Holding down the menu key is supposed to return to the top menu, but it only does this in certain functions, so this can be frustrating.  When recording something the files are put in the FMIN.DIR, or MCIN.DIR which is not mentioned in the manual.  For playing movies it is necessary to convert them to the AVI/MTV format using the supplied software.  The movie is turned sideways to fit on the rectangular screen, but you should select the small screen size to save space.  When you select a song it shows you the title, but not other things like artist, performer...  The title scrolls slowly, so if you have it set to quickly turn off the screen, you may not be able to see it all.    The software for the movie conversion and to convert other formats to MP3 are included inside the device in the Program folder.  But this is not mentioned in the the manual.  Apparently at one time they included a CD, but when they switched to the sensible&economical idea of including it on the device, they did not include the instructions on the manual.  There is also a copy of the manual on the device.  You must setup the video converter which is in the \\"MP3 Utility Tool\\" folder inside the \\"Programs\\" folder.  The MP3 converter is in another folder, but there are so many good MP3 converters available for free that this is not mandatory.    While listenging to either music, or FM you adjust the volume by pressing the VOL button, and the quickly press the << or >> keys.  The speaker icon turns red while you can adjust the volume.  Unfortunately it only stays red for a couple of seconds.  So there is a large tendency to miss the window of opportunity and to switch tracks or FM stations.  This is probably one of the biggest annoyances.  For videos, the icon stays red much longer.  They really should have it stay red or better yet allow it to stay on so you can adjust the volume by feel as you walk around.    One feature that I particularly like is the capability of organizing the music in folders.  You can have it play everything, a playlist, or the contents of a folder.  I like to listen to long works in sequence, so the folders are ideal for this.  You can select audio tracks for a playlist.  Only 1 playlist can be created as far as I know.  With the folder organization you can repeat entire folders.  So while it may not be competitive with the higher priced units in terms of playlist capability, folder capability is excellent and not avaiable on some of the competition.    The device includes the USB cord, a charger, and earbuds.  It can also be charged from a standard computer USB port.  But you can not play it anytime while it is charging.  If you value the extreme light weight and you do not need it for an extremely long trip, it is a very good device.  Since it does not have a hard drive, it is good for exercising.  The main deficits are the inconsistent controls and volume control.  This review will hopefully make up for the incomplete manual.  It may be OK for educational videos, but not for big screen epics.

Sound quality seems good, volume is adjustable to coincide with the radio, etc. It's all good!  Installation, however, is a laborious process. Don't expect to buy this and install it in five minutes. Fortunately, modern Fords have a radio that is pretty easily removed, even by a novice. But after that, it's a bit tricky. As far as wiring goes, I ended up just splicing the power and ground of FRD-04 into the power and ground of my radio. Simple enough. But if you don't know what you are doing, YOU CAN DO DAMAGE TO YOUR RADIO. Don't guess when it comes to wiring.  Another thing to consider is /where/ this thing goes. In my case, I drilled a hole through the bottom of the radio compartment into a little coin holder/bin. The FRD-04 fits nice and snug down there. But please keep this in mind - you will almost assuredly have to drill a hole /somewhere/ around your radio for this rather bulky adapter to sit. Space is often a premium in vehicles and you obviously cannot undue a drilled hole, so be careful with this as well.  In short, if you are a complete novice when it comes to car electronics, get someone who knows what they are doing to install this for you. Otherwise you are going to spend needless hours installing this and possibly causing damage to your radio.  And always, always remember to disconnect your battery whenever you are doing any sort of wiring in a vehicle!  If you need assistance in installation, feel free to contact me. So, more often than not, the HEX sport band works pretty well. It's comfortable, adds protection, and makes it much easier to operate your Nano.
