I purchased one of these from another vendor for about $130 shipped. I have used it for several months, including the collar mic, surveillance kits, multiple antennas, both as an amateur radio operator and in public safety. It works fine with good audio quality, but there are a few issues:

The radio's scan feature is crippled. If the radio is in scan, and you press the button to turn on the backlight, it stops scanning. If you press the button to turn on the LED, it stops scanning. If you try to lock the keypad, it stops scanning. If you want to change which channels are included in the scan, you have to reprogram it from a computer. You can't even use the dual VFO feature while in scan mode - even though the second channel is still shown on the screen, it is never checked.

The radio itself has developed a problem. Under certain circumstances which aren't entirely clear, it will occasionally completely reset itself. I suspect this is due to a power connection issue inside the radio, but for something this cheap I'm not surprised. I'm probably going to replace it and use the broken one as a base station radio.

The belt clip, where it connects to the battery, is too tight. It takes serious effort to remove the belt clip. Which would be fine, except that it's also weak. The piece that actually fits in to the battery has broken on me, necessitating a replacement. In fact, all of the plastic pieces here are of significantly poorer quality than what you would get with, say, a Motorola.

I have used the longer antenna. It's too long to use in the field, but as a base antenna it works fine and does improve quality. While we're talking about antennas, on my original antenna the plastic piece has chipped, resulting in the actual antenna coming out of it at an angle. It still works, but yet another example of poor materials. The replacement antenna, the end cap fell off and got lost, so I had to cover it with gaffer's tape.

The surveillance earpiece works fine. The surveillance microphone does not. I am told that it results in a 'muffled' sound which is barely readable. The collar mic works fine.

Hello everyone. This is a review about the Android Player JXD that I have experienced so far.

THE LOOK OF THE DEVICE
======================
One thing to note, although it has the setup of a PSP, it is NOT a PSP, rest assured of that. It simply has buttons and layout of a PSP to give a PSP feel, but sadly will not play PSP games, not unless they have made a PSP emulator for Android. So don't let the interface or pictures fool you. This is strictly an Android based device to help you play android games better.

THE PACKAGE
===========
I got my system in about 10 days from purchase date, so the timely delivery was great for me. The whole package comes with the following...

- Android Player JXD (One thing to note, this was originally a Japanese only device, but DOES have english support)
- Power supply (With universal adapter to plug into USA power supply, as it was intended for Japanese power outlets)
- Ear Phones (Inside a white odd looking package, probably to show it hasn't made contact with anyone else's ears)
- USB cables to connect to your PC so you can copy Music, Videos, games, etc.
- USB extension cable.
- Main system has 2 gigs of storage space, but you can install an 8 gig Micro SD Card to it (Micro SD card Not included)

Now, one thing to note, don't be shocked when you see the box have Japanese writing, as stated above, this device was only suppose to be in Japan, but I guess with some support, they added English support for the device and everything can be read in English. Only down side is that the manual is Japanese only, no english manuals came with it. So, you are gonna have some fun learning about all the cool features on your own, or look online for support of some kind. Plus, some of the error or warning messages might be in Japanese as well.

THE SCREEN
==========
The screen is a very good size for this device. The screen is clear and sharp and videos play extremely well. One thing I do recommend is getting a screen protector to help protect from scratches. Also, if you happen to have the HDMI cord for this, there's a button or app on the device that allows you to transfer what's on the screen to your HD TV. The transfer rate from little screen to the big screen is great. Imagine playing all your games on a 96 Inch HD Plasma screen. Hell yeah...

THE CONTROLS
============
This is where it gets a little bit of a pain. When you first start using this device, you kinda have to do a little learning about which buttons do what for a while. Although, once you figure it out, you can pretty much fly through all the screens, icons, items, etc. with ease. The controller part works great and the feel is very nice, although I am familiar with how PSP and other portable devices are so I am used to the feel. The touch screen on the other hand is a little sensitive and not always accurate to your touch. My advice on the touch screen is to get a stylus, works much better. The analog control, located just below the controller part, works very well with games that use analog control, such as SixGuns and Dungeon Defender. Also, controls for the emulators work good, but you sorta have to get used to the controls for a while, although there are settings that you can adjust to make the game work the way you want them to. This is done by, first playing the game you want while in your emulator, and then pressing the \\"Return\\" key, the loop arrow key located just below the buttons. Doing so makes a menu come up and you can then go to your settings and adjust the controls and whatnot there. The only real controls issue you will have is when you play the Nintendo 64 emulator, as the buttons are not like what you would expect, since the original N64 controller has 10 buttons. (Counting the \\"Z\\" and \\"START\\" button) Since this device only has 4 buttons plus 2 shoulder buttons (\\"L\\" and \\"R\\" respectively), the buttoncount is not enough so you will have to figure each game for N64 to your liking. The rest of the emulators and games work just fine, you shouldn't have too much trouble figuring out how to setup the games to your liking and you will love the Arcade emulator for sure.

THE ANDROID
===========
The Android part is great. I managed to download a ton of Android apps & games and they all work extremely well so far. You will enjoy playing android games with the controller parts. Only issue is you will have to figure out what the buttons do for each game, but the control part works great. The interface is very nice and reacts will with the controls and buttons, as well as the touch screen, but personally, you may realize that you might want to get a Stylus instead of using your fingers, as it tends to not always register your finger.

THE EMULATORS
=============
The emulators that did come with it work pretty good for the most part. Mind you, most of the games I played were \\"Licensed\\" games and most of them worked pretty good. Any games that would be considered as Unlicensed may not work well, such as those made by Camerica. The only emulators that came with this system were Gameboy Advance, NES, Sega Genesis, N64, and arcade. One thing you will like is that the system does come with some good starter games for you to test out for each emulator, such as Contra for NES, Captain Commando for arcade, Golden Axe for Sega Genesis, and Metroid Zero for Gameboy Advance. (Now, to point out, I don't know if the games you get will be different from what I explained, but then you never know) Only thing is, some of the starter games you get are in Japanese only, so don't be discouraged. (One major note, NO, I will not help you find roms for your system, you are on your own, so do not ask me) Although each emulator has a lot of good things, I think it would be better to just list the issues you will have with each emulator that you may have to deal with as well as what \\"I\\" have ran into so far...

N64
===
- Graphic issues (Polygons missing, wrong textures displayed, slow gameplay at times)
- Control issues (Original N64 controller had more buttons than this system will allow)

NES
===
- Some Graphic Issues (A small handful of games showed graphic errors, one of them being Mike Tyson's Punch Out)

GAMEBOY ADVANCE
===============
- A few sound issues (Some games had a few scratchy music moments, but nothing major.)

SEGA GENESIS
============
- Small Graphical Errors (Only a small amount of graphic glitches, nothing major that prevented me from not playing further)

ARCADE
======
- Default controls are different per game (SELECT is coin insert, START is Start button, but only for Player 1)

A couple other things to note. If any game for whatever emulator does not have a screen shot for that game, it will automatically make one the moment you exit the game. Also, make sure you copy the roms to the proper \\"roms\\" folder, as each folder has its own setup for each emulator you run. The \\"roms\\" folder will be located on the system itself. I would like to point out I have not tested EVERY game, as that would take forever. Although so far, I have not had any more issues other than what's stated above, you may run into a game or 2 that may or may not work for you. Also, most games controller setup can be configured.

CAMERA
======
The camera part is pretty good. By default, it takes low quality pictures, but you can make a few adjustments to the colors and what not to take good shots. It will also do video capture as well.

ADDITIONAL NOTES
================
One cool thing about this device, it does have wifi on it, and it works pretty well. My issue is the \\"Google\\" ready web browser that comes with the system can sometimes halt the system and will get stuck and sometimes will not exit out, even if you use the \\"return\\" or other buttons to try to leave. Although if you can find the Firefox app for it, that would be much better. So, if you wish to browser the net, my advice is to get a web browser app for the system that is not so buggy or glitchy that would halt your system. The system also comes with about 10 free Android games to play and a few additional apps for fun and leisure. The File browser it has works pretty good, and will choose the best option for each file to view. It also comes with a few text files for reading, but sadly it did not come with a text viewer to read text files, so you will need to download and install a Text viewer to read the free text files it comes with. Just about every common as well as few uncommon video formats will play, and very clear, but that also depends on the quality of the videos you have. So far I have not had any video skip or slowdown on me. The only format it would not play outside a compatible app was .MOV. When I used the default player that came with the device, it stated \\"Unsupported Format\\". Probably due to the fact that they have no direct license with Quicktime.

OVERALL
=======
I have read some of the other emulator devices and how bad they seem to be with people who buy them. This emulator device is actually pretty good and works really well from what I have seen so far. I am a little sad that there's no SNES emulator, although I have heard you can buy an SNES android app. Also, the fact that it does Android is a major plus, so you can have hours of fun with the system. The sound is very nice and clear, especially with MP3. Battery life on a full charge is pretty good. About 4 hours or so if you use it to play games, watch movies, or listen to MP3s. Longer battery life if you are just doing web browsing or general file browsing. Although the power supply works pretty well, I just recommend you get a universal adapter, mainly because the power cord it comes with is about 3 feet long, and I personally like a little more length than that. One major issue you may have is that the Micro SD card is a bit hard to get into the slot. Although if you have some good fingernails, you should be able to get it in firmly and it will stay in place when you hear the clicking noises. I personally think this was a good buy as I have enjoyed it the moment I received it in the mail. A lot of my friends were jealous of the emulator programs and were begging me to help them get this system. As mentioned, the manual is in Japanese, but I have managed to work out a lot of info and figured out how to setup the system. My only advice for setting up the system is, if you happen to have an Android Cell Phone, you might use that as a reference to help you figure out a few things for this device.

I think the best way to describe this GPS/handsfree/headunit is that there is no other single comparable device that matches its price-performance ratio.    Its low price guarantees that there are cut corners here and there. It isn't the pinnacle of technical achievement. And rarely do multi-function devices do any of their various tasks as well as any single dedicated device. The AVN2210p is no exception to this rule. It's not perfect, but it comes unexpectedly close.    The sheer breadth of features is what appealed to me. I wanted handsfree calling. I wanted to keep my car free of a CD library (I'm graduating from an Empeg car MP3 player). I wanted an in-dash GPS. And this unit does all of them! For a song! If I bought single-purpose devices to do all of these things, I'd be up over $1,000, my dashboard and cockpit would be a spiderweb of wires, and I'd have three things competing to be plugged into my lighter. No thanks.    The shortcomings are legitimate, though. Check the list of supported phones or risk bluetooth disappointment--and yeah, here I thought bluetooth was supposed to be a standardized protocol. Some phones not listed do work, like my Palm Centro after some futzing around, but unfortunately you have to install the unit in order to really test the handsfree. If your phone isn't listed as supported, check web forums to see if others have had any luck with your phone model.    Where it sits in your vehicle can also diminish the experience somewhat. Glare can make it hard to see, and while the 6 tilt positions are handy, it's not exactly convenient to change the tilt to accommodate shifting light conditions when driving during the day. You oughtn't be watching the thing while you drive anyway, and the audio prompts are more than adequate to get you where you're going.    So I can't give the AVN2210p a perfect 5-star review, because it has deficiencies; however, I think they are largely outweighed by the device's price-performance ratio, and by its versatility.

I've ordered a reading light and will see if that improves my overall experience. Using medium text helps considerably.  I like the touchscreen, which is nicely responsive. Being able to charge via USB is nice - one less charger.      PDFs are rather disappointing as several reviewers have noted.  I think plain text is fine, but most people looking for PDF readers read scholarly journals that have a double column format.  This is a pain in that you have to scroll up and down and it takes time to get to the right magnification. Like a lot of iPhone owners I wanted to protect my invenstment, so I opted to try this product. Dust and lint are your enemy during install of this product.  One spec and you're toast, so be extremely cautious and deliberate while applying this to your phone.  If anything gets under the membrane during install it creates a bubble that doesn't go away unless you remove the membrane, carefully clean and remove the particle trapped between, and then reapply.  Getting it aligned is tricky too, and if you are a perfectionist like me then it may get nerve racking trying to get this aligned just right.  But I have to say once you get it the proper fit that is acceptable to you the product does exactly what they claim.  The anti-glare is just great, and it helps mask smudges too.  They aren't as obvious now, helps the phone look cleaner.  It's frustrating when I show my phone to someone and there are smudges all over, just looks bad.  Well this helps in that department greatly.  And the feel of the membrane on the face of the phone is very nice too, I like the way my finger just glides across the screen now.  Overall I would highly recommend this product to anyone that wants protection, glare reduction, and less obvious screen smudge on their iPhone.  Kudos to Power Supply!

UPDATE 9/26/2011  After eventually contacting the company through social networking sites and emailing various higher-ups directly, we did finally get the warranty madness sorted out. After reviewing the invoice the repair guy submitted, they went ahead and approved my claim. We also had several people apologize for the experience I had. Following approval, I was given two options -- equivalent replacement since the TV was no longer sold or full cash refund. The one they offered didn't look as awesome at Best Buy, so we took the refund via Amazon giftcard, which was sent to us today.  I'm happy to report we've ordered a replacement television, including a SquareTrade warranty. Obviously, the customer service experience was kind of nuts, but I've been assured this was an isolated experience.   ---------  09/08/2011ish - We purchased a one year extension on the manufacturer's warranty for an out of box Samsung Plasma television that we purchased through Amazon. We were concerned that it might have issues since it's out of box and that a one year warranty wouldn't be long enough, but thankfully SquareTrade was here to put our mind at ease.   Fast forward 18 months to a few weeks ago when we turned the TV on, but nothing was being displayed on the panel, despite having audio and the LED power light coming on. Further inspection revealed that there was a crack running from the top to bottom of the internal panel. So, I submitted a claim with SquareTrade. They asked for some pictures and additional questions to my claim, titled \\"Crack running down center of television screen\\". After sending in pictures, my claim was approved pretty quickly. Awesome, because this TV is 18 months old and stopped working. TVs shouldn't stop working if I'm still measuring their age in months.   Here's where things get sketchy. We're handled by an agent who has only been there a week by his own admission -- he also describes himself as being \\"completely overwhelmed.\\" After the claim was approved on Friday, it took four business days hear back from the agent after I called a few times and sent a few emails since we didn't get contacted by the repair company in the promised 48 hours. Apparently, they misplaced our paperwork. During this conversation, the agent casually mentions that if it's a crack, it won't be covered. In my brain, I hear that record scratch noise and ask, \\"Wut? You already approved my claim.\\" The agent quickly backpedals, saying that it's not a real approval, except I have an email from SquareTrade saying it was approved. In any case, they'll still send the tech guy out, which I get scheduled for the following week.  A full two weeks have passed since filing the claim when the repair guy from a local company comes. He fills out an invoice, describing the problem as \\"internal crack in panel, no exterior damage\\" -- consistent with what I've been describing to SquareTrade the entire time. I hear nothing from SquareTrade the following day and, since I already know what I'm dealing with, call them my own. I tell the same agent that I've been speaking with the the problem was described as a crack in the panel, but that the company said they could repair it. I ask them if I can follow up directly with the company or if SquareTrade needs to make some sort of final second approval, despite my claim being approved already. He says that is fine for me to set up the repair with the company and it's great to hear it can be repaired. I call the repair company and, while I'm on hold, get a call from SquareTrade.  Surprise! The claim that has now been approved via email and, just moments before, verbally, is not actually approved at all. It turns out that apparently any crack, whether caused by accidental damage or not, is considered accidental damage. My already approved claim is out the window. I am also told that if I do think it's a manufacturing defect, I can contact the manufacturer. The iRiver H320 hard drive/ MP3 player is definitely something great to have.  I personally felt that it was better than the iPod because of the color screen, image viewer, FM radio, and recorder.  On the H320, I didn't like how there are two places for a USB connection.  One connection is called \\"data,\\" which makes the player show as a hard drive on the computer for regular file storage.  The other is entitled \\"media,\\" which is for synchronization with Windows Media Player 10.  I just wonder why they couldn't make one USB connection so that a user wouldn't have to switch to use the H320 as a hard drive or for synchronization.  The line in/out feature is good.  You can record from and external analog source or even connect another pair of headphones.  The player comes with software that updates the database on the player.  No drivers are required for its use.  Just connect it using the \\"data\\" port.  I do not know about its compatibility with online music sources-I bought music from walmart.com and doesn't seem to synchronize with the player.  Windows Media 10 tells me that I need a security upgrade, but it doesn't download!  At first using the player was very confusing.  There are only a certain number of buttons that mean multiple things depending on the mode or option that you are in.  It takes a little while to learn about what everything means.  My H320 takes 15 seconds to load with about half of the 20GB filled.  The music organization isn't the best.  The player has the options of a file tree like in Windows Explorer to find music, by artist, by album, or by genre.  Since I have about 2000 songs I still find that I have to do a lot of scrolling to find what I want.  I wish that there were a search by name feature.  Making play lists was hard at first.  It seems that you can only use Winamp to create play lists, because there is not play list on the go feature.  Play lists can only be made out of mp3 files!  The FM radio is nice, and has many settings, including the country.  The reception is all right, depending on your location.  I like the fact that you can record in mp3 from the radio and from other outside sources.  There is also a text viewer, but only in the .txt format from Notepad.  The EQ/SRS settings are cool.  It is user friendly.  There are many different settings that you can use for bass, treble, etc.  There are also multiple play modes like random, repeat, etc.  The LCD is nice and bright, but viewing pictures is another story.  Pictures can only be under 1MB in size, and they load slower as the size becomes greater!  The recorder is ok for recording speeches, discussions, and music from outside sources such as the radio and external CD players, mp3 players, etc.  It is not good for recording live music!  The internal microphone can't handle the different frequencies of sound, making the recorded sound become distorted.  I guess if you connect a good external mic, it might be perfect.  Overall, the player is good.  It is a little on the heavy side, and slightly chunky.  The case makes it even bulkier.  The player itself can be compared to a deck of cards.  I wasn't happy with the double USB connection, picture viewer, and recorder, and the music searching.  I was impressed with the capacity, color screen, options, and radio.  The fact that it had more features and the same size capacity as the Apple iPod made it my choice.  There is no scroll wheel, but the button configuration is good.  All of the buttons are flat, which requires that you keep pressing or holding the down or up buttons to find what you want.  Pressing a button once has a function, while, if you hold the same button down, it brings you to another different option.  Anyway, I felt that this definitely was worth my $296.40.  I would recommend it for users who want to carry all of their music collection around all of the time.  It is good for use that does not require a lot of physical movement, because there are moving parts within the player! -Written by fet4.

I have tested several different configurations of Synologies, including the DS 1512 five bay storage system. This is the DS214 the two drive system.
The synology is not a backup system. It is a storage system. It is hot swapable if you suspend the standard usage of the term. That is what I found on alot of the claims as to what the nas does or can do.It will work with macs and pcs, although it takes a bit of tweaking to get the mac network to play nice with it. The Synology comes with 512 gb on memory which is barely enough, and will at some point give you an issue with lockup, slowdown, or a disconnect from network. When loading take it slow and don't to a huge migration. A few files at a time and you should be ok.

Setting up Raid 1 is an easy process. This is the Raid where the drives mirror each other. After you get all your data on the Synology do not remove any drives. Never let anyone ever pull out a disk for any reason. Use the locks. Once a disk is removed you cannot re insert into the has without all data being lost, and the drive being reformatted and then rebuilt with whatever is on the other drive. Not the biggest deal on a two drive / two bay storage array. This becomes more of an issue when more than two bay system is in play.
It is also advisable to get a battery backup and plug this Sinology into it. Storage systems no matter what brand hate power outages, and you never know how they will behave until its happening in front of you.

Synology software still tops everyone else's. Arguably drobo has better raid in case of total failure. With them you don't have to send off drives for data recovery like some synology failures. Note I am not recommending Drobo if that thought popped into your mind.

The thing with Sinology is that intro units like this are a tad slow due to the low memory on board. The higher the model number the faster they are. This is a good unit to get started in the high capacity storage arena. Even when you outgrow its capacity or speeds, you can still keep it around as a dedicated backup to your main storage unit, or use it to stream music and video.

The only reason I didn't give this five stars is that it came with no documentation at all. The information I needed was in the Amazon item description, but it would have been nice to have a copy included with the item as well. Here are the vital facts to using this:

1 Input voltage MUST be lower than the output voltage. So if you have a 12v input, you need to set the output to at least 12.5v
2 Output voltage cannot be more than 3 times the input voltage. So if your input is 12v, do not set the output greater than 36v
3 Turn the potentiometer (the brass screw head on the blue box) clockwise to increase output voltage, counter-clockwise to decrease.
4 Max continuous operating current must not exceed 3 amps, description is not clear on this, so I am operating under the assumption this is Input current.

Hints to get this unit set up safely.

1 use a lower input voltage than you plan to for the final installation. For example if you intend to run a 12v input, use a 5v input to adjust the output voltage, this will reduce the risk of setting the output less than the input.

2 use a 5 amp fuse inline with this module input to protect against over current.

Audio quality very good: noise-free and detailed. I recommend using higher-quality earphones. FM reception very good, remaining stable in challenging locations, however tuning and preset processes require some getting used to. The memory is limited to the onboard 256Mb, and is not &amp;quot;expandable&amp;quot; as claimed in Target's product description. Display is very clear, but the orange-blue thing isn't used to advantage. Navigation is snappy and easy (again, a learning period is required) and can be done while the unit is playing. Loading files is very easy and the unit behaves well as an external drive. I'm stuck with USB 1.1 so transfer rates are a bit pokey. A firewire and/or ethernet connection would be a welcome addition. Mic recording is good for voice in proximity to unit , but the quality is poor for area or ambient sound recording, including live music and natural sound. The max bit rate for recording of 192kB/s really shines on line input recordings.  Although the manual suggests a max bitrate of 320kB/s, the actual unit can be set no higher than 192, nor is there any adjustment for gain in either recording mode. iOps uses a subminiature input jack for the line in connection, so don't lose that adapter cable!! I would prefer a regular miniature jack for that connection which could be internally switched between line or mic level as a welcome step toward perfection. Still, the concept is sound, functional, and so is the player. Build quality is very good, and the player is a pleasure to carry and use. It looks great, too, but the silvering along the edges of the mirrored panel was somewhat deteriorated in the unit I purchased. Would love to have gotten the 1GB version, but that's only available in Japan right now. This unit is a diamond in the rough, that, with a little polishing, could become a true gem in the flashplayer game.

I had read reviews that said this was a bit too big but that it worked fine once cut to size. So I bought it, intending to trim it before application.
When I fit it against the screen before applying, it appeared to be the perfect size, so I thought the manufacturer had corrected the sizing of the product.
Turns out it was still a tiny bit too large. So I highly, highly recommend cutting it down a bit before you even start to apply it! The top-to-bottom size is OK, but the side-to-side size is too big. Just 1 mm or 1/16\\" off is enough.
If you don't already have a box cutter, you can get a two-pack at the dollar store. Doesn't have to be a heavy-duty cutter, so the dollar store version would be fine. I wouldn't recommend using scissors, because it would be very hard to get a nice finished-product that way. Use a box cutter and a straight edge of some kind, and you should get a professional-looking edge. If you don't have a cutting mat, just use a piece of cardboard under it when you cut.
I also highly recommend viewing the installation videos online first, at [...].

Anyway, I am still using the original 5 channel amp with a new Kenwood head unit, and the little sub seems to be doing it's job. It doesn't have any real thump to it, and at really high volume levels I get some distortion, though that may be the fault of the amp rather than the speaker. Of course, I only need really high volume when doing 80+ MPH with the top down, and who can tell how much distortion there is with that much ambient noise? At moderate to high volume levels the sub performs very well. It is everything I could expect for the size of the speaker and the limits on the custom box and speaker positioning.

Radio:

Overall, I have really enjoyed this device. Here is a detailed review of the installation and use. I hope it is helpful for others!

INSTALLATION
I installed the USA Spec PA15infi in my 2009 Nissan Altima. I have a factory Bose system with navigation and 6 disc CD changer.

I installed it through the CD changer rather than the satellite radio. This was my only option as the instructions for running it through the satellite radio seemed prohibitively difficult for my skill set.

Installation was pretty simple. I removed the panel surrounding the CD changer, unscrewed the screws that held it into the frame, slid it out, unplugged the wire from the CD changer, and plugged in the PA15 (the white male plug). You'll note in the photo of the product that the black connecting wire for it has 2 white plugs on it, a male and a female. One goes into your CD changer, the other is a female connector to plug the original wire from the CD changer into the PA15.

The device functions as a bridge between the CD player and your iPhone with this wiring set up.

I tucked the device into the dash framework and left it on top of the CD changer when I put everything back in. I chose to run the wire to my iPhone out from the dash console with a foot or so of slack on the outside so I could have my iPhone sit either on the passenger's seat or in the cup holder by the gearshift. The wire comes out from under the fold down ashtray underneath the CD changer. It was a tight fit because it's a thick wire, but I was able to get the ashtray panel put back in place successfully and with minimal difficulty despite the thickness of the wire.

I chose to do this versus running it into the glove box and leaving the iPhone in there because I usually listen to radio stations via the TuneIn app and need to be able to access the phone to change stations; you cannot control apps like this through the car stereo after installation, only the iPod functionality of MP3 files on your phone can be controlled through the stereo.

Be sure to test it out BEFORE you put the dash back together. If a wire is loose or if anything isn't working, you don't want to have to take the stereo panels apart again.

The hardest part of the install for me was cramming the wires for the device into the console area. There is a lot of length to the wires, probably because some installs would require running wire from the back of the car to the front, but I tied some of the cable up with a tie and got it all to fit in the extra space behind the CD changer in the dash.

USING THE DEVICE
You can control the iPod functionality of your phone through your car stereo controls after installation. You can browse folders, skip tracks, and the steering wheel buttons work also.

To engage playing with the install through the CD changer as described above, you hit the CD/aux button on the nav system. The CD changer and factory auxiliary input will still work with the device installed. The unit acts as a bridge between the CD changer and the factory auxiliary input, so what this means is you hit the cd/aux button once to switch to the iPhone, hit again to go to aux, and hit again to go to the CD changer - it ends up toggling between the iPhone and the CD changer.

The preset buttons on the nav will change the play mode of the iPhone. Button 5, for instance, will set it so that you control the music through your iPhone and not through the buttons on the stereo (this mode also removes the track/album data on the nav screen). The other buttons change music folders. I haven't completely figured out what the difference in all of them is. I mainly use preset button 1 because it gives me direct access to the playlists I've set up on the iPhone and I find it easier to locate songs that way.

As I mentioned previously, third party apps like TuneIn Radio will work nicely on the PA15. In fact, that is mostly what I listen to in the car. To use this, just switch the input on the stereo to play the iPhone, then open TuneIn, pick a station, and start playing. When you first switch the stereo input to the iPhone, your MP3 files will begin playing, but when you launch TuneIn and play a station, the MP3 music will fade out and the output from TuneIn will take over.

Depending on the station you are listening to, it will show the show/song titles on the navigation screen. Something always shows, but as to details such as length of the program remaining seems to depend on whether or not the radio station broadcasts the information.

The iPhone charges while it's plugged into the PA15. It keeps charging after you shut the car off if you leave the phone plugged in and will eventually drop power off to the phone and stop charging when the car remains off, but I haven't figured out what length of time lapses before this happens.

The device is \\"smart\\" in that when you get back in your car, it picks up playing whatever you left off; if this was an MP3 track on the phone, it picks right back up in the middle of the track. If it's Internet radio via TuneIn, it resumes playing the station.

Note to users with a limited data plan: TuneIn will continue to stream in the background if you close the app but don't stop playing a station to build up a buffer. This continues as well, for a few minutes at least, when you shut off the car and leave the app open, even though the playback of the station does pause. I like this because I can skip through commercials later with the buffer that gets built up, but bear it in mind as it will add to your data usage even with the car off.

GENERAL IMPRESSION
Overall, I really like the PA15 and I'm glad I bought and installed it. Installation was relatively simple (and I'm not the best at stuff like that!), it allows playback from third party apps and shows all of the show/song infoI would want on the nav screen. I used to subscribe to XM but when I recently let my subscription lapse, I bought this, hoping it would serve as a good replacement. Indeed it has and I have no plans to go back to XM since I can get Internet radio for free through my phone.

Bear in mind of course that with streaming Internet radio on your phone that if you frequently drive in areas where there is poor cell reception, you will not get a steady audio stream and won't be able to listen to online stations.

A FINAL NOTE
I had an idea of running the cable from the PA15 into my iPhone 4 dock ([[ASIN:B003TKMM2M Apple iPhone 4 Dock]]) that I bought from Apple and mounting that behind the gearshift to display/access the phone. It would have fit perfectly given the amount of space I had to work with. But an important note: running the PA15 cable into an iPhone dock and having your iPhone mounted on the dock will not allow playback through the stereo. Don't know why, but the cable from the PA15 has to go directly into the iPhone to allow you to get sound through the stereo, otherwise you just hear sound on the iPhone's internal speaker.

While not without a few faults, I have found this to be an excellent purchase.  In my other truck I have a USA Spec iPod adapter, which literally cost me ten times as much, including installation.  This car mount system not only has a better set up, but better sound quality as well.    Pros:  +Superb sound quality.  Even when I happen to be in areas where there is a real station broadcasting on the frequency I'm using I have never had a decline in sound quality.  In comparison, the much more expensive USA Spec adapter gives me a constant whine, even after having the installer change the cable a few times.  +Good layout.  The arm puts my iPhone exactly where I need it.  All the controls are easily accessible, and the screen is easy to see without taking my eyes too far off the road.  For example, the GPS is easy to use, and even though you shouldn't be texting while driving, having the iPhone \\"firmly\\" mounted makes it as safe as possible.  +Price.  What can I say?  [...] is basically nothing for this kind of convenience.    Cons:  -Most importantly the setup could be a bit more secure.  Cigarette lighters aren't made to support weight and many will spin around in the socket.  It would have been nice if they had accounted for this and bundled a separate arm that sticks to the dash and provides an additional point of support if your particular set up requires it.  And while the mechanism that locks the phone in place is pretty good, there is definitely room for improvement.  Bear in mind that the iPhone is probably the heaviest device that this car mount system supports.  Lighter devices will obviously have less trouble in this respect.  -My only other gripe is that I have no idea why they claim this rotates 360 degrees.  There is no way you can, say, flip your iPhone sideways to watch a video or something.  If you have a very secure cigarette lighter than you may be able to extend the arm to the side, but that is not exactly convenient.  Still this is better than theUSA Spec adapter, which has a cord that is so short the phone is virtually inaccessible while in use.    Suggestions to manufacturer:  *Make it more secure, both in the way it holds the actual device, as well as how it attaches to the car.  *Put the mounting arm on a rotating hinge attached to the back of the dock.  This way it truly would allow 360 degree rotation.    I have not owned any similar transmitter/mounting systems to compare it to, but I can confidently say that this is a very decent product and many times better than the USA Spec adapter.

I bought this because earbuds and even upgraded earbuds still make my iPod g5 nano sound tinny. I was looking for something practical to plug it into that would allow me to hear my iTunes in all their dynamic glory. This product fits the bill! Here are its good points:    a. Design is stylish, and it either stands or can be attached to a wall.  b. Sound is surprisingly good. I'm picky, too. Decent dynamic range, and every type of music I've played sounds good so far on this item. Jazz, classical, world, pop, rock, folk, country, alternative, dance... so far, so good.  c. It can be connected to my flat screen TV, and the result is a **significant** upgrade in sound quality-- hooray! A dual use product. And though I haven't tried it, it looks like there's a video out jack (L, R, V), so that you can hypothetically view your nano videos on your TV! There is also a miniplug IN jack, which is what I'm using to import TV sound.  d. It charges my iPod!  e. It's a snap to assemble-- I didn't even need the directions.  f. It has a remote. It's a tiny remote. I love that.    Here are its not-as-good points:  a. As others have pointed out, the volume reverts to the preset factory level (louder than I like it) whenever you turn it on. It would be a far better product if it reverted to the last set volume level. However, this is not a reason not to buy it.  b. No bass or treble controls, and no equalizer-- you have to adjust the sound on the iPod itself.  c. No adjustment for differing sound levels in original music files-- some songs are too soft, others are too loud-- but that is iPod's fault, not the speaker dock's.  d. It was a bit larger than I expected... but the sound is worth it. This is not an easily portable unit, if that is what you're looking for.  e. I wish it were energy star rated. That's important for me, and for the earth. My TV and DVD player are both energy star rated.  f. You need to unplug the sound IN jack for the iPod to work properly. If you don't, the docked iPod won't produce sound, so this is an either/or situation. I'm sure there's a work-around; it would have been nice to have a switch or a solution on the remote. Plugging and unplugging could get to be a pain, over time.    That's it! The product comes with a bunch of adapters for the slide out iPod deck, but my nano fits it just fine as-is. I would buy this product again, given a do-over, and I recommend it to others.

I installed this into a 2004 Ford F150 Lariat over 2 weeks to ago. I like to go with JVC products for the simple reason being, they may not be the absolute best product, but, you get a lot of bang for the buck. Here is a quick rundown of the hits and misses.

The Hits:
The auto dimming feature is nice! Swipe your hand near the face and it lights back up. You can customize the background screen as well as the screen colors. It is blue in the picture on this site, but, you can change it to whatever color you want. The hands free/bluetooth feature works great. I do recommend mounting the microphone on your visor so it will be closer to your mouth and give better outbound audio. My voice command did not work until I moved it to the visor ( iPhone 4 ). If you have a Verizon or Sprint iPhone, you will want to update it as soon as it is installed. Their is a bluetooth patch that was released for CDMA iPhones to help them obtain better BT connectivity. You will obviously need the adaptor for the iPhone.

It has a nice parametric EQ with pre-set sounds as well as slots for user made sounds. Each field of the radio has its own EQ, so just setting up the EQ on the radio does not change it for the CD or iPhone/iPod or USB, etc. You need to tweak the EQ on each source. I like this feature. Sound quality is great.

The dual zone feature is great. I have 2 screens mounted in the rear headrests. Bought a USB splitter and ran it to both screens and the kids plug their headphones into the screens.

Removable faceplate with carrying pouch. Great idea.

I have near 100% functionality using the SwiJack interface for my steering wheel controls. The only thing it does not do is skip songs on the CD. It does on my iPhone, however, just not CD's. My steering wheel controls are as follows: Vol UP, Vol Down, Source, Skip to next Song/change station.

The touch screen works flawlessly.

The misses:

This is on oversized Double Din. I tried Metra and Scosche mounts and it was too big for both of them. I had to use a Dremel to cut the opening out to make it fit. This means that the exposed part of the mounting bracket now looks like crap. A dremel doesnt really cut plastic, it melts it away. However, this stereo was not big enough to mount in the factory spot without a bracket.

The Motion X GPS works well.......but, only when it works. To clarify, if you do not have cell phone signal, it is completely useless. I expected this when I bought it. I would like to see JVC offer an add on, stand alone unit for it. I would not look forward to it as there does not appear to be revisions in the inputs for this feature.

The iPhone integration is a great idea and works well for the most part. The only hiccup I have run into is when I have a playlist in random mode and it wants to play the same 5-6 songs out of 100+ songs over and over when I use the skip feature on my steering wheel controls.

CD read and loadup time is a little slow....around 10-15 seconds. No big deal, but, its there.

This is a nice unit. Other than the mounting issue, the other things are minor concerns and shouldn't sway you.

The only drawback is the access to the headphone jack is restrictive with aux cords that have a wide jacket b/c the opening in the case is pretty deep. Overall, I like the access with the click wheel b/c mine has sensitivity trouble with silicone covers.

I received this as a review sample and would have given it five solid stars had there been instructions. There were none and I am hoping that is an oversight because of the half dozen dash cameras that I have tested in the past year this one is superior to all of them. If you know how to set up and use one (or even one of the many sports cameras on the market) you can muddle through without a manual. Otherwise I regret to say that this is not for you.

Since there are ample product specs I am not going to regurgitate them. I do want to note up front that this camera solution is missing the rear facing camera for backing up that many other brands include. On the plus side, that camera is difficult to install and the display on the models that I have tested is postage stamp size, inset in a larger display, and near impossible to read.

A few reasons why I like it so much. first the display is one of the best (at the time of this review), and it comes with a suction mounting system that will actually cling to the textured dash in my vehicle, but is designed to adhere to a windshield. Even through the glass the camera returns and displays sharp images. It also accepts SD cards (not included) up to 32GB. I currently have a [[ASIN:B009QZH7BU SanDisk Ultra 32GB MicroSDHC Class 10 UHS Memory Card]] in this camera and despite being an obsolete model it works well.

Note also that you need to connect the camera to a power source constantly. The USB cable that came with it uses the older mini connector versus the more common micro end, and is long enough to reach the camera in my vehicle. I have to admit that the cable snaking over my dash is a bit ugly, but that can be solved by using a cheap [[ASIN:B00NBZUQC8 3000mAh Lipstick-Sized Cell Phone Charger]] affixed to the included mount. If you do decide to go the cable route you will need a spare port in your car charger to accommodate the cable. This camera easily works off the 1 Amp port in my four port char charger, so you need not worry about high speed ones.

Finally, if you use a battery back-up like the 3000mAh one I mentioned above or have convenient access to a wall charger this makes a perfect security camera in house or even in protected areas outdoors.

What I love about Amazon is that they take items that do not perform or are broken back and even pay the return postage. After getting my gift card credit refunded, I started doing more research and read many reviews. This particular unit seemed to be better than most and still had a reasonable price. One reviewer recommended a particular Class 4 memory card and even had a link to where you could purchase it. I took his advice and purchased the dash cam as well as the 16 GB SD card.

The item arrived in less than a week and I eagerly opened the box. The camera was actually partially charged right out of the box, and I was able to read the instructions and do the setup. I will add that one must either use a magnifying glass to read the instructions or magnify the booklet on a copy machine (my choice). Next came the test to see if it actually worked.

I was a little disappointed with the suction cup device as it was really limited in the positions one could employ it. I finally put it by the rearview mirror and put the power cord straight down to the power outlet. I don't want to worry about someone stealing the camera, so I unplug it and lock the camera in my truck.

So how did it actually perform? The playback on the small camera screen is OK for a fast look but not very useful if you need it for proof in an accident. I actually only use the small screen to make sure the lens is pointed in the right direction. One reviewer also commented on the jiggly lens. I fixed this by wrapping a rubber band around the body and this holds the lens firm in the right position.

For playback, I pulled the micro memory card, put it into a special carrier sothat I could insert it into my laptop. I used Windows Media Player to view the .avi files and the video was surprisingly clear and detailed. Wahoo. I even downloaded the files to Windows Moviemaker but this did not solve the problem. I will keep investigating to find a solution but it is a glitch I can live with.

In summary, I think this is a worthwhile purchase if you accept the limitations for a +/-$60 camera and memory card. I believe the picture quality was quite acceptable. Was it HD? Don't know but will try using the enclosed cable to transfer video to HD TV at a later date.

This review is for the SUPERGRIP-BLACK 80GB Zune Case from the PCMICROSTORE.    --------------------------------------------------------------------    IF YOU DO NOT WANT TO READ MY FULL IN-DEPTH REVIEW, SCROLL DOWN TO THE \\"OVERALL IMPRESSIONS\\" SECTION!!!    --------------------------------------------------------------------    In general, this is a good product. I will break it down by parts.    Shipping: I received this product in 6 days, but it was over a weekend - so really took 4 days. I was happy with the shipping. (I chose the standard option)    Packaging: Came in a small plastic bag, sealed, something normal you would expect.    The Case: I am impressed. The case slips over the Zune 80 and fits very well. Clearly designed for my Zune. It does collect dust fairly easily, but that is not a big deal to me.  --Controls: The Zune pad is not hindered at all by this case. The Play/Pause button and the Back button are covered, but I have no problem using them. The headphone jack has clear and easy access. The Hold button is a little hard to reach, but it is not that bad.  --Feeling: The case grips well, is easy to hold, and doesn't slip. It has texture on the sides and back witch allow even easier holding.  --Screen: The case does not hinder the screen viewing at all.  --Bottom / Charge post access: There is a fairly large hole at the bottom of the case, but the zune does not come out or slip down or anything like that. The standard cable provided with the Zune easily fits in.   I also have the Zune brand dock ([...])  I was worried that the case would hinder my dock access, but it does not! The way the Zune dock works it that it is universal for all zunes, and it has a small plastic piece that goes over the port to adapt for each zune. If you use the dock without any plastic piece in place, it works with this Zune case perfectly. I am very please with that.    The armband: It works really well. I was expecting a flimsy little strap, but that is not the case. It has a Velcro attachment. It slips through two little (reinforced) holes in the back of the case. It holds the zune in place as good as you could expect. In my opinion, it flops around a little too much for running. The zune 80 is just too heavy, but that is not this case's fault. It works well for weight lifting and exercises that dont have jumping or fast movements. I am satisfied.    The belt clip: The clip screws into itself through a small hole in the back of the case. It works well enough but it is not very high quality plastic. If you are planning to hang your zune on the clip a lot, it may break after a while and I wouldn't recommend it too much. But...the clip was just like a extra add on for me. Semi-Satisfied.    Video Stand: First of all, you must understand that the stand is VERTICAL, and you watch movies with the zune HORIZONTAL... However, you can move the little plastic grips at the end to sorta \\"convert\\" it for horizontal viewing. It is not at the perfect angle, but it works well enough. The stand stored under a small plastic lip, witch works well enough, but it is not full proof. The stand also easily removes if you do not want to use it. I am Satisfied.    Screen Protector: The screen protector is in no way, shape, or form specifically designed for the Zune 80. It is way to big and requires cutting. Do not buy this case if you are no prepared to do some work to use the screen protector. It can be cut fairly easily however, and works well if you cut it right. I suggest using a straight cutting like seen in a FedEx Kinkos or OfficeMax Impress, doesn't take too long, and should work fine. The protector itself does it's job once it is on and it not too thick. I am disappointed in having to cut it, but satisfied once it is on.    Combination of all accessories: Everything in this package works well together. You can have your screen protector on, case over that, video stand on, belt clip hooked in, and using the arm band and it all still works. I wouldn't recommend using the arm band with the belt clip, because it hurts your arm after a while, but the clip and band hold up well.    ---------------------------------    OVERALL IMPRESSION:  This is a great case at a wonderful price. All the features work well enough to satisfy any normal Zune user, and the case gives you the feeling that much more durability has been added to your zune. It grips well, doesn't hinder functionality, and protects your zune!    Pros:  -Protects well  -Good grip  -Full functionality  -Armband quality  -Full dock usage  -Video Stand works    Cons:   -Screen protector not cut to size  -Belt clip not too strong  -Hold button can be a tad hard to access    MY RATING: 4.8 / 5.0 Stars!!!

I got this a few years ago when it was on clearance for about $30, but didn't bother installing it until I'd worn out my beloved Kensington FM transmitter which had worked so well, couldn't find a replacement Kensington unit, and didn't find good quality with other low-cost FM transmitters for iPod. So I bit the bullet and tried this out, and I had no idea how comprehensive this product was! Not only does it connect my iPod, but it pairs with my Blackberry over Bluetooth to provide hands-free calling, and Bluetooth audio streaming.

Pros:
- Closest thing you can get to having a newer built-in telematics system in your own car.
- Low cost, even at today's pricing (if you can get it)
- Possible to pair two or more different Bluetooth devices (though I have only managed to get one of mine to work properly)
- Allows hidden installation so not easily abused in-vehicle (my old Kensignton FM transmitter kept getting stepped on from lying in the passenger's-side footwell)
- Good quality Alpine design, nice look and feel.

Cons:
- Lots of thick and/or long cables to manage, and difficult to choose an installation location for the base unit and display. I wound up taking out the center console and sticking the base unit onto the transmission tunnel, and routing the wires to come out from under the console into the footwell. I will probably re-route the iPod connector to go straight back and then up through the console storage so I can just keep my iPod in there, as once it's connected it really doesn't need to be handled.
- Bluetooth audio streaming on Blackberry Bold was a bit clipped and audio played with a slower pitch.
- Bluetooth with my Samsung T401g would, for some unexpected reason, cause the phone to turn off. Not sure why. Haven't tried any other phones.
- Remote may be easy to lose, and is the only means of control. Also, not always immediately responsive, and requires remote to be pointed almost exactly at display.
- Control interface not quite as intuitive as usual iPod clickwheel for selecting songs, playlists, etc.
- I have the microphone installed behind the steering wheel, but sometimes get complaints about my voice quality during calls. I really didn't want to go through the hassle of installing in the A-pillar and routing the wire behind the A-pillar and instrument panel. We have these WMS 450 systems deployed in more than a dozen classrooms. We equip classrooms with two transmitters: belt pack and handheld, and we include the CU400 dual-station charging dock. They have some very specific advantages:

- They are rechargeable mics
- The LCD display shows the number of service hours left on the charge
- The battery packs do not have to be removed from the mic for charging (this is the ONLY system we could find with this feature)
- Just drop the mic into the charging dock and it automatically kicks into charging mode

The biggest challenge is with syncing the mic to the receiver. It's an IR procedure and the manual is heavily icon-based, so the directions for syncing mic to receiver are very cryptic and hard to understand. We ended up making our own version of the directions and storing them in the cloud to techs could access them when/where needed. It's also worth keeping in mind that since each transmitter must be synced to its receiver, if you lose a transmitter you can't just carry another into the room and have it work - you need to go through the sync procedure first. If you have a few minutes that's not a killer, but it's not trivial and an unskilled person will not succeed in attempting it.

The only weak point we have discovered is that the lav mic plugs into the top of the belt pack transmitter with a mini-XLR connector which sticks up. If a presenter gets in the habit of leaning against the lectern and hits the point where the XLR connector plugs into the transmitter, it puts a lot of strain on the connector.

The transmitters are powerful enough to cover a large classroom 80 feet or more in depth and width. We really like them, and we haven't found any real problems. If they are treated with moderate respect they will last pretty well. We do recommend keeping a spare transmitter around so that if a transmitter is abused or damaged, you have a backup.

I tend to be very particular about my ereader cases and I don’t think that I am in the minority of Kindle Voyage owners in that regard. I have tried a number of different styles until I found one that suited me, the ACcase Vintage folio case.

I recently was given the opportunity to try the GMYLE Vintage cover and , naturally, I had to compare it to ACcase I have been using. I find that they are both well constructed and beautiful cases. For anyone considering this folio style, there are a couple of major differences and the best choice depends on one’s priorities.

The GMYLE cover weighs slightly more, 4 ounces compared to 3.4 ounces for the ACcase. The GMYLE case is definitely more attractive. I have attached pictures. Unlike the ACcase, the detail is not only on the front but also on the back and spine. It does indeed look very much like a vintage book and gives that feel when holding it.

The construction of the spines is different. The GMYLE has a firm spine but that makes it a bit more difficult to bend the cover back. That may ease with use but it is very stiff at first. That also prevents it from standing alone in a horizontal position if that is important to anyone. It will stand alone in the vertical position. The extra thickness of the GMYLE case, especially around the corners, provides a lot of protection for the Kindle if dropped. The front cover is easy to open and close on both. Both cases have cutouts for page turning, charging and power but the GMYLE case lacks the cutout for the auto brightness light sensor and that may be a critical defect for anyone who regularly uses that feature.

There are features that are unique to each and worth comparing. The GMYLE has a hand strap built into the front cover and the ACcase does not. This is important to a lot of readers who like the convenience of slipping their hand through the elastic while holding the book. A feature that the ACcase has is the automatic wake/sleep feature, . The GMYLE case does not have automatic wake/sleep when opening or closing.

If you are looking for an absolutely beautiful vintage cover that actually feels like a book in your hands and has a built in hand strap too, this may be an ideal choice. If having automatic wake/sleep and using the automatic brightness adjustment that is built into the Kindle Voyage is critical to you, then the GMYLE cover would not meet that need. It really is a choice of form over function.

The stitching is beautiful on this case as is the embossed design. The gold accents on the dark brown synthetic leather make this a unique and attractive case. I give it a full five stars for appearance but must deduct one star for the lack of full functionality, particularly having the case obscure the light sensor since the adaptive light function is one of the innovative features of the Kindle Voyage.

I bought this to watch TV sometimes at late night without disturbing my better half.
The product performs flawlessly and has a very tiny form factor. Others have written in detail about it so will spare the pairing etc details which are simple.

The few points to note for someone who plans to hard-wire it to their TV sets and leave it plugged in.

1. The unit works while its charging - so thats a great thing. You can leave it permanently connected to the TV
2. The charging cable is standard USB on one side and pin type on the other end - so you cant use just any usb cable to charge - don't lose the cable that came with the unit.
3. The little headphone pin cable is permanently attached to this unit - so you can stick that into the headphone socket of your TV - however for most TV's if you connect anything into their headphone socket - you lose the sound in the main speakers - so a better solution is to get a 3.5mm female headphone socket to RCA cable adapter ( http://www.amazon.com/Cables-To-Go-03182-Y-Cable/dp/B0002GUBIS/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1358117044&sr=8-1&keywords=3.5+mm+female+to+rca+male ) and plug this into the Audio In sockets at the back of your TV - so you have a choice to either listen through BT via this device or just listen normally on TV.
4. THE MOST IMPORTANT "quirk" that I found with this device is that even though it works when charging, if for some reason the power is cut off from the charge, the unit turns itself off - and has to be restarted via the small button located on the device. Originally I had connected it to charge via my TV's built in USB port and hidden it behind the TV , but as soon as I would turn the TV off, the device would switch itself off, and the next time I had to reach behind the TV to turn it back on again. The solution was to connect the charger to the mains and have the device behind the TV in such a way that if needed I could easily reach it to turn it back on again.

I swim 4-5 days a week. Boy let me tell ya it's BORING! Problem with low quality (read: CHEAP) earbuds is they sound HORRIBLE. It's already a challenge to produce good quality audio UNDERWATER, somehow these X-1s were able to produce crisp treble, rich midtone and thumping bass.

The real plus with these earbuds are the different size buds provided. If you have somewhat large holes in your ear, with the cheap ones the water is going to leak and break the seal, often ruin the sound. However the fairly large and jumbo sized XL buds this X-1 provided makes a GREAT seal. The material used in the earbuds are very flexible and high quality. The wetter the better seal.

However the downside is sometimes when removing the earbuds from the ear might have the buds stuck and it can get tricky to remove it and reattach to the headphones.

The cords are not as flimsy as the cheap ones. I suggest you wrap them around your ear. Most of the problem I experienced with ear buds become loose during swimming is due to the movement of the cords leading to the buds. Sometimes repeating tugs would eventually loosen them and might end up falling out. What I suggest you to do is wrap the cords leading to the buds around your ear, you can swim all you want and they shouldn't become loose.

As for cleaning I usually rinse out and shake any water lose. Sometimes they do get stuck inside the buds. You don't want that.

Overall this pair of earbuds sounds good, fits comfortably and built sturdy. Give them a try and skip the cheap ones.

service\\" while I recharge it's expensive built in battery. I

FM tuner. When I first bought one of these it was hard to

Lousy software. Windows media player is NOT good for
managing this unit. I use Rhapsody and it works great. It
took some time and persistence on my part but I now under-
stand how to use and manage these players.

No video capability.

Relatively small capacity. The largest unit available holds
4 gigs. That's more than enough for me but it's not for
everyone.

Bad headphones. So what else is new? I can't remember the
last time I got decent headphones with a music player whether
it was a tapedeck (I am a member ofthe over 50 set who used

mini disc player, or mp3 player.

I really like these units. I know what their limitations are and I can easily live with them. I am sorry to see that none of the newer mp3 players (not even SanDisk) run on \\"disposable\\" batteries. They are all powered by very expensive to replace built in batteries. January 2012.

I had spent over 3 months researching players and finally settled on the RCA2850.  There isn't much bad to say about this model, although a few things kept it from getting 5 stars.  My principle concern was space and having 20Gb makes the difference.  I've got over 1200 songs on it already and still have over 14Gb to spare.    Keep in mind however, the majority of my music is ripped 128K WMA.  I've found MP3 at the same rate to be slightly more expensive spacewise, and I personally haven't noticed a sound quality difference.  So obviously higher bitrates will result in more used space.    Physically, the construction is solid.  Metal is the primary material (instead of cheaper plastic) and the controls don't feel flimsy.  The one minus is that sometimes it takes a few times for the control to register with the player.  Don't know if it's a firmware or a hardware issue, but every now and then it can become annoying.  The size surprised me.  It's much smaller than I would've thought and I am very happy with it.    Integration with PC.  Since it's a portable HD, my PC (Windows XP) recognized as such and had no trouble dealing with it as a normal drive.  Drag and drop files as you choose.  Most of my music is already in folders since I've ripped my entire CD collection on it using Windows Media Player and it puts everything in self named folders.  The profiling tool (either on the player itself or the software) does a GREAT job.  If your tags are correct, it'll sort them all for you.    The other minus I see is that when you have so many songs and artists, navigation can slow down.  Albeit, it's still easy to browse, it's just not very fast.  Clearly nothing beats the iPod on physical navigation.  Some pluses.  The display is fantastic.  It's backlit and sizable so normal sized song and artist names show entirely on the display.  While playing, there is a visible progress bar that shows where you are in the song as well as time elapsed, song, artist, genre, year, format, and bitrate.  All very informative.  The sound quality is very good and I haven't noticed drop offs in playback versus the CD.  128K seems to be fine.    The controls.  It would certainly do RCA well to include a manual as there is a bit of a learning curve.  The online manual is fine, but there's something about reading a book that makes the difference.  I have yet to figure out if there's a way to randomize the entire contents of the player rather than by folder (artists, genre, etc).  The are some other quirks with the firmware (as probably all do).  I've had it freeze up once, particularly when using the pause feature when shuffle is enabled.  Again, not often enough to make you mad but sometimes enough to be annoyed.    The FM-record is a nice include.  However, in practice it probably doesn't give you much considering the quality is only so-so.  My primary use for it is to record songs off the radio that I want to remember to acquire.  A voice recorder would do better for this purpose and another minus is no line-in functionality.    Packaging of the player is very good.  RCA did well to include all of your necessary peripherals.  A soft cover case, cassette adapter, audio plugs, headphones, power supply, and car power adapter, and USB cable.  The cassette adapter was very cheap and did not sound good.  I would recommend getting a good one.  And obviously the headphones as well (as most of them are when bundled with players).    Overall, I'd highly recommend this player.  If RCA could improve the navigation speed and fix some of the quirks, I would say it's right up there with the iPod (Obviously, I'm saying the iPod is the top at this point).  I'd also appreciate more format support.  Right now it supports WMA/Secure WMA/MP3.  But if you've been agonizing over a decision, let me sway you toward this model.  This choice wouldn't be good for you however if you needed line-in capability.  Otherwise, go with this model.

I've used this unit since Feb '10, purchased it from Crutchfield when it came out.    Pros:  1) The Garmin based GPS navigation is far and away better than most factory navigation programs that I've seen.  Secondly, the unit is essentially a Garmin Nuvi.  One look at the file structure on the unit (hooking your computer up to the mini-USB port in the back of the unit) shows a typical Garmin based directory which also means that the maps should be upgradeable using the Navteq updates Garmin sells - or using the version you have if you bought a Garmin GPS unit recently.  I don't see why you would have to wait for the unit-specific upgrade, the normal GPS data should work just fine.  We'll see when I upgrade it myself.    2) The unit comes with a rolling color scheme.  It's a small thing, but the option to match your interior lights in your car is nice.    3) I have had zero problems with the unit since February.  I have not fiddled with any firmware or other major software updates.  My wife plugged her iPhone into the unit and it worked just fine as well.  Bottom line, 10 months of use and no problems.  If you want to bypass the video lock feature so your passenger can watch movies as you drive, just look on the kenwood USA forums.  It's easier than on the Pioneer units, from what I understand.    Cons:    1) Boot up time is pretty slow.  The unit is, naturally hooked up to your car power, so if you drive a manual tranny, and you happen to stall in slow traffic, driveway, etc., when you restart the engine, the GPS will go on/off.  However, it will resume navigation from the last set destination immediately upon reboot.    2) I'm thinking of purchasing the KNA-NT100, which is the Navteq FM based traffic information source.  Frankly, the unit should comes with this.  Combined with the DVD player and the aux-in and iPod/iPhone connection, you have everything that you and your passenger could use during a long drive.  However, you will have to pay for the wiring for the apple products and the FM traffic receiver.  El cheapo mp3 players, like the one I have, can be plugged into the USB port, but I don't think players like Microsoft's zune or more advanced ones which hide the directories on the device will work with the USB function on the receiver.  You can, however, plug an aux-in cable in and just play your audio through that (as I do).    3) Menus are slow and the UI looks pretty dated.  However, you have a user upgradeable GPS unit, with a nice big touch screen (which is resistive, so you can use it with your gloves on - something you can't do with a capacitative screen such as your smartphone during the winter in the Northeast) which has quite a few nice features.    The unit only got 4 stars because my brother's HTC HD2 simply won't get detected by this unit.  My blackberry bold 9650 and the wife's iphone 4 (and her old LG KF900) were detected just fine, but apparently there are some bluetooth incompatabilities, and the HD2 is one of them.  If you want to use that phone in particular with your navigation unit...well, SOL.  Since this unit is in my car and not his, however, it's a great unit for me.    No complaints here.
