Brief Summary:

Pros:

-Exceptionally fast charging output: when compared to my ANKER (great for a completely dead phone)
-Integrated input (standard USB) and output (micro-USB) cables w/included extension, you don't need to carry a seperate micro-USB cable, though you might have to lug an extra extension (see Cons below).
-Attractively designed
-Dual port charging: there's actually 3 total outputs if you count the integrated microusb cable.
-Affordable
-New Trent Support: I haven't had to use it for this device yet, but I called for a question regarding my car charger from New Trent and customer service was friendly, quick and IN AMERICA. They certainly gave me the impression that they care about customers, which is really outstanding for a smaller tech company, just search their reviews on Amazon... they do good work.

Cons:

-Size: for the capacity of this device, I think that they New Trent might have either added more battery power or make it a bit smaller, but I'm no engineer so I'm not sure if this was a trade off for the integrated input/output cables. It's not really something you'd want to carry in your pants pocket unless you're wearing cargo pants. Fits nicely into smaller bags/purses though.
-Charging: It takes a while for the device to charge even when using 1Amp chargers. From a completely drained device to full charge, I'd say it took about 4-5 hours, though this is still much better than my Anker Astro2 which seems to take a good 6-8 hours (though to be fair it has a higher capacity of 8400 mAH), but that's to be expected. The issue I run into was forgetting my extension cable and having to plug this into the wall with my HTC charger. The device had to dangle off of the wall since the integrated cable was so short. So it's a bit of a trade off to have to make sure you carry around an extra extender cable. Also the one that's included is fairly short. So it's nice to have the convenience of not having to worry about having a micro USB cable, but the one thats built in is REALLY short. An integrated retractable cable would be AWESOME. so perhaps in a future revision.
-Documentation: There isn't much in the way of documentation in regards to whether or not it's okay to use the tablet port for charging a phone device, or info on how you would use it to charge a Nintendo 3ds.

Additional comments:

I'm a fan of New Trent's devices and service, and own two of their other devices already. I also have an ANKER Astro2 8400mAH device of similar nature that works similarly to this so I have been fortunate to have a few other devices to compare them to. The things that really impressed me about the NT70T was how quickly it charged my phone (HTC One X/Evo 4G LTE) vs my old and comparable ANKER Astro2 8400mAH. Both devices have a 5V/2.1A output port, however the New Trent device was able to charge my phone to from 0% charge to 30% in about 15-20 minutes, which was more than I needed to make an hour long phone call. This is superior than even the HTC supplied power adapter.

Design:

The size of the device is bigger than my ANKER Astro2 which also has a larger capacity (8400mAH vs 7000mAH), in comparison the Astro2 has a much denser feel to it, and feels noticeably more compact. If size of chargers is going to be an issue because you plan on carrying this in your pocket WITH your phone, you will need some fat pockets. It is perfect for thowing in a purse or backpack though, which I think is the intention anyways. I find the NT70T to be reasonably sleek and attractive, however the back plastic does have a cheap hollow feeling to it, and durabilty might be an issue as the device sees more use. I don't know if this is a tradeoff for having integrated cables for charging and output.

The glossiness of the front surface is very much a fingerprint magnet similar to the front surface of a phone, but being that there is no screen being lit, fingerprints are very obvious, it looks pretty grimy after playing with it a few days.

As far the location of the primary button, I think it might be better if there was a button the the outer edge of the device. If I were to grasp this device in the dark, moving my fingers around to search for the button is a bit harder to do. I can see that it might be an APPLE like design, but I think that the function would just work better on the top or side of the device. The added bonus of integrated usb charging input and microusb is really nice, even though the cables for charging are so short. This generally isn't an issue when the device is charging other devices, however, when plugging this into a computer or wall plug it can be difficult to extend, and having to make sure you are carrying the extension cable means that you have one additional cable you are required to carry unless you are able to rest the device on to something. This can be a bit of an issue if you lose the extender and may be forced to leave the device hanging from a wall or USB port. It's a trade off but something to keep in mind. I think having an extra microusb port for charging, or having a longer retractable cable for charging would resolve this issue.

Function:

It takes a while to charge the device, but this is pretty much true for all devices in this category, as I tried to use a few different chargers, including my IPAD 10volt/1amp charger, and my 5v/1amp charger. It took about 4-5 hours from an empty battery on either one. With that in mind however, the output charge rate was phenomenal for my phone. I was able to charge my 2100mAH phone at a rate that seemed faster than my wall charger by far about two times before running out of energy. The device itself works wonderfully for its primary function, and I trust New Trent as a brand.

I purchased one of these from another vendor for about $130 shipped. I have used it for several months, including the collar mic, surveillance kits, multiple antennas, both as an amateur radio operator and in public safety. It works fine with good audio quality, but there are a few issues:

The radio's scan feature is crippled. If the radio is in scan, and you press the button to turn on the backlight, it stops scanning. If you press the button to turn on the LED, it stops scanning. If you try to lock the keypad, it stops scanning. If you want to change which channels are included in the scan, you have to reprogram it from a computer. You can't even use the dual VFO feature while in scan mode - even though the second channel is still shown on the screen, it is never checked.

The radio itself has developed a problem. Under certain circumstances which aren't entirely clear, it will occasionally completely reset itself. I suspect this is due to a power connection issue inside the radio, but for something this cheap I'm not surprised. I'm probably going to replace it and use the broken one as a base station radio.

The belt clip, where it connects to the battery, is too tight. It takes serious effort to remove the belt clip. Which would be fine, except that it's also weak. The piece that actually fits in to the battery has broken on me, necessitating a replacement. In fact, all of the plastic pieces here are of significantly poorer quality than what you would get with, say, a Motorola.

I have used the longer antenna. It's too long to use in the field, but as a base antenna it works fine and does improve quality. While we're talking about antennas, on my original antenna the plastic piece has chipped, resulting in the actual antenna coming out of it at an angle. It still works, but yet another example of poor materials. The replacement antenna, the end cap fell off and got lost, so I had to cover it with gaffer's tape.

The surveillance earpiece works fine. The surveillance microphone does not. I am told that it results in a 'muffled' sound which is barely readable. The collar mic works fine.

DC/DC Boost Converter with LM2587S Voltage Regulator. Input: 3.5V to 30V. Output: 4.0V to 30V.

I want to thank all who contributed their insights on the DC/DC Boost Converter with LM2587S Regulator. Since the converters did not have their own instructions, the experiences of others were very valuable to me. So, I decided to do my own tests for a future thermoelectric generator application. Given my abbreviated verification testing was rudimentary at best; the results showed the converters work.

Note. The LM2587 is rated for 5A, but that's a maximum rating for a particular application. Other components in this converter impose limits: the SS34 diode has a 3A rating and 40V [repetitive] peak inverse voltage max. The capacitors are limited to 35V max. Please keep these limits in mind.

So, the purpose of this exercise was to test and compile instructions for the DC/DC boost converter. Test instrumentation and other equipment included a regulated DC power supply, a fuse assembly, digital multimeter and the requisite test leads.

The procedures included first placing a 2 ampere (A) fuse in series with the negative input lead from a regulated DC power supply and setting its potential to 5-volts (V). Initially, I tried to adjust the converter while connected to a 100 load resistor as others suggested. This closed circuit method did not work for me. Thus, all adjustments were done “open circuit”.

I then turned the converter’s potentiometer (blue trim pot) counterclockwise (CCW) with it connected to the 5V supply and adjusted the converter’s output to 18V.

The 18V output remained stable even with a 3V input potential. With a 3V input, the converter’s input current fluctuated from 0.01 to 0.02A, but the 18V output was essentially stable. Increasing the input to 4V stabilized the current at 0.01A. So, I set each converter for an 18VDC output given a 4VDC input.

I also checked each converter’s output before making any adjustments. In each case, the “factory default” converter output ranged from 20 to 22VDC. I could not verify the “3x rule” whereby the output should not exceed the input by a 3:1 ratio.

I reviewed the LM2587 specification sheet and applications notes; available from Texas Instruments and National Semiconductor websites. The LM2587 “Simple Switcher® 5A Flyback Regulator” is the only active component - the converter’s overall function relies on it. The spec sheets do not cite a “3x rule”.

Per the specification sheet, when used as a boost (step-up) switching regulator, the LM2587 produces an output voltage greater than the input supply voltage; it does not mention a specific ratio. Though this particular converter design could have this limitation.

If your PC cannot see the device from the beginning it could be a driver issue, or in some cases other devices on your PC could be interfering. Some built in card readers can have problems with Rock Chip devices. If you have the know how you temporarily disable the onboard reader in the Device Manager and try connecting the player. I have been quite happy with this player. It has most of the features of more expensive players without costing a lot.    Appearance: The feel of the unit has a velvety/rubbery texture to it that I find nice and easy to grip. The surface size is not much bigger than a credit card, which is something I like, but it does mean that the viewing screen is not very big. I'll be mainly using this for playing music, so that wasn't a big factor in my decision. The color display is pleasant and sharp, with several options available to display information about the track being played. There is no belt clip or wrist strap attached to it, so it must go in a pocket or armband (again, not important to me but I state this purely for information).    Sound: This unit does not have speakers, so it must be used with headphones or external speakers. I have noticed no distortion of sound through either earbuds or my car speakers. The included earbuds (which I was not sure I could expect as it's not in the product description) are the large variety with the Sansa brand. I find this type of earbud to be difficult to use so I opted to use a different set.    Features: Internal memory is 4GB and there is a MicroSD expansion slot which I have yet to use. The FM radio picks up stations quite well. An equalizer function is available from the main menu for adjusting sound. The connecting jack is not a USB type but the wide type that is standard on most iPods. My understanding is that iPod docks will work with it, although I have not yet tested this. A voice recording function is included. A clock function is not.    Navigation: For the most part I like the way this navigates. It has a standard click-wheel and a dedicated main-menu button for easy switching of modes without interrupting the track or station currently playing. A playlist can be easily assembled on the fly, even as tracks are playing. Supposedly there is a way to load playlists from a computer to the unit, but this has not workedfor me so far, and it's the only reason that I did not give my review 5 stars.     Miscellaneous: This unit was not shipped with a user manual, but one can easily be found online at the manufacturer's website. I use mine with Windows Media Player with no problems, and I believe that iTunes and others also work seamlessly with it.    Conclusion: If you want a low-cost MP3/MP4 player with a fair number of bells and whistles, this is a unit you would do well to consider.

They all sound really quite nice with the exception of the horrible ear buds that come with the player.  But hey, they are ear buds and will sound bad anyway.  The radio thing is nice but not a deal maker or breaker IMO. In any case, it draws good clear signal.  My biggest complaint is the interface.  The menu set-up is not extremely intuitive and the controls take some getting used to.  Maybe I'm old fashioned but the wheel thing seems like a way to make something that should be easy more difficult.  When I am in a song menu, I can't tell you how many times I've tried to simply press down and nothing happens. In most menu's it forces you to use the wheel.  The other part about this is that it is not always consistent.  Some menus you press the middle button to select and others you press to the right.  Sometimes you can use up-down other times you can't.  Really kind of a mess in that regard.  Finally, there is an expandable memory slot but the manual itself does not really explain anything about this at all.  I put my SD card in and expected the player to prompt me about formatting it or something much like my cellphone did when I put one in it.  I scrolled through the menus and couldn't find a thing about it.  The manual they provide is also mum on this point.  I have not filledthe player past internal capacity yet so I'm not worrying about it but it seems to me if you have a feature like this that sets you apart from your main competitor - IPOD - you would make a huge friggin deal about it in the owners manual.    In, summary:    Pros -    1. Great MP3 player.  Nice sound.  Decent equalizer.  2. Expandable memory.  3. Radio.    4. Radio and Sound recording.  5. PRICE!!!  6. Good Battery life (so far).    Cons -    1. Small screen.  2. Moderately difficult and cumbersome menus and interface.  3. Manual is not comprehensive.  4.  No wall charger included.

Pros:

-Portable. How many other speaker systems can fit in a shirt pocket for transport and use found objects as the sounding board?

-Scalable. Daisy chain together for more output

-Entertaining. It's fun to place the speaker on different objects and see what kind of sound you get. A hollow-core bifold door makes for a terrific speaker box. An aluminum cookie pan... not so much, but creates cool metallic sound effects.

-Educational. This is a great physics toy for kids. They learn all about material pliability and sympathetic frequencies.

-Surprisingly good bass, depending on the material and the size of the enclosure. Try a large shoebox or a fitness ball.

Cons:

-Obviously this isn't the highest quality you'll get from a speaker. As long as you keep in mind that this product is about convenience, not quality, you'll be okay.

-The winding mechanism for the audio cord can be a bit tricky.

-I don't like having to use replaceable sticky pads. This product might be better served with a clip attachment rather than a stick-on, but I understand that would increase the form factor and wouldn't work for every application.

Useful for:

-Beach or poolside fun

-Any outdoor situation where you already have a sounding board available (like a styrofoam cooler or beach ball)

-Office. Attach to the side of your trash/recycle bin :)

We installed these in a 2010 Highlander with cloth seats. The beige matches the cloth close enough that they don't stand out much. We were worried that the leather-esque material wouldn't look right with cloth but it's actually an unobtrusive contrast.
Quality of materials seems pretty good and the workmanship is very good. The adjustable posts made getting them in very straightforward once you figured out which size adapters might be needed. The plastic sleeves that slide over to beef it up are marked so it didn't take long to match up what we needed.
As other reviews have mentioned, if you're looking for installation instructions with this you won't find anything useful. A few videos online later and we figured out how to lift the seat covers enough to fish the wires down. Every make and model is different so this step was probably the most difficult. Once you get the wires down we found that one of the wires was too short to pull out enough and connect, so we skinned up our knuckles after slipping a hand in to connect the pin ends correctly.
Once you get the posts in, the wires pulled through, and the wires connected to their individual cords, you've hit the fun part. Since there are no instructions we're still not sure we connected the RGB cables correctly for the "master" player feature. It seems like this is something you have to set up through the remote controllers, and unfortunately the useless operation instructions are even more useless at this point. Luckily my husband is a whiz with that stuff so he mashed buttons and they worked. You will also need to decide how you want to power these things up. The power lines aren't incredibly long and are just two plain wires. Using w/ E11 and ATH-M40fs and iPhone 4. The design and idea is a great one. Keep the E11 in close to the iDevice w/ the rubber band provided w/ the E11/5/your#, and: keep the bundle in one secure place. The ATH-M40fs has a long cord- something to deal with in its own right- but that is an advantage to keep from bumping or yanking on the bundle. The i-connection is very very stable and does not move.  The 3.5 mm Male end, on the other hand, is remarkably lean, and I'm not sure how else to describe it: if you bump or pick up or tug the bundle, you'll get static, possibly a disconnect. I tried using the LOD to a female-female to my ATH's and the same thing: if the connection to the f-f gets moved, you'll get static. Not sure why it's so picky; the male-male cable that comes with the E11 to the headphone on the iPhone doesn't have this problem.  So, just be aware that the 3.5 male end is a little finicky about any movement. Otherwise, it's a great design, and attractive, and useful, especially if you use the rubber band that comes w/ the amplifier. Some other reviewer mentioned hissing, and I think they may be on to something. Everyone mentions 10 hours as the magic number for burn-in, and I already hit that with the headphones- and there is still a little less hiss, but it's only around w/ the L9: that should go away as well. There is much better audio using the L9 versus the headphone cable: that is probably the other reason people buy it besides the attractive design. Once you get it connected and you're music is playing: don't move the bundle. 'Nuf said here!

I bought this for my 2011 Buick Enclave. It had the GM factory radio with XM but w/o navigation. The fit and look – form factor, shade of black, texture and matte of the plastic – are perfect matches for the vehicle. Even the backlight is the exact green of the Buick (the backlight color is not changeable, not that I can see anyway). The integration is also very good – steering wheel controls work w/o a separate steering wheel interface; all the chimes for key in the ignition, power lift gate up/down, turn signals, etc. work as before, though the chimes sound different; XM radio integrates through the factory wiring harness to the vehicle’s XM receiver and antenna, with nothing special required.

As for function, it is obviously not a GM product. I’m comparing it to the factory nav unit in my ’07 Suburban. The user interface is different – cooler in some ways and not so much in others. In my Suburban I can get a split screen – half nav, half radio/CD. In this unit you play an FM station let’s say, then you go to nav, and you still hear the FM station but see only the nav. When you change stations up/down the stations change, but you don’t see what station you are on. If you change modes (go to XM) it leaves the nav screen and goes to the XM screen, but you can go back to the nav screen and the destination you punched in is still there. There is another mode that automatically switches between nav and media display, but I don’t like that mode at all.

Other than the lack of the split screen, the display looks great, the touch screen works great, and the audio sounds great. However, switching between modes (radio, XM, DVD, etc.) is a little slow in my opinion. The navigation is your typical navigation. It does the job, and whether you like the look or not is subjective. It doesn’t look like Garmin, or GM factory, or Android, but it works fine. When I first start up navigation it takes a while to acquire all the satellites, but when it does the signal meter shows full strength. When you switch from radio to nav there is a brief cut-out of the front audio, and then it cuts back in (rear audio continues seamlessly). The ability to load a ton of music and videos on an SD card and play it on the unit is very nice. Selecting the file to play is very comparable to selecting a file on your computer and clicking on that file to play it – no frills.

Bluetooth is just okay. The Astrium phone interface is cool, but it’s not highly functional for my Android phone – I can use the keypad to dial out, but my work’s VM system struggles recognizing the digit presses when I use the Astrium interface, whereas it recognizes them perfectly when I use my phone. The placement (to the side and not the bottom) of the *, 0, and # buttons is very cumbersome to a spatially oriented person like me. Also, for me the call history is not populating at all. Plus, there is no voice-activated dialing, no ability to synch contacts, and no viewable device list. Because I can’t see a paired device list, I do not know if the unit remembers multiple paired devices (I’m assuming it does). I just know it pairs with my phone and remembers my phone. To the person I am calling the Astrium microphone sounds fine, but not as good as the GM integrated microphone in my Buick. The phone’s music through BT sounds great, but it’s cumbersome to switch to it.

It turns out my Buick’s BT is integrated into the vehicle, not the factory radio, so my wife’s phone auto-synchs with the Buick BT, and my phone auto-synchs with the Astrium BT (intentionally). When I’m synched with the Astrium BT the car doesn’t know anything about it; it’s all handled by Astrium, which means the talk button on the steering wheel does nothing for Astrium BT phone calls. When my wife is on a call the steering wheel talk button works, and the vehicle turns down the radio volume and takes overthe speakers for the phone call. She can use the Buick voice-activated dialing, but of course she can’t listen to her phone music.

For installation, if you’re familiar with car audio/video installation and/or have watched a dozen YouTube videos on how to do it, this installation is very straightforward and simple. You don’t need to create a wiring harness or splice wires; you don’t have to worry about any kits or adapters; it really is plug-and-play. But if you’re not familiar with car audio/video installation, the documentation is insufficient, and it was obviously written by a non-native English speaker. Astrium is a Canadian company and my unit shipped from Canada, but I don’t know where they manufacture the unit or write the docs.

There were a few loose wires on the wiring harness that I couldn’t figure out and that the documentation didn’t explain clearly, so I emailed eTraverse (the dealer) for help, and they sent me a set of dropbox links for better documentation in PDF. You want to get those docs. I took a photo of the unit with wiring harness attached before I installed it.
1. This is the included wiring harness for my vehicle which does not have Bose audio. There is a separate wiring harness, also included, if you have the Bose audio. The two connectors at the end mate directly with the factory connectors in the dash.
2. These are the loose wires that I didn’t fully understand at first. Three (yellow, black, red) are to provide power to an external CD changer. The blue wire labeled BACK receives a signal when the car is in reverse to switch the Astrium unit to the rear camera input signal. My Buick already has a rear camera with the display sent to the rearview mirror, so I didn’t use this. The blue/white wire labeled BRAKE (most units use a light green wire for this) is supposed to be tied to the parking brake. Here’s how that works…
You punch in a code on the unit and it takes you to factory configurations, one of which is for BRAKE CTRL. The OFF setting lets you ignore the brake signal and play the DVD or SD video whenever (car is in park or in motion). The LEVEL and PULSE settings expect a ground on the BRAKE wire when the car is in park, and will only play the video when ground is present (car is in park). If you set it to LEVEL or PULSE and the BRAKE wire is not connected to the parking brake, you’ll never see video because there will never be a ground on that wire. Look, I am a disciplined driver but my teenage children are not. I don’t want them to be able to watch a video while they’re driving. I thought that since this unit is so plug-and-play the wiring harness had that brake signal in there somewhere, but mine doesn’t, so I have to go back in and connect that wire. In other units you (or better your passenger) also cannot punch in a new navigation destination when the vehicle is in motion, and that is controlled by the same wire, which means you have to pull over to punch in a new destination. In this unit you can enter in a new destination when the vehicle is in motion, regardless of how the BRAKE CTRL is set.
3. This is the radio antenna plug. Apparently GM uses a smaller antenna plug than what’s considered standard/universal, and this mates directly with the GM antenna wire in the dash. With a generic unit I would’ve needed an antenna cable adapter.
4. This coax connector is for the GPS antenna. The antenna comes with the unit and has a very long wire to route the antenna to the top of the dash. I mounted the antenna on a flat horizontal surface inside the dash, and it works fine. On the car’s exterior is ideal; on top of the dash is good; inside the dash is adequate depending on how much bulk is above the antenna.
5. It’s tough to make out but this is an auxiliary wiring harness connector array. The jumper cable that you see there from the main wiring harness is justaccessory power and ground I think. There is a wire for iPhone/iPod in, which I am not using. There is a wiring harness for 5.1 audio out, which I am not using. There is a wiring harness for rear camera and radar (parking sensor) in, which I am not using because those things are already integrated into my car. There is a wiring harness for audio/video out to an overhead monitor or two headrest monitors, which I am not using now but may add later. There is a wiring harness for audio/video in from an overhead or headrest DVD player, in case you want to route those signals directly into your stereo. If you don’t care about the video signal, most car DVD players have an FM modulator to send the audio to your stereo via an FM signal.

I took several hours to read through the documentation and view some YouTube videos. If you can’t find a YouTube video that shows you how to remove your car’s dash panels, just watch several videos for other cars and you’ll get the idea. The actual installation took me about an hour to remove the dash panel, uninstall the factory radio, install the new unit, and replace the dash panel. The only tools I used were a plastic panel remover and a screwdriver with a 7mm socket head. I also used one cable tie to bundle up the loose wires on the harness that I’m not using. That’s it, very easy, too easy. If I had mounted the GPS antenna on top of the dash, and connected a rear camera, and connected an external DVD player, I’m sure the installation would have taken hours. Good luck.

1. Length - I have a automatic on the floor, and when in park this sticks out so far as to run into the shifter. If I dump a book onto a thumb drive or SD card, and fire it up, more often than not, it will start somewhere in the middle, even if the book consists of 200 files, numbered 1-200. This (I have found can be remedied by instead of copying files onto the drive / card by syncing a media player play list containing all the files to it instead. Not a huge pain, but it would be nice to have it always unerringly start at the beginning, when you are beginning.

Look VERY carefully at the picture for this product.  Note 3 things:  1) The louvers are horizontal  2) The louvers are FIXED (do not adjust up or down)  3) The position of the louvers in relationship to the driver.    Let's look at these three areas more closely...    1) There are two support posts on the back of the mount which will go over and attach to the top horizontal louver... so the louver MUST be horizontal.  2) If the louvers are NOT fixed (up or down), the weight of the Garmin unit will cause the mount along with your Garmin to hang flacidly downward in a position where you can't see the screen (it will face the floor).  3) The mounting bracket swivels left and right... but not up or down.  Therefore, if the position of your vents are too high or too low in relationship to the driver,  you might be disappointed in your ability to see the screen clearly in different light conditions.    However.....    If you meet all the above criteria,  this IS the unit for YOU!  I loved mine... I just wish someone had told me about the \\"fixed\\", non-adjustable (up or down) louver requirement...     Of importance to note:  When I realized this was not the unit for me, I e-mailed the seller, and was cheerfully and promptly issued an RMA and a refund.  So, even if this is not the right unit for you, (there are others)... I recommend this seller very highly.

Just took this for a 40+ mile bike ride in Washington, DC and Virginia (the WO&D trail) and it worked extremely well. Not a completely flawless device but very pleasantly surprising in some ways as well.

Here's how this product breaks down:

PROS:

- Loud, rich, clean mono sound from its single top firing speaker
- Internal mounting of iPod inside the speaker is solid and well thought out
- Overall construction of speaker and bike mount is very solid and rugged
- Battery life is good, device stayed strong for over four hours of riding
- Easy in-speaker recharging of the iPod so it doesn't have to be removed, although that is simple and fast as well
- Nice protective cap for the speaker in case it starts raining or gets muddy, easily stowed on bottom of speaker otherwise
- Easily mounted and rugged remote control for handlebars
- All parts firmly snap together for easy stowage (speaker, cap, remote) in the high quality heavily padded storage bag that comes with it

CONS:

- The device uses four regular non-rechargeable AA batteries to power the speaker instead of a rechargeable battery like most iPod speakers in this price range.
- Unit's remote control batteries arrived dead, indicating that these will have to be replaced often (uses 2 CR2032s)
- Shock mounting for the iPod is not all it could be, had one lock up on the trip that could be attributed to it.
- There are no support pages for this device on the company's Web site, unlike their other products.
- The device points the speaker up at the rider but the sound is sometimes hard to hear on some tracks when moving at high speed.

Overall a complete win if you ask me, there is no competing iPod speaker products that even come close for bike use.

First, if you’re looking for a solid dash cam and have found that reviews are few and far between you can finally stop looking, this is the camera you want! That said let’s get into the details!

Un-Boxing- Remember your first iPad or iPod or iPhone, these guys were paying attention! They have put this thing together in a very Applesque design, the box opens from the middle, the cam is packaged to be seen once the box is open and there is another box under with accessories.

Let’s look at the accessories and get them out of the way, a Micro-SD to USB key, they include what you need to actually use the device! No fiddling around at a Max or Depot to find a card reader if you don’t already have one, they have it in the package along with several wire clips to neatly trim out the power adapter once you mount the cam with the included high temp 3M tape. They thought of everything for you so this rig is ready to be used once you get it… Almost but we’ll get to that in a minute.

The cam is sleek, 1 inch in diameter and about 4 inches long, both ends have functionality like turning on/off the Wi-Fi or disabling voice prompts and the mount has a lock that will keep the cam in place once you install it but it’s not too difficult to remove when you need to.

There is a Micro-SD in the cam that ships standard, it’s 16 GB and should hold about 5 to 6 hours of footage in a FiFo format so once it’s full it will re-write the oldest file. The software to view footage is on this card, load the card into the provided USB key and browse to the software folder, install the viewer and not only can you view footage along with moving maps via Google (the cam has a built in GPS) but it’s also the fastest and easiest way to configure the settings.

Now here is what I suggest, there is newer firmware online, find it and download it, there are a few improvements on how the camera handles bitrates for recording and video quality. My cam shipped with the previous rev and the latest had come out nearly 2 months prior, once upgraded I found the camera to be much better in WiFi connection stability and better bitrates at High Quality video.

The firmware installs on your machine then copied to the MicroSD card which then applies itself to the camera once it’s rebooted. There are several warnings in the process, don’t remove the card when the camera is on, don’t pull power while it’s updating, the basics.

The complete process is painless and the steps are simple, install their software, install and run the firmware update tool, make sure the MicroSD is in your card reader or the supplied USB Key, let the process complete (2 mins) re install the MicroSD card in the cam and power up the cam in your car, 2 minutes later you’ll hear her tell you she’s recording and you’re up and running.

Install the cam in the middle of the windshield just behind the mirror, run your wire to the power port / lighter adapter in your car and download the BlackVue software to your i-Device or Android phone, this is the cool part, the cam has WiFi and you can view your cam LIVE in your car to set it up! The app will also let you view recorded files so you can actually show the officer what really happened and even give him a copy of the files for their report. All you have to do is tune your device to the cam’s WiFi and enter in the password, the default is blackvue however when you had the MicroSD card connected to your computer you had the option to change the password of the cam (best if you do) so type that in and navigate to LIVE, setup your cam (Aim etc), disconnect and let it run.

Important, if your power port is live all the time (mine turns off with the car) then you’re going to need to remember to remove the plug to power down the cam or your battery is going to drain. BlackVue makes a battery saver (charge guard) for about 30 bucks, it’s little harder to install and is basically a timer that after a set period of time will power down the cam. The cam that while your car is parked is also a security cam! If you leave it running it just records while parked so if something happens, you can view it later and find out what, when etc.

Bottom line there is a lot of GOOD in this unit, it’s pricey compared to its cheaper competitors but the quality is there from the minute you turn it on and watch the footage.

Last thing, the footage, the cam is HD but only because there is a 2 mega-pixel camera that qualified it for HD, trust me the video in your iPhone is possibly just a tad better and It’s not the HD you see on your TV at home, it’s good don’t get me wrong but the video’s on YouTube aren't quite telling you everything. For instance, I've found that the only way to read the license plate on a car in front of you is if you’re 3 to 5 feet from their bumper and forget about the ones to your left or right. The cam has an excellent wide dynamic range sensor, what that means is if you’re heading into the morning or afternoon sun, the camera is smart enough to block out the super bright sun and balance the rest of the image so it’s usable but this isn't a broadcast quality 3 chip HD camera by any means.

Is the image good, yes, is it the best you've ever seen, probably not nor will it be from a fewer than 300 dollar device. That said, the image quality is still superb and the software package is sweet when working with the integration to Google Maps.

The CON’s: Poor ability to capture and read license plates off angle and more than a car length in front of you.

The PRO’s: Comes with EVERYTHING you need to get up and running, excellent software package provided on the MicroSD card (no need to download anything and that includes the manual), Good image quality even in low light and especially in hard direct coming at you sunlight, GPS and WiFi integration and excellent mount that keeps the cam behind the mirror and out of the way and good 3rd party phone/device apps.

What would I change, I would like to see the 720p and 1080p modes both run at 10 megabit bit-rates, currently the 720p mode is constant at 8 megabit and 1080p is at 10. I would also be happy if the firmware was changed to 720p/59.94fps from the current 29.97fps. I think that the pixel density of 720p should provie a better image but this firmware steps the bitrate down at 720p rather than keep it the same as 1080p. I'm nitpicking now actually.

Install was a bit of a pain, but that is fault of the CRV and not the camera. If you look above the license plate of the CRV, you will see the OEM light that illuminates the license plate. This is the light that you remove and replace with this camera/LED.

That takes us to the bad, or at least not so great. There are two little LEDs that are supposed to take the place of your license plate light. The image doesn't catch the bumper of the car which would be great so that you know when you are actually going to hit something or not. I like to use backup cameras to get as close to possible to something when backing in (parallel parking for example) and this camera lets you get close but not within a few inches. I suppose that is a positive and a negative.

Lastly on the negative side - it is a great fit but not perfect. It is a tad loose once installed so I used some super sticky tape on the side of the hatch to keep it in place.

Aside from all that, the image quality is fantastic - especially for the price. The image is darn near crystal clear when there is sunlight, and in pitch black the CRV backup lights provide plenty of light to see what you are doing.

The manual is poor, but I suppose you really don't need one. The RCA (video) cable that is included could be a little longer, but you can find 6 foot extensions (or 25' cables if you want to avoid extensions) here on amazon for under 5 bucks. I tied the LED lights to the wiring for the license plate light and the camera power to the nearby reverse light.

Don't get me wrong, this is an excellent mp3 player. Excellent sound quality, build quality, etc. Its only fault is that it just doesn't have enough features to fit my taste. For what it does have, however, it performs excellently. Here are some pros and cons:

PROS:
-Extremely easy to use and upload music. On some other sites with reviews for this player, people complained that it was difficult to understand and upload music. I just don't see how that's possible! I'm far from tech-savvy, and I didn't even have to read the manual. I just clicked the SD card into its slot, plugged in the USB cable into the player and my computer (which recognized it instantly as a removable drive), went to my music folder and copied and pasted songs into the player, and VOILA! that was all there was to it. Even if that was too hard to understand, the manual explains everything even more clearly.
-Nice and compact. It can literally fit in the palm of my hand (and I have a small hand). Even if its in my pocket I sometimes forget its even there!
-Great sound quality. Even with the included no-name brand earphones, the quality was excellent. When I used some of my own earbuds, it got even better.

CONS (Warning: there are a lot more than pros, but these are really just annoyances that can be gotten over and don't lower my high opinion of this player in any way.):
-Practically impossible to see screen without backlight lit. But I just set the backlight to always be on, and that solved the problem without eating up too much battery life in the process.
-Scratches easily. Not as easily as an Ipod Nano (trust me, I've seen how those scratch), but still, a little roughousing with it and some pretty ugly scratches can show up. I cover it with plastic most of the time so there aren't too many on mine. I wish they made cases for it.
-Flimsy battery cover. I wish it was attached to something, it can easily get lost (and I do NOT feel like paying $10 for another one on eBay)
-SD card sticks out slightly. This isn't a problem for me, but it may be for you if you're worried about accidentally pressing the card while the player is on and losing or corrupting an expensive 1 or 2GB sd card.
-*This is only for people who haven't upgraded the firmware* The player does not support folders until you upgrade on the mymusix website, and it does not save settings until you e-mail customer service asking for the 0.25 version (however, I recommend asking for the 0.24 version instead because in the 0.25 version you must manually select settings to be saved on restart and in the 0.24 version it automatically saves the last setting you selected on restart. It also resumes at the last track playing on restart (although not on the exact time, only the beginning of the track.
-Not enough features for me. This player is a solid mp3 player, and that's about it. It has a hole for a microphone function and an icon on the lcd screen labeled \\"PRE\\" for an FM tuner function, but when I e-mailed customer service asking about them they replied that they were not supported for some strange reason. I was disappointed, but decided to get another SD mp3 player - the Coby MPC-751 - which supports these features. It's supposed to be coming in the mail today. Hopefully I'll have another good review to write soon!

I discovered that the flutter is some kind of pick-up that depends on the location and on what you place the unit on.  So for those who get loud hums (especially if they are intermittent), occasional pops and wow, try moving the unit and placing softer mats under it; this will tell you to what extent the noise is coming from the unit or is a pick-up from the environment.  In my case, careful choice of location eliminated the noise.

Just to let everyone know, I have a 2011 KIA Sorento LX and that I bought this system from ANOTHER company, not Koolertron.  This system is a very nice attachment to the dash of the Sorento. This product was made specifically for the 2011 KIA Sorento and it looks like an OEM product when installed. I had the system professionally installed and it couldn't look any better! The product has everything needed to install into your vehicle, however, I had an issue with the wheel controls. It turns out that the KIA Sorento in the US needs an extra harness/wires in order for the wheel controls to work, so check with technician beforehand just in case you need it as well. Once the controls are all set, you can set which buttons you want to do what.  There is a downfall, once the system is connected you'll be giving up a big quality of bass in the sound system, although you can adjust a bit of the bass it won't sound the same as the original but this system can also connect a sub-woofer (if you have one in your car). It can also connect to the flip down DVD/TV console in your car as well which can give the back passengers entertainment as well.   Onto the more important things about the system.   The main screen looks exactly like the picture shown you can make the screen look sharper and clearer by adjusting the contrast, brightness, and it applies for everything else as well.   Radio:   I love the fact that there are 3 different memories that you can store up to 8 each (which makes 24 FM stations in total, if you have that many!). There are also 8 addition slots for AM stations (just in case if you listen to talk shows). DVD:   This is my favorite part of the whole system. The DVD is so clear it looks like you're watching it on TV or your LCD laptop computer! Warning: do not watch while you're driving or else you might end up in an accident but this is a great time killer for your passengers or when you're  not driving and you have time to kill.   TV:  I didn't buy an extra converter box for this function so I won't be able to review it.  Bluetooth:  The Bluetooth works quite well. It works through the speaker system just like the OEM radio. The person receiving the calls will hear everything clearly (tested it quite a bit of time when I called my parents), however, on your side, there might be a small static. Navigation:  The navigation program works adequately. The company will provide you with an SD card that'll have the files to work the navigation system already inside. However, the SD card they might provide will be crap and the system might not recognize the files which as a result, the navigation program won't work. You might need to transfer the files onto a better SD card and put it into the system instead. The Navigation program is I-go. It is pretty good, it'll just look like any other navigation programs on Magellan or Garmin system, but from all the times I use it, it's a bit slow to update turns when you take a different route than the one that they set for you. Also if you have it in \\"Picture in Picture\\" function, the GPS voice will over-ride the radio/dvd/cd every time you turn, so it could get very annoying, especially when you're going on long trips.   USB:   I rarely use this function so I won't review this.  Overall:  I like the system and it works perfectly well with your car. After buying SMC Wireless Receiver (on eBay, that should have been my first clue) and a ZyXEL Music Box, and spending hours on trying to get them to be recognized by my wireless network, I gave up and decided to spend a few more bucks for the Soundbridge.  You get what you pay for, that's for sure.    I had this unit up and running in about 15 minutes.  It immediately recognized my wireless network and allowed me to enter my WEP password.  Immediately after I did, my network software on my desktop popped up a window recognizing that the device was attached to the network.  Hallelujah!  No hassles, easy set up.    Now, the reason I gave it a 4 instead of a 5:  the documentation is weak.  Not nearly as bad as the others, but it could be improved.  The area where it is weak is in navigating through the menus on the device, but after a little experimentation, I mostly figured it out.    What I really like about it is that it will play literally thousands of Internet radio stations without your desktop even being on.  There is an online program called RokuRadio which allows you to preload your favorite stations (accessed on your desktop) - it's user friendly - easy online, then the unit will pick up the stations as you add them.  New stations not already on their list can be added as you find them.  Documentation says that you can create radio favorite playlists with I-Tunes, but I didn't try that.  It also mentions Windows media to do the same, but it gave no instructions on how to do that.  But the online RokuRadio works fine, so that wasn't a real concern.    For playing your wma files (it also plays other formats, but wma is all I have), your desktop has to be on and you have to have a media server working - I have Windows Media Player 11, and it has a media server (Windows Media Connect) embedded in it.  You can create playlists on your desktop, and then the unit will allow you to scroll to and play the playlist.  (NOTE- the unit documentation also lists a couple others including I Tunes that is supposed to work - I didn't have to verify that, as my Windows Media 11 works fine).  It even has a shuffle feature.    I'm having a difficult time figuring out why some of my content is protected - all my music was downloaded to my PC from original purchased CDs.  I'm trying to get some answers about that online in the user forum.    All in all, I'm very satisfied.  Forget the others.  Buy this one.

After watching footage for other cameras out there, both above and below this price point, I found this to be the best \\"bang for the buck\\".
However, while it is a great cam in the daytime, it falls short at night, especially if there are no streetlights around.
Driving at dusk, the iris was constantly adjusting while driving away from the setting sun on a cloudy evening, but what the camera picked up was brighter than it actually was. Images are clear, and you can make out enough of the surroundings that in the event of an issue, you can clearly see what is going on, so long as its in front or to the front-side of you.
Once it got completely dark, the camera became near useless. I could make out lines in the road my headlights illuminated, but not much else on unlit back roads. In the city with streetlights it is better, but again, the constantly adjusting iris means while you can see great UNDER a streetlamp, in between is very much darkness.
The sound quality is great, however, except when I recorded some test footage at its full 1080p resolution, there was background noise which could bother some people. I've read reviews that lower resolutions may not have the noise, I will look into it. However, vehicle noise, outside noise (windows closed) and in-car conversations were picked up beautifully.
I only have two problems, the poor night performance, and the listing on Amazon. BEWARE BUYERS, this camera takes a MICRO SD card, not a 'flash' or regular 'SD' card as suggested by Amazon and the product specs.
Also, if you're like me and have a long commute, get a card larger than 8gig. On my card at full 1080p I have about 50min of space, and that only jumps to 58min at 720p.
Since this is only my first day of having it up and running, I will be playing with the settings, and reporting back if I need to change my review at all.

The G-sensor function is crap. No matter what you set it to (2g, 4g, 8g) it will write-protect files if you hit a bump in the road. You can turn it off, sure, but when I restart the camera, it defaults to the 4g setting. Utterly useless, unless you are pulling the memory card daily to wipe files, because given enough time and enough bumps, the card will be filled with write-protected video files.
I might try to return it, its a major annoyance.

Also, image quality at night is still horrible. Adjusted the white balance through its range and nothing helps. Even with the high beams on driving down a dark country road the image recorded is BLACK. No details at all, unless you happen to have a car's tail lights in front of you, or you're within 20 feet of something. Trees, cars, people, deer, etc.

My family has a two Galaxy S3's, an iPhone 4S and an iPod Touch. We're always on the go, and our devices frequently run out of power. When I go on business trips, the same thing happens to my colleagues and me. The solution? Buy a portable backup battery charger that will work with and charge multiple devices throughout the day, and have enough power to spare in case you lost your charger or the airport charging kiosk is overcrowded.
I used another battery backup device before: The 10,000mAh Anker 3e. It was a great device. It had enough power to charge phones, tablets, and almost anything you could attach to it. The bad? It was too big and heavy to carry around in a laptop/messenger bag when space and weight are a premium.
Enter the New Trent Easypak NT70T. This device weighs only 6.8oz, and is slightly larger than an iPhone 4S, but it has a 7,000mAh rated battery. It's a good balance between being portable, yet powerful. As soon as I received the NT70T, I saw the device had about 75% power. I charged it for a couple hours until it was 100% full, as this is recommended by most battery manufacturers anyway.
Then, I gave the NT70T its first test: Completely recharge the dead battery in a Galaxy S3. The NT70T comes with three charging ports one built in micro-USB, and two USB ports for attaching your own cables. I used the built in cable, which I believe charges at 1.2 amps. With this configuration, it took about 3 hours to charge the S3 to 100%, and the NT70T's auto-off feature shut off the device.
With about 4,300mAh of power left, I used the NT70T to recharge my iPhone 4S. For that, I used the 2.1 amp charging port. The Easypak topped off the battery my iPhone in about an hour. Since I was leaving work that day, I kept the charger attached to my phone while I listened to an audio book for the 45-minute drive home. The result? A fully charged iPhone upon arrival at my house, and still enough power to recharge another Galaxy S3.
As I mentioned, I like the size, weight and capacity of this battery charger, and the built in charging cables (one for power in and one for power out) are handy to have. However, for this to be a fair review, I must comment on some things I don't like:
1.) The charging cables are a good idea, but they are too short and impractical. For example, while trying to charge the NT70T with an AC outlet USB charger, I had to prop-up the charger in order for it to reach the charger. Yes, New Trent includes a USB extension cable, but I would prefer to have the least amount of cables as possible.
2.) The NT70T does not allow for pass-through charging. Thus, if you need to recharge your NT70T and a phone or tablet, you better be sure you have two power sources to charge them concurrently. It's not a deal-breaker, but it would have been nice to have this feature.
In conclusion, if you are looking for a backup battery charger that will recharge your iPod, smartphone, or tablet 3-4 times on a single charge, while not bogging you down with bulk, then this New Trent Easypak NT70T is for you.

Configuring this thing is pretty easy except for the time. Every time I try to configure the time through the I-Road Blackbox Viewer on my PC it tells me invalid date. I set the date for a day ahead of what it currently was and it accepted it, but when I put the micro SDHC card back in the unit it reset the time back to 2012. It was frustrating, but I was determined to have the correct date and time. I spent a while trying different things, and I finally got the time and date to stick.

Here's how to adjust the date and time and make it stick. When you go to set the current time in the I-Road Blackbox Viewer on your PC it will say its invalid, so set it to a day ahead or behind what date is currently at. Go to my computer, and open up the location of the SD card. When you open it up you will see 3 folders providing you have used the unit. The folders will be config, normal, and event. The config folder is what you are looking for. Open the config folder and there should be two .cfg files in there. They are system.cfg, and time.cfg. Depending on the setting of your computer you might not see the .cfg extension, so it will just be files that say time and system. You can edit the time.cfg with notepad. DO NOT attempt to open the system.cfg with notepad because you will corrupt the file.

When you open up the time.cfg there should be one line that looks like this:

time=1404683400,lang=0

The number 6 you see is the dayahead that I set the unit to so I simply changed the 6 to a 5 and saved the file. Next I right clicked on the system.cfg and selected properties. When the properties window pops up set it to "Read Only". When you do this it will prevent the unit from changing the system.cfg back to what it originally was. I also set the time.cfg to read only too. When you put the micro SDHC card back in the unit, and take it out for a test drive it should display the right time and date now. My time was 8 minutes off, but I can live with that.

My unit was running the firmware version 02.00.04 and the I-Road Blackbox Viewer version was 1.0. Depending on your firmware and viewer versions you may, or may not experience the same difficulties in setting the time on your unit.

I don't know why Barnes & Noble decided not to make a full case for their NOOK Glowlight, but that lack sent me looking for a third-party item to fit the bill.

This is a nice little case which fully protects the NOOK, and looks pretty good, for all that it's "2nd class" leather. It certainly beats out the "clip-on" cover sold by Barnes & Noble, which costs more, and only covers the front of the NOOK. This case has a leather pocket, with a cutout for the screen and Nook button, which securely holds the NOOK, and protects bot the front /and/ back of the device. The edges are also covered by the leather hinge and magnetic clasp. There is a mysterious 1/2", prefectly round hole in the back, about 1/4" from the top edge -- but perhaps the case was designed to fit other devices as well as the NOOK Glowlight.

Now the caveat: Although this case is specifically advertised as being for the NOOK Glowlight, I'm not sure that the manufacturer actually had one of these devices available, passibly designing the case from a photo of the NOOK. I say this because the NOOK's power button is located on the upper left edge of the device, which falls right -under- one of the straps that holds the inside pocket in the case.

I was able to remedy this by making a small cutout in the strap with an X-Acto knife, to expose the button. Only took a few minutes, but be careful if you do this -- one slip and you could sever the entire strap. Anyway, this cutout should have been done at the factory, or else the strap should have been located elsewhere.

Once that small modification was made, however, the NOOK slipped right in to the case, and everything worked properly. For the price, this is a good cover for the Glowlight, until and unless Barnes & Noble offers a better one.

I purchased the HP F310 after researching several car dash-cams. I installed it and was able to access its menu to customize some features; 6 screens for a total of 25 items. It has a wide angle view, acquires GPS signals relatively quickly. I set the date and time and set up satellite synchronization; (remember to compensate for Day light savings time). The buttons are \\"soft\\" buttons meaning their function changes depending on what screen your on. The so called \\"emergency\\" recordings are kept in a separate folder so they are not over written until its folder is filed up, then it over rights the oldest one. The regular video files are over written oldest first when its folder fills up; that statement is vague because it depends on the size of the SD card you installed. I installed a 32GB card. You can also set the size of the video files by changing recording length(3 or 5 min) and/or resolution (HD/Full HD). The device itself only displays Km/hr but the supplied application \\"Super Car\\" displays Km/h as well as MPH. The video is a movie file and GPS data is a separate file. Quick Time can play the video file which does display the Date/Time, GPS data which includes recorded speed in Km/H. Super Car will play the video as well as display the GPS data which includes the sensor data, number of satellites available as well as used, compass heading and position using Google maps. It seems to want to load only 1 files at a time and loops it so when it finishes it restarts ( manual alludes to being able to list multiple files). Won't let you setup a play list to display all the files on a trip. It also has about a 30 sec lag between the video file and GPS data display so as you watch the video and compare to your mapped position you are not in the same spot. If you live in an area with speed cameras you can manually enter them in (up to 200) and the unit will warn you as you approach one. You can also set up a speed limit (Km/H) to warn you if you exceed it. The supplied CD contains a users manual (useful-read first), Super Car application, Quick time (down load a newer version), PDF reader (down load newer version). The unit does NOT come with a SD card (required storage device) so go shopping or make sure you purchase one when you purchase this unit, rated class 6 or greater up to 32MB.

I actually rate this camcorder as a 4.5 stars. I bought this camcorder as a replacement for the first one I owned; the first one was stolen at the Natural History Museum in NYC. I decided to replace it only if I could find the exact same one again. Luckily, I found it here at Amazon. This camcorder is sold through an outside vendor, 6Ave. Note: this camcorder records video clips and will take photographs. In this review I use camcorder and camera interchangeably.    The camcorder measures approximately 4.5\\" X 2.0\\" X 2.75\\" (excluding the strap). It weighs 11.1 ounces; it will weigh more once the battery is added to it. I have a 2 hour battery attached and together it weighs a little over 14 ounces. It will come with a 1 hour battery. The total weight will differ because the batteries (1, 2, 3 hours) are different sizes. The left side of the camcorder contains a flip out screen; the screen will rotate up and down (but it will not rotate a full 360 degrees). Once the screen is opened, the camcorder turns on. The screen size is about 2.5\\" by 1.5\\" and is in color. This screen is not a touch screen. Do not touch it or you may end up damaging the screen. In the interior, are 5 buttons; the circular one is the power button (on and off), the three diagonal buttons are for transferring video and photo clips, and the \\"select play/rec\\" will play selected video clips on the camera's view screen. On the right exterior side is the camera strap. All you have to do is simply slide your palm in between the camera and the strap and wrap your fingers around the top and your thumb around the bottom; this is how you hold it. It fits in your palm.    When your fingers are wrapped around the top, your index finger will be in position to manipulate the \\"W-T\\" switch (the zoom mechanism) and the snapshot button (for pictures). This camcorder has a 35X zoom lens. It's amazing how close to the action you can get with this zoom lens. However, be warned: the closer you zoom in, the shakier your video will be or the blurrier you picture will be. Any 'barely there' movements made by your hand will be magnified in your video. I recommend using a tripod (if possible) if you use the maximum range on the zoom lens.     On the back side of this camera, where the battery is located, are three things: a rubber cover that says \\"DC\\" which allows you to plug the camera into a wall to charge the battery, a switch that allows you put the camera into video mode or picture mode, and the \\"start/stop\\" button which is used to record video clips. The \\"start/stop\\" button is placed right where your thumb would rest on the camera.     The bottom of the camera contains a tripod mount and a door where you can place a Micro SD card. This card, an accessory, stores the digital pictures you take. If it is not installed, you will not be able to use the picture mode (take pictures). On the front of the camera, down at the lower left corner of the lens is a rubber cover with the USB logo. This is where you plug in the cord to connect your camera to your computer when you save your clips.     The quality of the video is amazing. It truly reflects an image that is true to the scene you record (i.e. colors). Sound is a different issue. When playing back clips, there will be sound as long as there was noise during the event you record. For example, I recorded a band playing a song standing on their front lawn. Background sound will always be \\"quieter\\" than the sound of the person holding the camcorder. So be warned; this camcorder will pick up the voice of the person recording the scene much more than of the other noises. I speculate that the person making the recorder is the closest person to the microphone.     This camera is very light and portable. I have put the camcorder in its bag and then put the bag in my backpack so I can carry it around when I am out and about. This camcorder is good for all types of situations. I have used mine for: walking tours while I was in England and Ireland, graduation ceremonies, at Seaworld in San Diego, recording my brother's wedding ceremony, in the Monterey Bay Aquarium, and so on. This camcorder works fairly well in low light situations like aquariums, which are fairly dark. If you plan to travel with it, I encourage you to do so! However, I suggest that you have the TSA hand check the camera. This is only a precaution; I have no evidence that the X-ray scanner will damage it. Carry it on the plane when you travel.    The only reason why I didn't give this camcorder 5 stars is because of the computer software. The supplied software is for PC based computers; there is no software for Macintosh. I have not yet been able to figure out how to put my movie and photo clips onto my Mac Book Pro. I would enjoy this product even more if I could work with my clips on Mac in either IMovie or IPhoto.     I hope this review gives you a good description of the physical camera and how it works. Overall, I'm extremely excited to have my camcorder back!

From the product specifications, I understood with this product that it was the audio adapter and a 3.5mm headphone jack, so no surprises with what I found in the envelope. Since I have multiple devices (apple and android) I'll use in my car, the headphone jack was the easiest choice. There is a USB port for charging but I didn't run an additional cable to expose it.

Installation was easy enough. Plenty of videos on the web to see how to install it (I found one that showed how to remove the cupholder and cover over the gearshift with out any special tools). I was able to place the GROM unit behind the radio head without having to secure it with tape or anything, things are pretty snug in the compartment. Some other posters commented that mounting brackets would be nice, but I'm not sure where it could mount easily in the limited space. I ran the audio cable behind the console and through the slot where the ashtray sits and slide the ashtray back on top. The ashtray is snug, but not quite as secure as before. I didn't want to drill if I didn't have to and this arrangement works out well. As an alternative, I laid out the cable that connects from the head unit to the grom adapter behind the radio and ashtray under the gear shift to front section of the cup holders. In that area is a component for the airbag but there looked to be plenty of space to try and mount it there with tape or something more rigid. Taking that route, you'd have to make an opening for the audio cord.

The sound quality is as good as what you hear from the device with headphones plugged in. Definitely better than the FM transmitter I bought years ago. You'll need to find the balance between device volume and car radio volume.

The only interesting behavior I've seen is when I switch the head unit to play the audio from the GROM device, it plays for a split second, then a split second of silence and then it continues playing. It is consistent with doingthat (turning on the car, turning on radio, changing audio source from cd to CD changer...) so I don't know if it's GROM or the head unit. Not a big deal.

Overall, with only a 30 minute installation this is a great option for Mazda owners looking to utilize their personal devices through the car's audio system!!

Nowadays, USB chargers come in all sorts of shapes, sizes, number of ports, and current capabilities. Some have external cords, and others (like this charger) plug directly into an outlet. If you're looking for a USB charger, you've got a lot of choices. :) Only you know the best set of specs for your needs, so I'll just try to describe what I think are the relevant qualities of this model.

First, it's very well made. Rock solid with no loose parts or rattles at all. The retractable plug snaps firmly into place in both the open and closed position, and it's not difficult to move. The USB ports are sized properly so that cables plug in with ease but are not wobbly or loose inside.

The whole unit has an Apple-ish look and feel to it. Well, old school Apple, that is. :) Back when they went with glossy white plastic versus the current aluminum look. I really like it. It reminds me of my older Airport Express unit.

Personally, I really like highly compact units like this because I think that they are great for travel. Assuming that wherever you are staying has a power outlet readily available, that is. Luckily, most hotels seems to have one or more power outlets exposed on top of a desk (such as the two on the base of a table lamp at the hotel that I stayed in last week). If you stay somewhere in which the outlets are further out of reach, you'd probably benefit from a different charger that comes with a power cord unless you get an extension cord for this.

Two outlets is perfect for me because I tend to take a phone and a tablet with me, and this can charge both with ease. Both ports can handle up to 2.4A, which is beyond what I need on any of my phones or tablets.

I have nothing bad at all to say about this charger - I think that it's a great product. If it meets your needs for number of ports, current capability, and outlet accessibility, I recommend it.ets your needs for number of ports, current capability, and outlet accessibility, I recommend it.

They sound good at low or high volume and do stress a little when pushed too hard, but so far everyone who has heard them in this setup has been amazed that they are only 8's.
I don't want to sound like a raver or a fanboy, there are still some issues. The extension is not as low as I would like and I think they should have more excursion than they do. After MUCH deliberation and research, I decided to purchase the Sony touch e-Reader. After using it for a month, I have these things to say, both positive and negative:

1. The screen does sometimes have a slight glare as other reviewers have commented, but it's not a big deal at all. Adjusting the angle at which you are holding it solves the problem. In direct/bright sunlight, there is no glare and it is at its clearest.

2. PDF files are not perfect, especially if they were not formatted to be read on a reader. For example, I uploaded a bus schedule, thinking it would be excellent to be able to carry it on my e-Reader, not to have to write it down or look it up or deal with paper (the reason I bought the e-Reader in the first place). The bus schedule had to be zoomed in to XXL and even then it was not easily readable. That said, I have made pdfs of articles I've wanted to read \\"on the go,\\" and it's been great.

3. The battery does not last 14 days. Maybe it's because I use it a lot, but I need to charge it every few days.

4. I love that I can put ePub books and pdf e-books on the reader. I love that I can buy books from the Sony store and from Borders and other sellers of e-Books. It's important to have a choice where to buy your books.

5. The number one reason I bought the Sony reader is that I can check out library e-books and read them. This is great.

6. ...that said, the library books sometimes mysteriously disappear (become content-protected and therefore unreadable) even before they have expired...I haven't quite figured out the pattern but it has something to do with having too many library books on there at one (shouldn't matter!) and uploading them at different times.

7. I love that it's touch screen. The touch screen is very responsive but not too responsive. It is more user friendly than some of the other readers I looked at/tried, even the other Sony e-Readers.

8. Even with the case I bought, it's thin enough to fit into my fairly small purse.

9. I love the built in, click on, dictionary, but it doesn't find \\"form\\" words. (It won't recognize a word with an -ing ending, generally speaking).

Alpine doesn't use any sketchy math loopholes, they just give you what they advertise.    Enough with the hyperbole.  When this box arrives at your house, what you get is a sleek looking amp with a small footprint that is power efficient and keeps on chugging.  I have this amp installed in the glove box behind the passenger seat in my 350z and after 2 hours of driving around listening to dubstep cranked up to 11, it's still less hot than some plates that have been handed to me at restaurants. I would recommend, as other reviews have, to leave the bass boost alone.  It's a pretty abrupt difference in volume with it adjusted any higher than 0.    I'm using this to drive to 10\\" Rockford Fosgate Punch subwoofers I found laying around, and for the price of this amp, I definitely got MUCH more than I bargained for.

This remote came with my Viper 4204V two-way remote start system that I had purchased and had installed at Best Buy on July 22, 2013. I must say the range for his remote is absolutely AMAZING. The signal works to about 2000 ft. and goes through walls and needs no direct line of site to work. The signal can even be used through a cell phone in case of emergency (see below) I think other reviewers here have laid out the functionality, bells and whistles very well, so I won't waste your time with what each button does.

I will say it uses two CR2016 lithium cells that last between 3-6 months of normal use. An optional leather case is available on Amazon for about $15. I HIGHLY recommend it as you do not want to drop this remote without protection, and the case provides just that.

BTW, If you were wondering, the \\"two-way\\" part of this remote's name simply refers to the remote's ability to receive an acknowledgment signal of any command you give. In other words, the remote notifies you, using its ghost LED lights and sounds, that your car did in fact start or did in fact lock. This is unlike a one-way remote that cannot tell you anything, like most garage door openers. Anyway, this remote communication is excellent.

I have a tip that may help you; ALWAYS leave your one-way remote at home or with someone you trust and hide an extra ignition key somewhere in the car. Now, if you ever get locked out of your car for any reason, simply call home or your trustworthy friend from a cell phone. Have them point the one-way remote into their phone while you simultaneously hold your cell phone to the windshield receiver, and presto.... they can unlock your doors, deactivate the alarm and even start your car right through the phone. You will then have access to your extra key, which can get you home. Just remember to treat them to a nice dinner for getting you out of a jam.
Hope this helps.

Overall, I am very happy with the power and features of the NT70T and will continue to use it as my primary battery back-up.

I've read on sparkfun's website that people have an issue with the case breaking as soon as they open it.  Here's the trick, the tabs on each side holding the top on need to be lifted just slightly. It would be nice if they labeled some of the different components a little better.  It should be pretty obvious what they are when reading the manual, but a little better separation and labeling wouldn't hurt.  Also, the manual doesn't fit inside the box because of a raised spot in the middle.  It would be nice if the raised portion could be lowered and a holder for the manual be placed on the inside of the lid. Nothing too serious, just some layout issues causing text to be cut off and some formatting of text that I think could have been better.  Overall I'm very please and can't wait to see what I can create with the Arduino.  Also, go over to sparkfun.com for all kinds of great parts and helpful reviews.  They also have a nice message board. Jameco.com is also a great website for tutorials and parts.
